news.title: Subramanyam: Alaska Ballot Stacking 'Part of the Process' of Ranked-Choice Voting, Wish My State Had Ranked-Choice
news.text:
On Thursday’s broadcast of “NewsNation Now,” Rep. Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA) said that because Alaska has ranked-choice voting, “if you recruited a third-party candidate who can take votes away from your opponent, that’s part of the process,” and he wishes his state had ranked-choice voting as well.

Subramanyam said that “Republicans pushed third-party candidates against [Mary Peltola], against me, against many other Democrats over the years.” And people on the right “tried to get the Green Party a higher profile to take away votes from Kamala Harris.”

Host Connell McShane then asked, “[I]f it was you, would you have done this, tried to find someone with your opponent’s name…what do you say?”

Subramanyam answered, “I wouldn’t, but I also don’t have a ranked-choice voting system in Virginia. I wish I did, honestly. But, in Alaska, they have ranked-choice voting, and third-party candidates are very relevant. And so, if you recruited a third-party candidate who can take votes away from your opponent, that’s part of the process, and that’s just how it works in Alaska.”

news.title: Georgia Early Voting Breaks Record Amid Obama, Trump and Harris' Final Push
news.text: In-person early voting has passed a recent record in Georgia with one day left, as 2,294,275 Georgians have voted as of Thursday afternoon, the Secretary of State said. In 2022, a total of 2,289,951 people had voted early in-person, the secretary's office said. Overall, this year's numbers, including absentee-by-mail ballots, are on pace with overall 2022 turnout. “Georgians continue to head to the polls in record numbers because they trust the system,” Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger said in a news release about the record on Thursday. “This record-breaking in-person early voting turnout wouldn’t be possible without our county elections officials who work every day to ensure our elections are free, fair, and fast.” The record comes as high-profile Democrats, including former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris, have stumped in the state to back Democratic candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms for governor and incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff. President Donald Trump also rallied in the Peach State over the weekend to support Republican gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson and U.S. Senate candidate Mike Collins. What To Know About Early Voting in Georgia The Secretary of State's office added that in addition to the number of early in-person votes, 108,251 absentee ballots have been accepted on Thursday as of 1:35 p.m. ET. As of a 4:35 p.m. ET update, the state has accepted 2,359,330 early in-person votes, according to the state's election data hub interactive chart. So far, Fulton County has the highest number of ballots accepted with 285,482. Cobb and DeKalb Counties had the second-highest number of ballots accepted. Robert Y. Shapiro, a professor of political science at Columbia University's School of International and Public Affairs, told Newsweek on Thursday when asked about the early voting numbers, "This is more welcome news for the Democrats than Republicans in that the statistical models that have been run show a big edge in this vote is for Democratic candidates." Shapiro continued: "This is evidently spurred by Democrats' greater enthusiasm to go out and vote against Trump's Republican party in holding the Republicans accountable for the poor performance of the Trump administration. This may be epitomized by the crowds and enthusiasm that former President Barack Obama has found and spurred on at the rallies he has been attending, as he has campaigned as well for the candidates for governor and the Senate there." Early voting in the state continues on Friday and Election Day voting locations are open from 7 a.m. until 7 p.m. on November 3. Trump, Obama and Harris' Final Midterm Push Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during them. Trump won Georgia, a swing state, during the 2024 presidential election versus Harris by roughly 2 percent. Former President Joe Biden won the state in 2020 versus Trump by less than one percent. Trump's overall approval rating and ranking on specific policy issues like the economy, immigration, jobs and the ongoing war in Iran have recently slipped as households across America are consistently flagging affordability concerns. The polling lows come as Trump has crisscrossed the country in the lead-up to November 3 to rally for potentially vulnerable GOP candidates, including previous stops in Georgia. Democrats are keen on flipping the governor's mansion in the state as outgoing Republican Brian Kemp is term-limited. Both Obama and Harris have visited the state to throw their support behind Ossoff as well, as polling shows him leading. On Wednesday, Obama rallied in Morrow, Georgia alongside Bottoms and Ossoff and took swipes at Trump on affordability and the ongoing war in Iran. “He is spending time supergluing gold medallions to the mantel in the Oval Office,” Obama said. “He is literally doing arts and crafts while we are fighting a war and trying to deal with out-of-control prices.” Over the weekend, Trump held a rally in Perry, Georgia, and called out Obama's crowd size at a previous rally he held in Michigan. “You know, I saw Barack Hussein Obama was in Michigan and the place was empty,” Trump said to the crowd. “And they were saying, ‘Oh, this is a large crowd coming, the people are trickling through’—they don't talk about my crowds, they never talk about them.” In a post to Truth Social before the rally, the president said: "I will be doing a BIG RALLY today in the Great State of Georgia, in honor of Mike Collins, one of the hardest working and most respected Congressmen in D.C., and the phenomenal Rick Jackson, who will hopefully be Georgia’s next Governor. They are two incredible people! Their opponents are Radical Left Lowlifes and Lunatics who want to Take Away Your Guns, Open Your Borders, Allow Men To Play In Women’s Sports, and have Transgender nonsense for everyone. I Won Georgia in a Record Vote. See you later!!!" Harris traveled to Macon on Thursday along with Ossoff, highlighting how soon the election is. "We have five days left. We have a moment now to turn pain into purpose," Harris said in part. What Polling, Prediction Markets Show 5 Days Ahead of Midterms A Quantus Insights poll this month shows Bottoms with 46.6 percent of the vote compared to Jackson's 48.2 percent. For the U.S. Senate race, Ossoff has 51.8 percent versus Collins' 44.9 percent. The poll was conducted from October 15–17, 2026, among 755 likely voters and had a 7.6 percent margin of error. A YouGov poll last month placed Jackson ahead with 45 percent compared to Bottoms' 44 percent. One percent said someone else, 1 percent said they would not vote and 9 percent were undecided. The poll also showed that Ossoff landed 51 percent to Collins' 41 percent, while 6 percent were undecided, 1 percent said someone else and 1 percent would not vote. The poll surveyed 3,447 Georgia registered voters from September 15-18, 2026, and had a margin of error of 2.7 percent. Prediction market site Kalshi shows that Ossoff is leading with over 95 percent on Thursday afternoon compared to Collins' 4.1 percent. For the governor's race, Bottoms has 61 percent on Kalshi compared to Jackson's 39 percent. On Polymarket, Bottoms has 62 percent compared to Jackson's 39 percent. Ossoff has 96 percent compared to Collins' 3 percent. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Early in-person voting has passed a recent record in Georgia, with one day still left.

Former Senator and West Virginia Governor Joe Manchin joins Sean Hannity for a candid conversation about Joe Biden’s decline, the Democratic Party’s radical shift, the future of the Senate, and the collapse of bipartisan politics.

In this wide-ranging episode of Hang Out with Sean Hannity, Manchin reveals what he saw while working with President Biden and says Biden was a “cognitive mess” during his debate with Donald Trump. news.title: Jesse Watters Claims AOC Has the 'Most Upside' to Becoming Next President — After the Democrat Accuses the Fox News Star of Sexual Harassment
news.text:
Jesse Watters made his thoughts about Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez known on The Five, RadarOnline.com can report.

During the Fox News show, Watters weighed in on a few potential Democratic presidential candidates, delivering his unfiltered takes on Kamala Harris, Gavin Newsom, and more.AOC Rejects Jesse Watters' Show InvitationWhen he got to Ocasio-Cortez, he brought up some comments she made about him outside the U.S. Capitol in January. At the time, Fox News producer Johnny Belisario invited her to appear on Jesse Watters Primetime, an offer she promptly rejected.

"He has sexualized and harassed me on his show," she said of the conservative commentator. "He has sexually harassed me on his show. He has engaged in horrific, sexually exploitative rhetoric."

"That’s not true, Congresswoman,” Belisario insisted.

As for Ocasio-Cortez's hypothetical presidential run, Watters claimed she'd have the most "upside" among 2028 Democratic candidates, even though they're not on good terms.Jesse Watters Claims AOC Has 'Potential'"AOC has the most upside," he explained on the show on October 26. "It was almost like she was seeing America for the first time and that’s good," Watters continued. "And that's what I kind of want to see from her."

"Her problem is people with money don’t want to give it to her because she hates business," he argued. "It would make her more comfortable with us and America," Watters clarified.

"She feels fine about you," Tarlov suggested.

"That's not what she said,” Watters asserted. "She accused me of sexual harassment."

"I don't wanna get between you two about that," Tarlov concluded.Jesse Watters' AOC JabsIn 2025, Watters claimed that Ocasio-Cortez wanted to "sleep with" Deputy White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller.

news.title: Trump Doesn’t Hate Black Women—If They Sing His Praises and Show Their Asses
news.text:
After spending the last month’s run-up to the midterm elections siccing the Department of Justice on his Black, female political opponents, President Donald Trump graciously allowed a Black woman to join his sycophantic entourage at a recent rally in Michigan: rapper Nicki Minaj. 

This wasn’t Minaj’s first public appearance in support of Trump; she accepted a White House invitation to speak at the United Nations last year. But it was the first rally where the president made a talking point out of her…anatomy.

“I looked at one hell of a beautiful ass before, Nicki Minaj,” said Trump, as the crowd hooted and hollered in approval. “That’s hard to miss.” 

He then licked his lips and told Minaj to stand. She did, smiling and waving to the crowd in a moment that I can only assume is making bell hooks turn in her grave like a rotisserie chicken. 

The entire interaction only fueled rumors that Minaj is slated to become the new White House press secretary after Katie Zacharia’s historically brief tenure, gossip that was directly referenced in a tweet by White House Communications Director Steven Cheung:

It’s hard to say whether the Trump administration is seriously considering Minaj for the position. But what’s clear is that Trump’s “admiration” of Minaj’s backside isn’t an isolated instance of sexism; it’s an example of white supremacy’s centuries-long legacy of fetishizing and exploiting Black women’s bodies.

Trump’s comments reminded many commenters of the treatment of Sarah (also known as Sara or Saartjie) Baartman, an enslaved woman born in the late 1700s, who was paraded around in European “freak shows” and circuses where people ogled her large derriere. Dubbed the Hottentot Venus, Baartman would wear next to nothing while she was locked in a cage, with a “trainer” ordering her to sit and stand “in a similar way that circus animals are ordered.” 

After her death at the age of 26, Georges Cuvier, a famed naturalist who believed Baartman was the link between humans and animals, reportedly made a cast of her body before her autopsy. He then pickled her brain and genitals in formaldehyde, which would go on to be displayed alongside Cuvier’s cast at the Paris Museum of Man until 1974, 159 years after she died.

The exploitation of Baartman is often cited as one of the most clear-cut examples of the fetishization of Black women’s bodies, encompassing the morbid curiosity, hypersexual stereotyping, and blatant dehumanization that Black women face to this day. This fetishization falls under the umbrella of misogynoir, a form of sexism that’s propelled by racism and specifically affects Black women and girls. And Trump perpetuates it constantly.

From calling ex-White House aide Omarosa “that dog” during his first term to describing then-vice presidential candidate Kamala Harris as “a mad woman” with so much “anger”, Trump loves leaning into negative stereotypes when tearing down Black women. But none more so than denouncing their intelligence. And the evidence of this is more than anecdotal. It’s backed up by data. 

In 2025, Mother Jones correspondent David Corn interviewed the director of a research group whose team found that Black women are overwhelmingly the demographic on the receiving end of Trump’s “low IQ” insults:

This team examined his Truth Social posts for the past four years, ending on April 10. In that stretch, Trump called individuals and communities “low IQ” at least 50 times, and 60 percent of these instances involved Black public figures and legislators. These targets included Vice President Kamala Harris; Reps. Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas), Maxine Waters (D-Calif.), Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.), and Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.); the Rev. Al Sharpton; New York Attorney General Letitia James; and political strategist Donna Brazile.

The tilt is clear. Trump reaches for this characterization more often when he’s denouncing Black people. Notice, though, that it’s not just Black people but Black women who draw much of Trump’s wrath.

Trump’s comments on Minaj’s body may seem on their face like run-of-the-mill sexism. But in the larger context of the president’s penchant for misogynoir, they paint an even more unsettling picture. And as we can see from the raid on Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home to the arrest of Sen. Louise Lucas, his animosity towards Black women leads to tangible consequences.

As Nicki Minaj, who has much more agency than the enslaved Baartman, willingly plays the helpful Jezebel for Trump and his goons, she is doing nothing but aiding and abetting an administration that’s proven over and over and over again that they despise women who look like her.

news.title: It’s Not Just ‘The Economy, Stupid’: Political Corruption Giving Inflation Run For Its Money As Top Voter Issue
news.text:
Corruption has become a top issue alongside affordability for many voters ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Polls show that corruption has joined affordability as the issues voters are most concerned with in the 2026 midterm election cycle as the latter issue is often linked to President Donald Trump’s war against Iran in voters’ minds. Trump, his family and administration officials have been accused of several corrupt actions, including accepting a plane from Qatar and pardoning a cryptocurrency exchange CEO tied to Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump’s business ventures. 

Sarah Chamberlain, the president of the Republican Main Street Partnership, told the Daily Caller News Foundation that corruption became the “number one issue” because of current economic conditions. 

“Usually, the polling is much better for the Republican than it has been,” Chamberlain told the DCNF. “I think it’s just across the board, people are tired of the corruption … If the economy were healthier, no one would pay attention to the corruption. But because they’re struggling, corruption is a bigger deal on their minds.”

A Fox News poll found government corruption to be the top issue, with 60% of registered voters being “extremely concerned,” while 58% expressed the same level of concern about inflation. Seventy-two percent of Democrats said they were “extremely concerned” about corruption and 47% of Republicans said the same. (RELATED: Top Trump Dinner Bidders Stash Cash On Exchanges That Shut Out Americans)

Thirty-six percent of voters said government corruption was their top concern in a CNBC poll from Friday, while 34% said grocery costs were their biggest concern. Nineteen percent of registered voters said corruption was their top issue in a CNN poll from Wednesday. 

A Financial Times survey found that 91% of Democratic voters and 72% of independent voters were “concerned about corruption, self-dealing or conflicts of interests” in the Trump administration. Another survey by Navigator Research, a Democratic-aligned polling organization, found that 81% of voters believe corruption in government is contributing to rising costs. 

Former U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned on Oct. 13 after the administration asked her to step down. Guilfoyle allegedly asked Trump donor Eric Deters to wire $100,000 to her American Express account in exchange for getting access to Trump. The wire transfer never occurred.

The State Department’s Office of Inspector General is investigating Guilfoyle after her alleged solicitation. 

Democrats vowed to investigate Trump and administration officials for corruption if they take back Congress in January, including Trump’s family and their finances. Trump made more than $1 billion off of cryptocurrency and promoted companies after buying their stock, according to a CNN investigation. He accepted a jet as a gift from Qatar to use as Air Force One, which is supposed to be transferred to his presidential library. The White House repeatedly denied any allegations of wrongdoing. 

Trump pardoned Changpeng Zhao, the former CEO of cryptocurrency exchange Binance, in October 2025. Zhao and Binance had established business ties with World Liberty Financial, a crypto venture that Trump launched with his sons, Don Jr. and Eric. Trump planned to host a dinner on Nov. 22 for the top 185 holders of $TRUMP meme coin after hosting a similar event at his Washington, D.C., area golf club in 2025.

Melissa Toufanian, Navigator’s managing director, said people would not be “so worried about all this corruption if I were doing better,” according to The Financial Times. 

“It’s when people are not doing so well financially and they see others benefiting to an obscene degree that the frustration begins to build,” Toufanian said. 

Voters remained dissatisfied with the economy throughout the election cycle, which commonly is a top issue for voters in elections. The issue prompted Democratic strategist James Carville to coin the famous phrase, “It’s the economy, stupid,” while advising former President Bill Clinton during the 1992 presidential election. 

Gas prices increased over $4 per gallon on average, while Diesel prices exceeded $6 per gallon since the Iran war began. The price of food also increased since the start of the war. 

Republican Utah Sen. John Curtis urged the Senate Judiciary Committee to subpoena Donald Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden as part of an investigation into the use of presidential family relationships for private financial benefit in a letter from Sept. 22. The committee has not appeared to address the letter or began any investigations. 

“[Corruption] is the number one issue right now, and it’s across the board. It’s not just Republicans,” Chamberlain said. “[Voters] are struggling to pay their bills, and they’re seeing the fraud that [Democratic Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz] was involved in. They’re seeing different types of fraud and they don’t like that because they don’t have the money to go out to dinner. So usually, fraud is not a big issue, but when you have an economy that is stretched, fraud is a big issue.” 

Chamberlain said the fraud in Minnesota and a Russian oligarch paying for Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding caused corruption to become a top issue. She stated that fraud could have a major impact in the Senate races, particularly Texas and Minnesota. 

Republican Minnesota Senate nominee Michele Tafoya trailed Democratic Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan by an average of five points in a state where former Vice President Kamala Harris won by a 51.1% to 46.9% margin, according to RealClearPolling. Tafoya centered her campaign around the fraud that took place statewide throughout Walz’s administration, in which Flanagan was apart of. 

“I think you could really see a surprise there in which [Tafoya] wins because of the corruption out there,” Chamberlain said. 

Fraudsters, most of whom were of Somali descent, allegedly stole hundreds of millions of Minnesotans’ taxpayer dollars from state programs since 2018, such as Feeding Our Future, which provided meals for low-income children during the COVID-19 pandemic. The Department of Justice (DOJ) charged 80 suspects with stealing around $250 million from Feeding Our Future.

Somali fraudsters allegedly stole over $90 million from Medicaid and child care programs throughout the state, including $46.6 million in autism fraud (EIDBI), $22 million in individualized home supports and $15.7 million in housing stabilization services, according to the DOJ.

“Billions were stolen under Peggy’s watch while she became a millionaire in public office,” Tafoya told the DCNF. “Minnesotans are tired of career politicians who let corruption run rampant while taxpayers are left holding the bill. I will be an equal opportunity pain in the ass for any corrupt politician.” 

Flanagan’s campaign did not respond to the DCNF’s request for comment. 

Corruption became a front-and-center issue in the Texas Senate race, where Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democratic Texas Senate nominee James Talarico face a competitive matchup. The Republican-controlled Texas state Legislature impeached Paxton in 2023 on bribery and abuse of power charges, although the state Senate acquitted him. 

Paxton was accused of misusing the office of the attorney general to protect and assist Austin real estate developer and political donor Nate Paul, who faced federal investigations. He allegedly intervened in lawsuits, issued favorable legal opinions to protect Paul’s properties from foreclosure and hired a special prosecutor to investigate claims helpful to Paul. 

Paul allegedly paid for expensive renovations to Paxton’s home and employed a woman with whom Paxton had an extramarital affair. Paxton denied all wrongdoing. 

During the Republican primary, Republican Texas Sen. John Cornyn and his allies referred to Paxton as “Crooked Ken” and called him “corrupt to the core” in one ad. Talarico and his allies released attack ads calling out Paxton’s alleged corruption. 

“Ken Paxton was impeached by his own party for taking bribes from wealthy donors while blocking overtime pay for Texas workers and gutting our health care,” one of Talarico’s ads said. “We cannot afford Ken Paxton’s corruption.”

An October University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll found voters trusted Talarico more on handling corruption than Paxton by ten percentage points. 

“Ken Paxton has taken on the federal bureaucrats and the corporations ripping off Texans, and he has beaten them,” Paxton spokeswoman Madison Cercy told the Post. “Democrats have spent years trying to destroy him, just like they tried with President Trump, and every attack has come up empty.”

One Republican said he was voting for Talarico over Paxton because of corruption. 

“It’s just confusing to me that people are willing to throw away their morals or what they would call their Republican morals, in order purely to support keeping a Republican majority in the Senate,” Sam Clark, a Dallas Republican, told The Washington Post. 

Paxton and Talarico’s campaign did not respond to the DCNF’s request for comment. 

Talarico said during a Fort Worth town hall that Paxton’s net worth shot up while he was in office and argued his legal entanglements should disqualify him from being senator. Paxton’s net worth rose from $174,000 when he first entered the state Legislature in 2003 to an estimated $13 million currently, according to Forbes. 

Corruption advertisements were the second most common topic for Democrats after the economy, according to a Washington Post review of more than 8,000 ads. Democrats spent about $306 million on ethics-focused ads in early October, while Republicans spent $187 million.

Former Democratic Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola’s campaign reportedly plotted to sabotage Republican Alaska Sen. Dan S. Sullivan’s reelection bid by recruiting a candidate with the same name, The New York Times reported Wednesday. 

Peltola’s team actively searched for other Dan Sullivans to be on the ballot in November to boost the Democrat’s chances of winning, a review by the Times found. An operative introduced by aides from the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) made secret trips to Alaskan communities while using a fake name and pitched his idea to would-be candidates over beers at brew pubs. 

Peltola’s campaign lawyers and senior aides at the DSCC participated in regular conversations about the effort and considered forming a new political party to draw conservatives to the ballot, according to the Times.
news.summary: ‘If the economy were healthier, no one would pay attention to the corruption’

news.title: Kamala Harris breaks with left flank, warns Dems that impeaching Trump is 'not a good idea'
news.text: Former Vice President Kamala Harris broke with some on the left flank of the Democratic Party on Wednesday over whether Democrats should pursue impeachment proceedings against President Donald Trump if they regain control of Congress in November. "The Parnas Perspective" host Aaron Parnas asked Harris what she would recommend Congress do if Democrats regain control following the midterm elections. "Would it be to go the investigations route and potentially an impeachment one day," he asked, "or would it be go past policy and force the president to veto it?" JAMES CARVILLE WARNS DEMS AGAINST IMPEACHING TRUMP IF THEY WIN CONTROL IN MIDTERMS "I think that going on in the direction of impeachment is not a good idea. OK, just to be honest with you. Because we have limited resources and I think the energy and the resources need to be put into accountability, need to be put into investigations and that's where the time should be spent. Remember I was in the Senate for the last go-round and the votes aren't there, right? So that's how I feel," Harris said. She argued Democrats need to focus on getting things done and that they should be "ruthless." HOUSE DEMS PLOT TRUMP INVESTIGATION BLITZ IF THEY SEIZE MAJORITY "When I say we should be ruthless, I don't mean cruel, but we should be uncompromising and not sit around, you know, being genteel about the relationships and instead actually get stuff done, whether it be about accountability or restoring, for example, what they took in terms of the Medicaid cuts, restoring what we need to do around some check and balance around this war nobody wants," the former VP said. Some Democrats in Congress have pushed again to impeach Trump, who was impeached twice during his first term in office but acquitted in the Senate on both occasions. Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, forced a vote on a resolution to impeach Trump over his administration's immigration enforcement policies, including the deaths of people during federal immigration operations earlier this year. The move divided House Democrats, whose leaders have largely avoided emphasizing impeachment as they work to regain control of Congress in the November midterms. Florida Democratic Senate candidate and state Rep. Angie Nixon said in an interview with Politico that she would not oppose impeachment hearings and would vote to remove Trump if elected. "The Daily Show" host Jon Stewart expressed a similar sentiment during a question-and-answer segment at the end of his "The Weekly Show" podcast. He was asked whether Democrats should seek to impeach Trump if they regain control of Congress in the midterm elections. REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: DEMOCRATS FACE AN IMPEACHMENT TRACTOR BEAM THAT COULD DERAIL THEIR AFFORDABILITY MESSAGE He said he wanted Democrats to make a full-scale effort to rebalance the economy rather than hold performative hearings. "I don't want to see a f---ing five-act performative play of House hearings," Stewart said. "I just don't want to see it. I don't want to see everybody having the opportunity to pantomime accountability because you know they're actually not going to bring it." "There will be enormous pressure to seek accountability if Democrats win control in either or both chambers next week, but the push to make things better for the American people may be even more intense. If successful, Democrats would be wise to try to strike some balance and to work on parallel tracks to deliver results. Voters want justice and accountability, but they want affordable gas and groceries more," Costas Panagopoulos, a professor of political science at Northeastern University, told Fox News Digital of Harris' remarks. Republican strategist Liz Mair, head of Mair strategies, said Harris was "right," in a statement to Fox News Digital. She added, "Democrats will win these midterms not because swing voters who deliver those victories want them to spend the next two years impeaching the president, but because they want them to focus on bringing costs down or at least limiting ongoing price hikes." DEM MAKING SENATE COMEBACK BID SAYS HE WOULDN'T SUPPORT A TRUMP IMPEACHMENT PUSH "Every second Democrats spend trying to impeach President Trump again is a minute they're not spending addressing affordability challenges, and appeasing their base at the expense of doing what they will literally have been elected to accomplish," Mair said. Harris has endorsed several big institutional changes, such as Supreme Court expansion, possibly getting rid of the Electoral College, and Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico statehood. news.title: Eminem Called 'Spineless' Over MAGA Star Kid Rock Collaboration As Song Misses Billboard Hot 100
news.text: Eminem has faced 'spineless' criticism over his collaboration with MAGA supporter Kid Rock, while their song 'Heal My Faith' missed the Billboard Hot 100 in its debut chart appearance. news.title: Trump's Latest Attempt To Salvage the Midterms: Bribe and Extort the Voters
news.text:
The midterm elections are just days away, and while anything can happen, the broad consensus among pollsters suggests a bad night for Republicans.

Hoping to shore up a victory for his party, President Donald Trump seized upon an idea: bribe the voters.

"If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate, both of them," Trump pledged in September, "I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000."

According to Vice President J.D. Vance, this "dividend"—which would cost more than $1.3 trillion—would come from the "extraordinary amount of revenue" generated by Trump's tariffs. Of course, that math doesn't work: According to the Penn Wharton Budget Model, the U.S. took in just under $300 billion in tariff revenue between January 2025 and July 2026, not counting the amount it has had to refund after the Supreme Court found they were illegally imposed.

At that rate, it would take years of tariffs just to pay for Trump's dividend. Adding insult to injury, of course, is the fact that tariffs are paid by Americans, meaning we would be taxing ourselves to pay for our own disbursement.

But in the campaign season's closing days, Trump has made a number of other threats and offers, contingent on his party's success—a completely risible use of government power.

In September, three Ohio Republicans—Rep. Mike Turner and Sens. Bernie Moreno and Jon Husted—petitioned the president to build a planned Space Force training academy in their state.

"Every other state wants it," Trump said this month at an Ohio campaign rally. "If we win the midterms, Ohio will be very, very strongly considered."

Some of his pledges have been much more explicitly transactional.

On October 17, the Department of Defense—which Trump calls by its original name, the Department of War—announced a conditional $80 billion loan to pharmaceutical manufacturer Antheia. That same day, at a campaign rally in Kentucky, Trump made a pledge to the state's voters.

"If the Republicans win, the Department of War will be investing $100 million in the pharmaceutical company Antheia to revitalize a gigantic drug manufacturing facility in Winchester, Kentucky," he said. But he prefaced it by telling Rep. Andy Barr, the Republican running for the state's open Senate seat, "you have to win, Andy. Otherwise, forget it."

Days later in both Kansas and Iowa, Trump brought up E15, a gasoline blend that contains up to 15 percent ethanol derived from corn. It has advantages and disadvantages as an alternative to traditional gasoline, but it's a boon for corn-growing states.

"Normally, E15 is not allowed during the summer because warmer temperatures increase fuel evaporation and thus the formulation of ground ozone ('smog')," writes Benjamin Zycher of the American Enterprise Institute.

The government can waive that restriction to address disruptions in the fuel supply, which it did in March amid gas price shocks related to Trump's war in Iran. The House passed a bill in May to make the waiver permanent and allow E15 to be sold year-round, which Trump backed in June; the Senate version of the Farm Bill includes a year-round E15 amendment, but Democrats have held up its passage.

"With Roger Marshall in the Senate," Trump told Kansans last week, "we will make year-round E15 permanent. But if [Democratic candidate] Adam Hamilton is in, I'm not doing it."

He then made the same pledge in Iowa, where Rep. Ashley Hinson is the Republican Senate nominee. "With Ashley in the Senate, we will make it year-round E15," Trump said. "We'll make it permanent."

Of course, it's nothing new for politicians to make big promises in exchange for your votes. Typically, they're all hollow to at least some degree.

And Trump's pledges do reflect some version of reality: Keeping the Senate in Republican hands will make it easier for him to do certain things. But some of his others have been downright indefensible, less like typical political bribery than outright extortion.

At a rally in North Carolina last month, he tied hurricane disaster aid from the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) to Senate candidate Michael Whatley's election.

"We spent more than $2 billion [in] FEMA funding," he told attendees. "You're waiting for some additional money…and I'm gonna get that to you, Michael. Now if Michael loses, I'm not sending it." He added right after, "I'm only kidding, you're gonna get it."

Other times, he didn't take it back: Trump appeared at a campaign rally in Georgia this week, stumping for Rep. Mike Collins to unseat Sen. Jon Ossoff, and part of his sales pitch was that if Ossoff wins, he may just ignore the state.

"President has a lot of power," he said, and there's "a big difference when he likes the people representing a state. Collins could call me anytime he wants." But if Ossoff wins, he added, he won't take the call, and he even narrated a hypothetical conversation to make his point: "'Tell him I'm not in.' 'But he needs money for Georgia.' 'I don't give a damn what he wants!'"

Also this week, Trump railed about the Senate race in Alaska, where Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan faces not only former Rep. Mary Peltola but a retired teacher also named Dan Sullivan. The New York Times reported this week that the Peltola campaign actively recruited the second Sullivan to run explicitly as a spoiler, to siphon votes away from the senator.

"I have delivered for Alaska at Historic Levels," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "The Democrats are trying to steal this important Republican Seat and, if that happens, everything we've done for Alaska will come to an immediate hault [sic]."

It's one thing to say the federal government shouldn't provide aid to states—and since taking office, the administration has cut or paused such disbursements by $177 billion. Last week, the FEMA administrator indicated that going forward, states should expect to shoulder more of their own disaster aid.

But this goes much further, with the president explicitly conditioning aid on whether or not the state's voters have displeased him.

Perhaps, as in North Carolina, Trump was simply joking; the White House did not respond to Reason's request for clarification.

But there's certainly precedent to suggest he was serious.

"Last September, the Department of Energy (DOE) recommended cancellation of 624 grants for clean energy projects that had been approved by the Biden administration," Reason's Jacob Sullum wrote in July. The government then "winnowed it down to 284 grants, all but one of which had been awarded to projects in states that were represented by Democrats in the U.S. Senate and had voted for Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election."

In March, Politico reported that Trump had approved 89 percent of disaster aid requests from states with a Republican governor and two Republican senators but only 23 percent of requests from states with Democrats in those offices.

According to the Idle Rambling Substack, the trend continues: Trump has rejected nearly half of aid requests from Democrat-led states in this term while only rejecting 18 percent from Republican-led states.

But perhaps worst of all, he threatened not to pay out damages to people who suffered harm.

Between 1953 and 1987, the water at Camp Lejeune in North Carolina was contaminated by leaks of fuel and dry cleaning chemicals. The government estimates that as many as 1 million people, both service members and their families, were exposed to toxic chemicals. The Department of Veterans Affairs officially recognizes eight diseases stemming from exposure, including multiple cancers and Parkinson's disease.

In 2022, Congress passed the Camp Lejeune Justice Act, which waived any federal government claims of immunity and allowed veterans to sue over exposure to tainted water. As of September 2026, the Department of Justice says it has paid out more than $879 million, out of more than $1.1 billion in settlement offers.

"We're also fighting for our great veterans, and taking care of those veterans who brought claims related to water contamination at Camp Lejeune," Trump told North Carolina rallygoers last week. "And if we win the House and the Senate, I am directing the Department of Justice to settle all remaining legitimate claims as soon as possible." But "if we don't win, there's no money. If we do win, you're getting it."

It should be clear by now that Trump values personal loyalty over all else. To that end, there is nothing he finds more disreputable than failing to do what he says.

In the closing days of this campaign season, he is making that more explicit than ever, tying his party's success in a state to whether the state is entitled to equal treatment under the law.

Trump was right that presidents have "a lot of power." He's also a living example of why they shouldn't.
news.summary: As the election approaches, it is more clear than ever that the president values loyalty over all else.
news.author: Joe Lancaster

news.title: Everyone's predicting a Blue Wave... but I'm the pollster politicians hire for the MOST accurate data - and my private survey reveals a totally different outcome: BRENT BUCHANAN
news.text:
In the closing days of the 2026 midterms, I am not mincing words with my Republican clients. Put simply, angry voters tend to punish whoever is in charge – and right now that negative sentiment falls on the shoulders of the party in control of the White House and Congress.

Voters who believe that the country is on the wrong track plan to vote for the Democratic party by 61 points, according to Cygnal polling. Back in 2024, when President Donald Trump roared to victory in an electoral landslide over Vice President Kamala Harris, those voters backed Republicans by 45 points.

Another warning sign: Independents, who make up about a fifth of all midterm voters, lean Democratic by 14 points in our survey this week. That is half the 28-point gap we found in early October, but it is still more than triple the amount that Independents leaned Democratic in 2024.

A third problem is widespread public concern about the cost of living. Voters earning less than $50,000 per year have moved 22 points toward Democrats since 2024. Democrats also now hold a 12-point edge (48 percent to 36 percent) on the question: Which party do you trust more to handle the cost of living?

Thirty-one percent of voters who call inflation and the economy their top priority back Democrats by 28 points.

Even voters without a college degree, a critical part of the Republican coalition of the past two decades, have shifted 14 points toward Democrats. Non-white voters without a degree drove most of that shift, moving 28 points toward Democrats, while white men without college degrees moved seven points.

This is a difficult political landscape for anyone with an 'R' next to their name to navigate, but whether this election becomes a rout of historic proportions or preserves Republican control of the Senate is still to be determined.

As the founder and CEO of the top private polling firm in the US, as recognized by The New York Times and statistician Nate Silver for the accuracy of our 5,000 polls conducted across all 50 states, I am advising my clients to focus on four key groups of discouraged and persuadable voters who will make the difference.

Soft Republicans

On the campaign trail, President Trump has told his supporters to pretend that he is on the ballot, but to some voters that makes little difference.

The President may not like to hear that, but Republican candidates should.

'Soft Republicans' are the 55 percent of Republicans who say they see themselves more as traditional conservatives than Trump Republicans. They make up 21 percent of all voters – and represent a 'soft spot' in the GOP base.

Only 43 percent of them view Trump 'very favorably,' compared with 80 percent of Trump Republicans. Just 21 percent say they are voting to express support for Trump. Instead, nearly six in 10 say they are voting based on Republican principles.

But here's the rub: 86 percent of them still plan to vote Republican in congressional races.

They might have cooled on Trump, but most haven't completely abandoned the party. Traditional conservatives favor Republican candidates by 76 points, down from 86 points in early October, while Trump Republicans are at 96 points.

You can see these dynamics unfolding in the races that will decide control of the Senate.

In Texas, Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico appear to be in a dead heat. A late-September Fox News poll had Talarico ahead 51 percent to 49 percent among likely voters and found that 22 percent of Republicans who don't consider themselves MAGA, back Talarico.

In these final days, highlighting Talarico's prior support for far-left social positions, like opposition to banning transgender athletes from girls' sports and a belief in 'six genders' may make the difference. 

Double Haters

Sixteen percent of voters tell us that they dislike both parties in Congress.

These 'Double Haters' tend to be higher-income, well-educated men.

While all voters making over $100,000 per year are almost evenly split (as they were in 2024), these 'Double Haters' lean toward the Democrats by 37 points, up from 29 points in early October.

They say they value candidates who will act as a check on the President, but they aren't completely lost to the GOP, either. A quarter of them are voting Republican and another 13 percent are undecided.

The key for Republican candidates is to appeal to the third of 'Double Haters,' who indicate that they may turn out for the GOP, if their candidate demonstrates some independence from Trump.

In Maine, Republican Senator Susan Collins is an ideal candidate to test this theory.

She was only one of seven GOP senators who voted to convict Trump during his second impeachment trial in 2021 on charges of inciting an insurrection at the US Capitol.

Collins is currently locked in a tough fight against Democrat Troy Jackson. If she can demonstrate her autonomy to 'Double Haters,' she may win.

Undecided and Unmotivated

Next are the true undecided voters, (mostly made up of men under age 55 and black voters) who are 5 percent of the electorate and tell us they do not know how they will vote for Congress.

Nearly half of them (48 percent) are independents. Seventy-two percent say the country is on the wrong track and they view Trump unfavorably by 41 points, even though 34 percent of them backed Trump in 2024.

And they are also not just unsure of their choice; they're checked out of the political process.

Only 42 percent are extremely motivated to vote, compared to 70 percent of all voters who say the same.

Men under 55 are the clearest swing group in the electorate. They favored Republicans by eight points in 2024 and favor Democrats by 11 points today. But only 63 percent of them say they are extremely motivated to vote, compared with 77 percent of voters 55 and older.

As for black voters, Trump's coalition moved some of these Americans toward the GOP previously. Today, their support for Republicans has fallen from 28 percent in 2024 to 14 percent and the Democrats' advantage has grown by 26 points to 68 points.

Their motivation is improving, with 64 percent now extremely motivated, up from 52 percent in early October. In that early October survey, only 33 percent of black voters said they believe their vote makes a difference.

These voters may be under-motivated, but they are not unpersuadable.

In Minnesota, Republican Michele Tafoya has sought to link her Democratic opponent, Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan, to an unfolding scandal in the state, in which individuals with ties to the Somali community allegedly obtained billions of dollars in public benefits fraudulently.

A recent Star Tribune/KARE 11 poll showed Tafoya leading among independents, 38 percent to 32 percent, with 29 percent of them still undecided. Those are the voters who may be outraged at the misappropriation of tax dollars.

Fatalist Republicans

Finally, you may have heard quite a bit about Democrats having an enthusiasm edge, and they do, with 80 percent of party loyalists saying they're extremely motivated to vote compared to only 67 percent for Republicans.

But when you count voters who are 'extremely motivated' or 'very motivated,' the gap shrinks to six points (92 percent to 86 percent).

The group that GOP candidates must specifically target are 'Fatalist Republicans.'

These are voters who are voting for the Republican candidate, or considering it, but who expect Democrats to win control of Congress. They make up about nine percent of all voters.

What sets them apart is expectation, not preference. Fewer than half (48 percent) are extremely motivated to turn out, compared with 70 percent of Republican voters who expect their party to win. In early October, only 31 percent of them said they think their vote actually matters in this election.

They are not a fringe. Fourteen percent of all voters backing Republican candidates expect Democrats to win. Fatalists skew male (63 percent, against 46 percent of all voters) and younger, with only 19 percent aged 65 or older, compared with 30 percent of all voters. Most are Republicans (55 percent) or independents (35 percent), and 69 percent voted for Trump in 2024.

This is a group that doesn't need persuading. Its members need convincing to show up.

The bottom line is that Democrats currently have a strong upper hand because voters are frustrated with the party in power, and anger and frustration are powerful motivators.

Our latest national survey has Democrats ahead on the congressional ballot, 51 percent to 43 percent and the 28 percent of voters who have already cast ballots favor them by 28 points.

But with just days left in the midterms, Republicans can still narrow the gap. Voters who plan to vote in person on Election Day favor Republicans by 15 points, so GOP candidates need to keep finding ways to win over persuadable voters and give their supporters a reason to go to the polls.

Brent Buchanan is the Founder and CEO of Cygnal, a national polling and analytics firm, and author of America's Emotional Divide.
news.summary: I'm the founder and CEO of the top private polling firm in the US, as recognized by The New York Times for the accuracy of our 5,000 polls conducted across all 50 states.
news.author: Brent Buchanan,Editor

news.title: Facing racist attacks, South Asians in Texas back Democrats, says survey
news.text: Washington, Oct 29 (PTI): At the receiving end of racist attacks, South Asian voters are backing Democratic candidates in Texas, including James Talarico for the US Senate – a key seat to wrest the upper house from Republicans. More than 60 per cent of voters surveyed by the South Asian American Voter Empowerment of Texas Education Fund (SAAVETX EF) and the University of California San Diego said they would back Talarico for the US Senate over Republican Ken Paxton, and Gina Hinojosa for Governor over incumbent Greg Abbott. Among registered voters, 66 per cent preferred Talarico, while 21 per cent preferred Paxton. In the gubernatorial race, 63 per cent preferred Gina Hinojosa, while 27 per cent preferred Abbott. As many as 58 per cent respondents reported at least one experience of hate, including online harassment, threats of violence, and damage to places of worship in Texas during the past year because of their race, ethnicity, religion, nationality, accent, or immigration background. Sixty-four per cent respondents said they frequently or sometimes heard South Asians or immigrants described as “invaders” or “outsiders” in the past two years. Separately, when asked about their 2024 presidential vote, 65 per cent reported voting for Kamala Harris and 25 per cent for Donald Trump. South Asians account for 19 lakh of Texas’ 60 lakh population and Indian-Americans number 5.5 lakh, the second-largest presence after California. The rising numbers of Indian-Americans in Texas have made them a target of racist attacks from MAGA supporters of President Trump, which also became a campaign issue for the upcoming midterm elections. Last month, Bo French, the Republican candidate for the Texas Railroad Commissioner’s post, triggered a political row when he described, in a social media post, South Asian students celebrating a Texas football game as a “problem”. The remarks were condemned by outgoing Texas Senator John Cornyn, who was defeated in the Senate primary elections by Paxton, a Trump-backed candidate. “Our community is tired of being treated as outsiders and used as political pawns. When elected officials and candidates fuel hostility, people feel less safe and less confident in the institutions meant to protect them,” Chanda Parbhoo, founder and executive director of SAAVETX EF, said in a statement. A 90-foot statue of Lord Hanuman in Texas was in the spotlight of a political debate last month when a conservative YouTuber called for “tearing this down”, drawing a sharp backlash from Hindu groups and thinkers alike. The Statue of the Union, installed at the Asthalaxmi Temple in Sugarland, Texas, has been at the centre of a controversy since its consecration in August 2024, with a section of Christian conservatives describing it as a “demon God”, “unChristian”, a “false god” and a “character from the Planet of Apes”. “The survey reveals a community confronting exclusion, but also highly civically engaged,” Tom K. Wong, founding director of the US Immigration Policy Center at UC San Diego. According to the survey, 64 per cent of respondents said their community’s concerns were not well understood or not understood at all by elected officials, and 54 per cent believe their community holds little to no political power. The survey found that 78 per cent respondents would be much or somewhat more likely to vote for a candidate who speaks out against discrimination toward South Asians. news.title: Texan voters once believed Trump's 'lies' but they're now ready to vote Democrat
news.text:
As he prepared to leave his home in Houston, Lorenzo Salgado Sr had just over an hour to live.

The construction worker started July 7 the same way he had for the last 30 years. He woke up, grabbed his lunch and a coffee and left the house before 6am to put in another hard day's work.

On the way, he was followed by unmarked vehicles. By 7am, he was fatally shot.

He's the second person to be killed by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents in Texas this year.

Salgado Sr was an undocumented Houston construction worker who had lived in the US for 30 years, his sons say being arrested by ICE was his biggest fear.

Instead they killed him.

CCTV shows an unmarked vehicle pursuing Lorenzo's van, but there is no footage of the actual shooting. The agent who shot him through the passenger side window was not wearing a body camera.

Authorities claimed that Lorenzo drove towards an ICE agent.

"That doesn't sound like our dad," Lorenzo Jr says.

"Our dad had a great respect for the law. 

Ronaldo Salgado thinks his dad thought he was being robbed.

"I imagine him being scared of someone trying to steal his van, his tools, that morning, and I am fairly confident that some of his last thoughts were about us, because he cared a lot about us.

"He cared a lot about his wife, our mum, and I know he worried about him leaving us alone."

Four months on Lorenzo Jr wants America's Latino population to do just one thing to remember his father: vote.

"Voting is voluntary, so at least in some of the lower income neighbourhoods that are accustomed to not being heard, they feel that their votes don't matter," he tells 7.30.

"I think voter turnout is going to make the difference."

At the 2024 US presidential election America's Latino community was split between Donald Trump and Kamala Harris.

But at the midterms polls suggest Latinos will heavily favour the Democratic Party, largely because of a backlash against widespread immigration arrests and the deaths of at least nine people by ICE operations since Donald Trump was elected to a second term in the White House.

Living in fear

The arrests and killings have up-ended America's Latino communities. 

In Texas alone, more than 100,000 people have been detained by ICE agents in the past two years. Many of those arrested have been deported.

In south Texas, the prospect of being targeted by ICE has left many in the Latino community frightened.

At the sprawling Mercadome Flea Market in Alamo, near the Mexico border, customers are staying away.

ICE has arrested people in the car park of the market, says Rosa Martinez, who sells shoes and clothing.

"It's very slow.The sales have gone down, I think maybe 70 per cent," Ms Martinez tells 7.30. 

And nobody seems immune from immigration arrests — even Sister Letty Ugboaja, a nun from Nigeria who was arrested on her way to the Our Lady of Sorrows church in McAllen, Texas.

After a flurry of phone calls, Sister Letty was eventually released. Most of those detained are not so fortunate.

Parents have been arrested after dropping their children at school.

The church now asks parents to fill in a form allowing someone else to collect their children, just in case they are arrested after drop-off before eventually being deported.

"We don't call them illegal, we call them undocumented," says Father Jorge Gomez, the rector of the Basilica of Our Lady of San Juan del Valle.

"Mothers are afraid that the husband is not going to come back home after his job because there's a lot of raids, taking people, deporting people, mostly men, when they get out of work, a restaurant or a construction site or a store.

"We have a lot of mothers left behind with two or three kids that are in need, because the breadwinner has been deported or is in the process of being deported."

The evaporation of a workforce

As well as exacting a human toll, the arrests have had a significant impact on the construction industry in south Texas.

Local builder Mario Guerrero has lost much of his workforce. A construction project in Phar, Texas, is taking years longer than it should.

"We should have been done in year one because it doesn't take much to build these apartments," Mr Guerrero says.

"It's taking long to build because we don't have the proper labour force right now."

His skilled workforce, hired through sub-contractors, has evaporated.

He says ICE detains everyone on a job site, legal or not, and releases them only when they can prove they're in America legally.

Mr Guerrero voted for Trump two years ago — partly, because he vowed to stop the wave of refugees and migrants coming across the southern border but he says the wave of arrests will drive people to vote for the Democrats.

"Biden was a failure," Mr Guerrero says.

"He opened our borders. Nobody wanted that. Nobody wants open borders. So when Trump was like, 'we're gonna stop that. We're gonna close that. We're gonna send them all back.' Of course we want them to go back, but we never thought that he was gonna terrorise people that were here already working and, and providing a better living for their families."

'Make Quinceaneras great again'

Now the blue wave appears to be surging.

Three Texas Congressional districts may fall to the Democrats, including some that were gerrymandered to favour Republican candidates.

In the Fifteenth Congressional District, the party is pinning its hopes on a former teen idol, Tejano singer Bobby Pulido.

Early in the campaign, Pulido was mocked by his Republican rival as not worthy of being a congressman because he was merely "a quinceanera act". Quinceaneras are coming of age celebrations for 15-year-old girls.

Mr Pulido embraced the jibe and performs at quinceaneras most weekends as part of his campaign.

"That's when he said, "Well, let's make quinceaneras great again'," says Sandra Riviera, wearing a hat with the same slogan. 

Mr Pulido estimates he's since performed at 80 quinceaneras.

At a recent Saturday night rally in south Texas, he had a plea for his supporters.

"This election is so important for everybody to get out and vote," he tells them.

"Everybody comes up to me, 'Yeah, you got this in the bag'. No, we don't. We do not have this in the bag.

'Real change' putting an end to 'lies'

The rise of Mr Pulido and the south Texas Democrats is music to the ears of Julio Garcia, a committed Democratic supporter who has spent much of the past two years engaged in a peaceful, albeit noisy, protest against Mr Trump.

He rides high through local streets in his truck decorated with anti-Trump signs and has had an air-horn retrofitted to the vehicle so he can respond loudly whenever someone gives him a wave or a honk.

"There's a lot of Latinos who voted for Trump," Mr Garcia says.

He says that is no longer the case, judging by how often he's sounding his horn as the election gets closer.

"They are frightened of ICE, because ICE has done such terrible things," he says.

"ICE has gone up … to people's homes and workplaces, and they've taken innocent people."

Father Gomez is careful not to criticise Mr Trump or his policies but he is unhappy with the way the laws are being enforced, which he says has been "inhuman".

"Some people are being killed when they're [immigration enforcement] just trying to go and get them. Some of them haven't been running." 

Back in Houston, the Salgado brothers regularly visit a roadside memorial for their father.

They've been buoyed by the public reaction: every day there are are more flowers or tributes to their dad, left at where he was shot and killed.

"I hope that we've done enough to encourage enough people to vote, at least here in our communities," says Ronaldo Salgado.

news.summary: In south Texas, the aggressive enforcement of immigration laws has hollowed out restaurants, building sites and even churches — and the backlash is threatening to turn the traditional red state blue.
news.author: Adam Harvey

Welcome to At the Races! Each week we bring you news and analysis from the Roll Call campaign team. Know someone who’d like to get this newsletter? They can subscribe here.

By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari

White House officials and congressional leaders are on the final press to get out their voters ahead of Election Day. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, in particular, seem to be focusing mostly on securing the Republican and MAGA base.

And that’s leading to stops in traditionally red parts of the map, including a presidential visit Thursday to South Carolina, where a new New York Times/Siena poll found a dead heat between appointed GOP Sen. Darline Graham and Democratic nominee Annie Andrews. 

Republican Rep. Nancy Mace, who is leaving Congress after an unsuccessful gubernatorial bid, said she’s seen polls with Graham and Andrews each ahead. “South Carolina is notorious for not wanting to be told what to do, politically or otherwise,” Mace told CNN on Wednesday, adding that voters feel “boondogled” that Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, was not just a placeholder.

The president, who campaigned in reliably red Mississippi and Texas earlier this week, has upcoming stops in Florida and Iowa already scheduled ahead of Tuesday, though a planned visit to Kansas has reportedly been scrapped. He’s also doing tele-rallies, including a reported election eve event for Rep. Julia Letlow, the Republican Senate nominee in Louisiana.

Those are all states that the president carried by double digits in 2024.

Vance is expected to swing into a House race Monday, in an upstate New York district that could be a harbinger of the size and scale of a potential blue wave. As the (Albany) Times Union reported, Vance’s visit is to support sticker company CEO Anthony Constantino, who’s running to succeed retiring Rep. Elise Stefanik in a district Trump carried by 21 points two years ago. Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales rates the race Lean Republican.

House leaders will be busy, as well. Speaker Mike Johnson told Fox News he’d be in five states on Thursday alone.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries heads to Virginia on Saturday to support former Rep. Elaine Luria’s comeback bid against GOP Rep. Jen Kiggans. Jeffries, who is poised to become the first Black speaker if Democrats flip the House, will be in Alabama on Sunday, Punchbowl News reported, stumping with Rep. Shomari Figures. The freshman lawmaker saw his once near-majority Black district become more Republican under Alabama’s new map. Inside Elections rates the race Lean Republican.

Starting gate

Most vulnerable: We revisited our rankings of the most vulnerable incumbents for the final time this cycle, and things have changed dramatically since the spring of last year. On the Senate side, Georgia’s Jon Ossoff fell from the top spot to the bottom of the list, while red-state incumbents, including Roger Marshall of Kansas, Darline Graham of South Carolina and Cindy Hyde-Smith of Mississippi, have made unexpected debuts. Redistricting continues to influence the House list, with members in redrawn seats claiming most of the top positions, while swing seat Republicans round out the remaining spots. 

California ballots: A California federal judge ruled against the Trump administration’s effort to have set aside 20,000 ballots from alleged noncitizen voters in the state, our colleague Michael Macagnone reports. The Justice Department’s lead attorney on the case had previously indicated that the administration would appeal if the judge ruled against them. 

Going big in Texas: Will the Lone Star State go blue next week? That was among several questions journalism students from the University of Southern California sought to answer on a recent reporting trip to South Texas, where they interviewed more than 200 people across 1,100 miles at multiple early voting sites and candidate events. 

Two weeks in October: Democrats running for Senate kept up their massive fundraising in the first two weeks of October, according to pre-general election reports filed with the Federal Election Commission last week. For example, Texas hopeful James Talarico’s campaign reported raising $17.6 million in 14 days — far more than any Republican Senate candidate took in during the previous three-month quarter. 

Hoping for a “blue tsunami:” On paper, North Carolina’s 3rd District shouldn’t be all that competitive. But the Republican-led redraw of the state’s congressional map turned the district a shade bluer, bolstering Democratic hopes of defeating GOP Rep. Greg Murphy.

Roll Call on the road: CQ Roll Call photojournalist Tom Williams recently traveled to the Republican-leaning battlegrounds in Ohio and Kentucky, where he caught up with GOP Sen. Jon Husted, Democratic House hopeful Kristina Knickerbocker and Republican House nominee Ralph Alvarado, among a host of others. Come for the candidates and stay for the photo of the soaring bald eagle.

Stacking the ballot: Trump called for the criminal prosecution of Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola following a report in The New York Times that detailed her Senate campaign’s role in recruiting a potential spoiler candidate with the same name as Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. Trump also told reporters the former congresswoman should withdraw from the race. Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski said Alaskans “deserve the honest truth from Mary and her campaign,” while GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavey has ordered an inquiry into the scheme to decide whether any criminal charges or civil action is warranted. House Oversight Chair James R. Comer is also launching an investigation into the allegations. Peltola’s campaign said in a statement that it “has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign” and that the Democrat was staying in the race. 

Maryland’s map: Former President Barack Obama is urging Maryland voters to support a ballot initiative that would allow the Democrat-led state to redraw its congressional map ahead of the 2028 elections. 

More Alaska: Three former Alaska governors — Democrat Tony Knowles, Republican Frank H. Murkowski and independent Bill Walker — endorsed Democratic gubernatorial candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins in an op-ed for the Alaska Daily News. Murkowski’s daughter and Senate successor, Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski, is also backing the Democrat. Kreiss-Tomkins faces three Republicans in next week’s election, which will be decided by ranked choice voting if no one takes more than 50 percent of the vote. 

GOTV: The DCCC is spending more than $1 million on a get-out-the-vote ad campaign across dozens of House districts aimed at Black, Latino and Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander voters. 

House divided: Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens endorsed Abdul El-Sayed after losing a divisive Senate primary this summer, but her fiancé told the Detroit News that he would vote for Republican Mike Rogers next week. Jason Turkish, who is Jewish, said he saw an “escalation in [El-Sayed’s] rhetoric since the primary” that has made Jewish people feel unsafe. Stevens, though, confirmed on CNN that she would vote for her former opponent, though she called on him to “denounce the hateful ads that have hurt people,” including a campaign spot featuring Tucker Carlson.

What we’re reading

Sports to politics pipeline: Front Office Sports dove into the FEC filings of House hopefuls Jay Feely of Arizona and Mark Teixeira of Texas and Minnesota Senate nominee Michele Tafoya and found several notable sports figures among their campaign donors. Feely’s filings, in particular, showed strong support from the football world, including donations from two current NFL head coaches (John Harbaugh of the New York Giants and Kevin O’Connell of the Minnesota Vikings) and the owners of nine NFL teams. 

Small dollar, big dollar: Republicans outside groups have enjoyed a cash advantage over their Democratic counterparts this year, but a Politico analysis finds that the GOP’s small-dollar fundraising efforts have shrunk compared with the 2022 cycle.

Democratic DNA: Democrats are optimistic about winning a number of red-leaning districts in South Texas, Kentucky and Iowa. But such flips would be less a signal of a blue wave than a reversion back to the Democratic leanings of those seats before the Trump era, The Cook Political Report asserts. 

Musk connection: Republican Chris Gober, a onetime top lawyer for Elon Musk’s America PAC, is running for an open House seat in Texas. But Gober hasn’t exactly touted his connection to Musk or his PAC, CNBC reports.

Grading the maps: The New York Times analyzed the congressional maps of every state with more than one House district and found Texas and California to be the most gerrymandered, while the lines in Massachusetts, where Democrats hold all nine seats, were judged to be “quite fair,” with the newspaper noting that computer simulations to “draw compact districts without any consideration of partisanship or race” failed to yield GOP-leaning seats in the Bay State.

The count: 35.8 million

That’s how many early ballots had been cast by the end of Wednesday, according to calculations by voter data firm L2.

At the same point in 2022, 20.6 million people had voted early, while just 13 million had done so by the Wednesday before the pre-pandemic midterm election of 2018. 

Hispanic voters, who were key to Republican gains in the 2024 elections, make up 11 percent of early voters so far, with 3.9 million casting ballots. That’s an increase from 1.5 million at the same point in 2022 and 1.1 million in 2018. 

– By Roll Call’s Ryan Kelly

Key race: #PA01

Candidates: Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, a perennial Democratic target who held on to his Philadelphia-area seat in the 2018 “blue wave,” faces a challenge from Bucks County Commissioner Bob Harvie. 

Why it matters: Fitzpatrick, one of a handful of House Republicans who represent districts Kamala Harris carried in 2024, is considered a survivor of tough election cycles. But Democrats see Harvie as their best chance yet to oust the five-term incumbent.

Cash dash: Fitzpatrick has been relying on his campaign war chest all year, having raised $8 million through Oct. 14, with $709,000 on hand for the election’s final stretch. Harvie reported raising $3.2 million through mid-October and had $409,000 available. The pro-Democratic House Majority PAC has been the top outside spender, dropping $5.6 million through Oct. 26, while its GOP counterpart, the Congressional Leadership Fund, spent $3.3 million. The pro-Fitzpatrick Defending America PAC spent another $1.4 million. 

Backers: Fitzpatrick touts support from several labor groups and also won endorsements from the NRDC Action Fund and the League of Conservation Voters Action Fund, environmental groups that typically back Democrats. Former Democratic-turned-independent Sen. Joe Manchin III of West Virginia is also backing Fitzpatrick. Harvie has endorsements from End Citizens United, the New Democrat Coalition Action Fund and the political arm of Planned Parenthood, as well as from Pennsylvania Reps. Madeleine Dean, Mary Gay Scanlon and Chris DeLuzio. 

What they’re saying: A New York Times/Philadelphia Inquirer/Siena University poll released last weekend found a margin-of-error race with Harvie at 48 percent and Fitzpatrick at 46 percent. An internal Harvie campaign poll from early October showed a tied race. Fitzpatrick has emphasized his bipartisan record — he told Punchbowl News earlier this year that he would become an independent if Pennsylvania switched to open primaries. Harvie, meanwhile, has sought to tie Fitzpatrick to Trump, arguing that voting for the incumbent is a “vote to keep Republicans in charge of everything.” 

Terrain: The district sits just north of Philadelphia and includes all of Bucks County. Harris carried the seat by less than half a point two years ago, while Fitzpatrick won reelection by 13 points. Inside Elections rates the race Lean Republican. 

Wild card: Fitzpatrick is the most recent member to succeed a brother in Congress. Former Rep. Michael G. Fitzpatrick represented the area for eight years over two nonconsecutive terms before retiring in 2016. He died of cancer in 2020.

Early in-person voting is coming to an end as soon as Thursday in several states, including Maine, where Republican Sen. Susan Collins is seeking a record sixth term. The Voting Rights Lab tracks end dates in every state that allows early voting.

news.title: Young men have soured on Trump and the GOP. But will they vote on Tuesday?
news.text:
In 2024, unhappy with the high cost of living under the Biden administration, Steven Fitzgerald cast his ballot for Donald Trump. Now, the Generation Z real estate investor from western Maryland says he regrets it.

“The focus of the administration ... was supposed to be on making the economy better, houses more affordable,” says Mr. Fitzgerald, who also works as a compliance code inspector. “I don’t feel like he’s doing the job that I gave him to do with my vote.”

Economically squeezed and concerned about yet another protracted war abroad, voters of all backgrounds and ages are telling pollsters they’re unhappy with President Trump’s policies. But no group seems to be experiencing greater buyer’s remorse than young voters – particularly young men.

Mr. Trump won 55% of male voters between the ages of 18 and 29 two years ago, fueling his return to the White House and stunning Democrats, who historically have won younger voters. Now, multiple surveys suggest many of those same young men are moving away from the GOP.

Only 49% of young people who cast ballots for Mr. Trump in the last election approve of his performance today, according to a recent poll from the Pew Research Center. A survey of Gen Z men earlier this fall found that, among those most likely to vote, Democrats held a 17-point lead.

“Young men voted for Trump [in 2024] because they thought he would be better for their short-term and longer-term economic prospects,” says John Della Volpe, director of polling at the Harvard Kennedy School’s Institute of Politics. “Some of those young people will continue voting for Trump-aligned candidates and Republicans. But clearly not as many. Others may switch to Democrats, and others will stay home.”

Young people in general tend to vote at lower rates, but there are some indications their participation in this election could be lower than usual. A Harvard Institute of Politics poll released last week found only about one-third of Republicans ages 18-29 say they’ll definitely vote in the midterms, compared with 46% who had planned to vote before the 2022 midterm elections.

During the 2024 campaign, Mr. Trump made a concerted effort to reach young voters, for example by appearing on podcasts with popular figures like Joe Rogan and comedian Theo Von. Stylistically, he appealed to many younger men with his off-the-cuff approach.

“He says what he thinks, he says what’s on his mind,” says Charlie Sabgir, director of the Young Men Research Project in Washington.

On the trail, Mr. Trump promised to end “forever wars,” lower the cost of living, and boost energy independence, all in the name of “America First.” It was a message that strongly appealed to Gen Z men like Mr. Fitzgerald.

“Imagine what the country would look like if we spent $300 billion on the American people, the middle and lower classes, as opposed to sending [it] overseas,” he says. “I see people struggling every day.”

Hunter Hardy, a Gen Z electrician from New Lexington, Ohio, also regrets casting his vote for Mr. Trump in 2024. “He’s not keeping his promises,” says Mr. Hardy, who says that in his view the president turned out to be no different from any other politician. As a result, he’s grown “tired” of politics, he says. No matter how he votes, it seems like “the government does what it wants.”

In 2024, the Gen Z men who voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris were also generally more supportive of foreign intervention, according to exit polls. By contrast, younger men who voted for Mr. Trump often wanted a more isolationist foreign policy, Mr. Sabgir notes. For those voters, the war with Iran has felt like a sharp betrayal. Many also support ending aid to Israel, an issue that unites the younger generation on the left and the right.

Faltering support among young men could portend a rocky 2028 presidential run by Vice President JD Vance, Mr. Trump’s current heir apparent. Another poll released this fall found that a majority of young men have an unfavorable view of Mr. Trump, the Republican Party, and Mr. Vance.

During the 2024 campaign, Mr. Trump leaned into certain online conspiracies – calling for the release of the Epstein files and government documents around UFOs, for example. On those fronts, too, he wound up disappointing supporters with his actions in office. The Trump administration has released millions of pages of documents on Jeffrey Epstein, the convicted sex offender who died in prison, but critics have complained about heavy redactions and say that not everything has been released.

Some national Democrats say their party has an opening to win back younger men not only in this election, but in 2028 as well – if they don’t squander it.

“I think they’re going to take a chance on us this time around, but we need to actually do something with that power they’re giving us,” Democratic Sen. Ruben Gallego of Arizona says in an interview, after appearing on a panel earlier this month in Washington about issues facing young men.

That means Democrats need to deliver on legislation to raise wages and make it easier to buy homes, Senator Gallego says. “If we don’t have good policies, we could go on Theo Von, we could go on Joe Rogan, we could go on all these things, and they still won’t support us because then they feel like, ‘What am I getting?’” he says.
news.summary: Trump won a majority of young male voters two years ago, fueling his return to the White House. Now, many of those same young men are saying they will vote for Democrats or stay home.
news.author: Sophie Hills

The message from Corinth was loud and clear: Mississippi stands with President Trump, and we're not finished yet. Let's carry that same energy to the ballot box on November third.
