news.text: ATLANTA — Days before key US midterm elections that will decide the balance of power in Congress, Democrats are leaning on former president Barack Obama to energize voters and help propel the party to victory.'Yes we can,' the crowd chanted at a rally in Atlanta on Wednesday, reviving the slogan from Obama's historic 2008 White House run.'These are serious times,' he said, berating political leaders who 'enjoy insulting and dividing instead of bringing people together to solve problems.'The first Black US president headlined three rallies this week for Democratic candidates in next Tuesday's elections, with voters picking lawmakers who will serve for the remainder of President Donald Trump's term.Democratic control of Congress would place the Republican leader in a legislative straitjacket for his final two years in office.Trump has embarked on a blitz of campaign rallies across the country, including in traditionally Republican states where his party is facing competitive races.Obama was in Atlanta to support Senator Jon Ossoff. Running for reelection in Georgia and widely considered a 2028 presidential contender, the lawmaker with rolled-up shirt sleeves and a youthful vibe has drawn comparisons to the 65-year-old former president.'He has that energy nobody else has,' Jennifer Lee, a 21-year-old student at the rally, said of Obama.'He makes you feel something, and that's exactly what Democrats need right now. Get people fired up, get them to the polls.'Luc Brearley, a 32-year-old teacher, was more reserved about the Obama effect.'He can probably help with turnout in some places, like Atlanta or Philly. But in swing districts, I don't think one speech changes anybody's mind,' he told AFP.'People are voting on prices and their own lives.'Blue waveRepublicans fear a Democratic 'blue wave' on election day, with voters angry over inflation stoked by oil prices that have soared since Trump launched his war on Iran in February.Obama rallied voters earlier this week in Ohio, a normally Republican state which this time features heated governor and Senate races.Hours later, he took the stage in Michigan alongside Abdul El-Sayed, a candidate with a rising profile who Democrats hope can help the party retain a US Senate seat.In Obama, 'Democrats have found their true spokesperson for the midterms,' said Barbara Perry, an expert on US presidents at the University of Virginia.She described his 'ability to rouse the crowd' and 'sense of humor, which he's turned on Trump.''He's a young, energetic former president' who is still 'very loved and trusted, certainly among Democrats, but even more broadly,' Julian Zelizer, professor of history and public affairs at Princeton University, told AFP.'And so that becomes someone who's very valuable.'Campaign cultureAs Democrats search for a leader to stand in the 2028 presidential polls, Obama can easily serve as a temporary placeholder, Zelizer added.Obama's recent advocacy is a departure from his discretion in the first year of Trump's second term.'That is changing, and Trump, of course, has completely changed our civic culture and our campaign culture,' Perry said.In 2024, Obama backed Kamala Harris in the final stretch of the presidential election, which Trump ultimately won.When Obama opened his presidential center in Chicago in June, all living US ex-presidents joined a star-studded lineup -- with the notable absence of Trump.

news.title: Familiar faces and a trip back in time: 5 takeaways from the N.H. Senate debate
news.text:
They are both from storied New Hampshire families (one best known for governing, the other for its famous Manchester restaurant). They are both veterans of Washington. They are both kind of policy nerds.

On Wednesday night, Rep. Chris Pappas, a Democrat, and former Sen. John E. Sununu, a Republican, clashed in a tense debate at the WMUR television studio in Manchester, fighting over Social Security and the cause of the high cost of living, and seeking to yoke each other to unpopular figures in their respective parties.

Pappas and Sununu are running for a seat held by the retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, a Democrat. Both parties view the race as crucial to their hopes of retaking the chamber. Pappas, who leads in polling, seized opportunities to attack Sununu and present him as beholden to President Donald Trump — perhaps reflecting a degree of discomfort that Sununu has been able to keep the race competitive by presenting himself as independent of the unpopular president.

Here are five takeaways from the night.

 Neither candidate is new to voters. 

Sometimes, a political candidate bursts onto the scene out of nowhere. That is not the story of New Hampshire in 2026.

The Senate race pits Pappas, an understated, four-term Democrat who has spent much of his adult life in elected office, against Sununu, a former member of Congress and one-term senator who won this same seat in 2002 before losing it in 2008. Sununu is the son and brother of former New Hampshire governors. Pappas’ family is best known for its popular restaurant, the Puritan Backroom in Manchester.

Pappas, 46, sought to present himself as a “new generation of leadership.” Sununu, 62, insisted he could shake things up in Washington after being first elected to Congress 30 years ago.

And each nevertheless accused the other of representing the status quo.

“Chris Pappas talked about all the things he wants to do and wants to accomplish, but he’s been there for eight years, and he hasn’t gotten the job done,” Sununu said.

“This election is about Team New Hampshire versus Team Trump,” Pappas said. “Fact is, John Sununu was our senator before and, if he was as effective and as independent as he says he was, then he’d probably still be our senator today. But voters had another idea.”

 Both bragged about challenging their own party … 

Sununu’s candidacy depends on his ability to convince voters in New Hampshire — a state that has never really warmed to Trump — that he is independent of a president who endorsed him early in the race.

So he rattled of a list of his differences with the president: the trade war with Canada, the war in Iran, the $1.8 billion fund Trump proposed for victims of “weaponization” by the Department of Justice and his now-scuttled plan to televise a military execution.

“When Donald Trump leaves office in two years,” Sununu asked, “where does the country go?”

What was more surprising, perhaps, was how frequently Pappas made a point of spelling out his differences with national Democrats including former President Joe Biden.

“I called out Joe Biden when he was president because he let things get out of control on the southern border, and it created a crisis,” Pappas said. “And I’ve taken on my own party on immigration, and I’ve gotten a lot of flak for it.”

 … and working with the other side. 

It’s an era of deeply tribal politics, but things are split in New Hampshire. Republicans have total control over state government, while Democrats hold each seat in the federal delegation.

That might be why, in a somewhat retro twist, both candidates were eager to talk about how frequently they reach across the aisle.

Pappas talked about his support for one bipartisan measure after another: a ban on stock trading by members of Congress, a measure that would provide heating assistance to low-income people, immigration measures and more.

Sununu said that he had worked with Democrats plenty, and he praised Sen. Susan Collins of Maine — another Republican who likes to talk up bipartisanship — as a “model.”

“I even wrote bipartisan legislation with Hillary Clinton to improve auto safety and protect kids,” he said.

 Sununu climbed in his Wayback Machine. 

Clinton wasn’t the only reference Sununu made that seemed, well, dated.

He talked about demanding changes to the Patriot Act during the presidency of George W. Bush. He said he was the first Republican to call for the firing of Alberto Gonzales, Bush’s attorney general.

He grew visibly annoyed as he parsed an attack by Pappas over legislation privatizing Social Security during his term in the Senate.

“That wasn’t my bill, Chris,” Sununu said. “OK, you can’t ascribe every crazy bill ever introduced in Congress to me. That’s dishonest.”

He also chafed when Pappas said his net worth had grown to an “estimated” $35 million after he left the Senate.

“Goodness knows, I’m not worth $35 million,” he said, before accusing Pappas of being unable to read a financial disclosure form, the federally required filings that publish broad ranges for public officials’ assets. “Now, I blame that on the time he spent at Harvard.” (Sununu attended MIT.)

 Pappas demurred on impeachment. 

Some Democrats are hungry for candidates who want to punish Trump for what they see as the excesses of his second term — but that’s not the audience Pappas was playing to.

Asked about the prospect of impeaching Trump if the Democrats gained a majority in Congress, Pappas called instead for “focused hearings” and “oversight.”

“We need to stay focused on how we can solve problems, make lives better for Granite Staters and lower costs,” Pappas said.

Sununu nevertheless accused him of being too liberal for New Hampshire. He said Pappas voted too often with former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and knocked him for campaigning alongside former Vice President Kamala Harris and California Gov. Gavin Newsom.

“I don’t know what Chris’ infatuation is with California, but it’s not New Hampshire, and it’s not a good model for our state,” Sununu said.

Pappas reminded him that Harris won New Hampshire in 2024, and that Trump had not.

“Here in New Hampshire,” he said, “we welcome out-of-town guests.”

This article originally appeared in The New York Times.
news.summary:
Sometimes, a political candidate bursts onto the scene out of nowhere. That is not the story of New Hampshire in 2026.

news.title: Eminem’s Collab With MAGA Music Star Flops Hard
news.text:
Eminem’s new song with MAGA rocker Kid Rock is his least successful collaboration to date.

The Grammy-winning rapper stunned fans when he confirmed Halfway to Jesus. Kid Rock, a close buddy of Donald Trump known for his allegiance to the president’s MAGA cause, told fans to announce the song, “His verse speaks to something we’ve talked about, and that really needs to be heard: we differ politically and on other things, but we’ve stayed friends through it all.” 

According to music charts, the message hasn’t reached many people.

“Heal My Faith,” released Oct. 17, did not make Spotify’s U.S. Top 50 and fell out of the iTunes Top 100 just a few days after its release. It appeared only once on a Billboard chart, reports Consequence of Sound—namely, Hot Christian Songs, where it only reached No. 38.

Kid Rock’s Halfway 2 Jesus album debuted at No. 10 on the Top Christian Album Chart. 

The disastrous performance follows Eminem’s social media promotion of the song, with a message to peeved fans. 

“Not about choosing sides, just choosing to make music with my old friend. Praying for all of us,” the rapper wrote in the post. When Kid Rock announced the new song as a jam session between two old friends, fans were incensed, pointing to the “line in the sand” the rapper drew between himself and Trump supporters in 2017.

“Any fan of mine who’s a supporter of his, I’m drawing in the sand a line—you either for or against,” he rapped at the BET Awards back then, adding, “We love our country, but we f---in’ hate Trump!” 

Years later, the star campaigned for Kamala Harris in 2024 and introduced Barack Obama to Detroit rallygoers. 

His longtime friend Kid Rock was busy campaigning for Trump’s side, performing live at the Republican National Convention and speaking and performing at several Trump-backed campaign events. He’s also been Trump’s go-to musician and drunken phone-call buddy since Trump’s re-election. 

Eminem and Kid Rock’s relationship predates Trump’s rise, and they teamed up previously on Kid Rock’s 1998 album for the song “F--- Off,” and Kid Rock also appeared in Eminem’s 2013 video “Berzerk.”

Kid Rock said in an Instagram video in 2024, “Let me tell you, I love Eminem; we’ve been friends for many years,” he said then. “I don’t agree with his politics, but I do give credit to him…for standing up and not being afraid to be vocal for that which they believe.”

Despite their history, Eminem’s fans ripped him for the latest collaboration, calling it “spineless.” One wrote, “I will never take Eminem seriously again when he talks about politics,” wrote yet another X user. “What a f---ing disappointment.”

news.title: JD Vance, GOP Leaders Join Final Paxton Push as Talarico Rallies in Dallas
news.text: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton is set to get a boost from Vice President JD Vance in his Senate bid, as national Republican leaders make a final push to retain the seat. The race between Paxton and Democratic nominee James Talarico has become unusually close. Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso stumped for Paxton across West Texas on Wednesday, a day after Trump made his third visit to the state this month. "He's not the guy for you. He doesn't represent your values, and we can't take a chance," Trump said. Talarico has led most public polls since Paxton ousted Senator John Cornyn in the May runoff, and the seat could decide which party controls the Senate for the last two years of Trump's term. The prospect of losing control of the Senate has prompted Trump and the GOP to shore up Republican strongholds where Democrats are running closer than expected. Trump has rallied in Mississippi, Michigan, Georgia, Florida, Iowa and Ohio over the past week. He is scheduled to visit South Carolina on Thursday, Florida on Friday, Kansas on Saturday and Iowa again on Sunday. Newsweek reached out to the Paxton campaign for comment Thursday. What to Know About Vance’s Weatherford Stop Vance is scheduled to speak at 1:50 p.m. local time at JRJ Construction in Weatherford, west of Fort Worth, according to the Texas Republican Party. It is his third Texas rally in about a month, following stops in Harlingen and Tyler, as Republicans seek to boost turnout in heavily Republican Parker County. The Texas trip comes two days after Vance rallied in Howell, Michigan, where he said the Senate race between Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed highlights a “clash of competing visions” between the parties. Why Top Republicans Are Rallying in Texas Republicans rarely need to defend a Senate seat in Texas, as Democrats have not won a statewide race since 1994. This year, however, the party has deployed some of its biggest names to the state. Trump held events for Paxton in Corpus Christi and Lubbock on Tuesday, his fourth visit to Texas since Labor Day. Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso joined Paxton on the campaign trail in West Texas on Wednesday, making stops in San Angelo and Abilene. The money tells a similar story. Republican-aligned PACs backed by Trump, Senate Republican leaders and Elon Musk have committed more than $214 million to advertising supporting Paxton and attacking Talarico, according to figures from media-tracking firm AdImpact. Talarico, meanwhile, has raised $146.3 million in total campaign receipts, compared with Paxton's $22.3 million, according to Federal Election Commission filings through October 14. The GOP's closing strategy leans on the party's numerical edge. Paxton's tour has focused on rural areas and solid Trump country, and he has told supporters the math is on his side. "We can win this because we have more Republicans. We just have to vote," Paxton said in Victoria last week. He called the tight race "shocking." What Polls Are Saying Four surveys released this week show Talarico ahead, with leads ranging from 2 to 8 percentage points, depending on the pollster. A CNN/SSRS poll of 923 likely voters, conducted October 20 to 27, found Talarico at 49 percent and Paxton at 43 percent. Another 5 percent said they would back neither candidate, and 3 percent picked someone else. A YouGov Blue poll commissioned by 254 Labs gave Talarico his largest lead of the week. The survey of 1,000 registered voters, weighted to reflect likely voters and conducted October 21 to 26, showed him ahead by 51 percent to 43 percent, with 5 percent undecided. The Barbara Jordan Public Policy Research and Survey Center at Texas Southern University, working with YouGov, found a tighter race. Its poll of 2,000 likely voters, conducted October 21 to 25, showed Talarico at 49 percent and Paxton at 47 percent. Libertarian Ted Brown drew 3 percent, a share that could matter in a contest this close. An N+ Univision/YouGov survey of 1,000 registered voters, conducted October 13 to 21 and released Tuesday, put Talarico ahead 50 percent to 45 percent. Paxton trailed in all four surveys, with the Texas Southern University poll showing the narrowest margin, at 2 percentage points. Will Texas Finally Turn Blue? Democrats have not won a Senate race in the state since Lloyd Bentsen's victory in 1988, while Beto O'Rourke's 2018 run against Senator Ted Cruz ended 2.6 points shy. Turnout this fall has broken midterm records. Nearly 5 million Texans had voted by Tuesday, about 26 percent of a record 19 million registered voters, according to state data reported by KERA. At the same point, turnout was roughly 21 percent in 2022 and 24 percent in 2018. Harris County set a midterm record on the first day of early voting. Analysts caution against reading too much into those figures. Texas voters do not register by party, and Republicans have historically been more likely to wait until Election Day to cast ballots, Brendan Steinhauser, a Republican strategist in Texas, told Newsweek. Mark Jones of Rice University's Baker Institute, who co-authored the Hobby School survey, told Houston Public Media that Talarico's numbers amount to the strongest late-campaign showing he has seen from a Texas Democrat in decades. There are warning signs for Democrats, too. A CBS News/YouGov poll conducted October 8 to 16 suggested Talarico was receiving slightly less support among Black voters than Kamala Harris did in the 2024 presidential election. Why the Texas Midterm Matters Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority, so Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control. Their likeliest targets, North Carolina and Maine, would only get them to 49, leaving them to compete in states Trump won by double digits, including Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas. Texas has become a key target for Democrats and a firewall for Republicans as a result. A Paxton loss would end the GOP's three-decade winning streak in statewide races and could help Democrats secure control of the Senate for the rest of Trump's presidency. The stakes are also symbolic. Texas Republicans have long cast their state as the heart of the conservative movement, and a Paxton win would deal a blow to Democrats' hopes that the state's growing cities and suburbs will eventually shift it their way. Early voting ends Friday, October 30. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Rhian Morgan.
news.summary: Vance and other top Republicans are making a final push for Ken Paxton as James Talarico leads new Texas Senate polls.

news.title: Google Blames 'Technical Gap' for AI Refusing to Say Who Won 2020 Election
news.text: Google said a “technology gap” was responsible for its AI Mode telling users that Donald Trump won the 2016 and 2024 presidential elections, while saying that users should check the official Federal Election Commission (FEC) results to find out who won the 2020 contest. On Wednesday, X users drew attention to the issue, which appears to have been fixed. The discrepancy was particularly controversial in the context of President Trump’s repeated claim that the 2020 election was rigged against him, though this has been repeatedly rejected in court. Newsweek contacted Google for comment on Thursday by email outside regular office hours. Google AI Discrepancy Daniel Pearson, an editorial writer for The Philadelphia Inquirer, on Wednesday posted screenshots on X of Google’s AI mode being asked “who won the 2016 us presidential election” and “who won the 2020 us presidential election.” For the former, Google AI replied: “Donald Trump won the 2016 United States presidential election, defeating Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton,” citing election website 270 To Win. However when asked about the 2020 contest it responded: “To verify the winner and specific results of the 2020 United States presidential election, including electoral college and popular vote counts, you can consult the Official 2020 Presidential General Election Results published by the Federal Election Commission (FEC).” Pearson wrote: “Is Google Gemini trying to win a republican primary?” Writer and podcaster Charles C. Mann also shared screenshots on Wednesday of him asking Google AI “who won the 2020 US presidential election” and “who won the 2024 US presidential election.” For the former, Google AI said: “For official U.S. presidential election results and data certified by the Federal Election Commission (FEC), please consult the official voter portals and certified documents.” By contrast, for the 2024 contest, it replied: “Donald Trump won the 2024 US presidential election to become the 47th president of the United States,” citing CNN as its source. On X, Mann added: “I had real trouble believing that Google was actually doing this, but I just duplicated the result myself. The two queries were about a minute apart and identical except for a single digit.” San Francisco-based writer Zeke Hausfather also raised the issue, writing: “Google has specifically prevented its AI tool from telling users who won the 2020 presidential election, even though it happily tells us that Trump won in 2016 and 2024. This sort of political intervention into LLM [large language model] responses is deeply problematic. (h/t to Charles Mann).” Google’s Response The official "News from Google" X account responded to Hausfather and other X users raising concerns, saying: “We’re fixing the issue with 2020 election queries in AI Mode; the Gemini app answers the question more fully. Our systems verify election responses using news articles or AP data for recent elections, and historic records for older ones. “There was a technical gap with 2020 - same is true for 2022 Senate races, which we’re also working to fix.” Current State As of 11:30 a.m. ET on Thursday, Google AI gave equivalent answers when asked “who won the 2024 presidential election” and “who won the 2020 presidential election” by Newsweek from the United States. For the former, it said: “Donald Trump won the 2024 United States presidential election. He defeated the Democratic nominee, Vice President Kamala Harris, to become the 47th President of the United States,” citing CNN as its source. Similarly, when asked about the 2020 election it replied: “Joe Biden won the 2020 United States presidential election. The Democratic ticket of former Vice President Joe Biden and Senator Kamala Harris defeated the incumbent Republican President Donald Trump and Vice President Mike Pence.” 2020 Election Rigging Claims Trump has refused to accept the result of the 2020 presidential election, repeatedly alleging that the contest was rigged against him, blaming Democrats, election officials and even that suggesting federal agencies could be involved. In a statement published on November 5, 2020, Trump said: “If you count the legal votes, I easily win. If you count the illegal votes, they can try to steal the election from us.” On January 6, 2021, hundreds of Trump supporters rioted at the U.S. Capitol, following a "Stop the Steal" rally addressed by the Trump, in a failed bid to prevent the presidential election result being certified. During the ensuing violence, one Trump supporter was shot dead and more than 100 police officers assaulted, according to the Justice Department. Trump’s team launched a series of legal challenges arguing that the 2020 election result was compromised but failed repeatedly in court. They were also dismissed by neutral and even Republican legal experts. Trump Administration and Google Since Trump’s return to the White House in January 2025, Google has gone along with the president’s renaming plans for U.S.-based users. That month, Google followed Trump’s direction to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America on Google Maps when viewed from the U.S. This summer, it adopted the same policy when Trump renamed Lake Ontario to Lake America amid ongoing trade tensions with the Canadian government. Google said the decision was in response to the U.S. government’s Geographic Names Information System (GNIS) formally changing the name. In October, Trump told supporters at a South Carolina rally that he had spoken to Google CEO Sundar Pichai about potentially renaming the Atlantic Ocean but would “probably pass” after he replied: “Please don’t ask us to do that.” Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Rebecca Flood and Dave Siminoff.
news.summary: On Wednesday, social media users posted screenshots of Google AI saying Trump won in 2024 but not Biden in 2020.

news.title: Disappointed by Trump, dubious of Talarico: This Rio Grande Valley health official mulls his midterm vote
news.text:
Subscribe to The Y’all — a weekly dispatch about the people, places and policies defining Texas, produced by Texas Tribune journalists living in communities across the state.

McALLEN — Dr. Ivan Melendez was among the 110,000 voters in Hidalgo County who voted for Donald Trump in 2024 in a historic swing that amounted to the first time the predominantly Hispanic county has gone for a Republican presidential nominee in more than 50 years. 

In the Rio Grande Valley, Melendez serves as the county’s health authority, responsible for enacting health laws in an area with one of the highest uninsured rates in the country.

Naturally, healthcare is a top issue for the top medical official for the region. He cast that vote in large part because he viewed Trump as a major force in expediting the COVID-19 vaccine in early 2020. And after already enduring four years with Trump in the White House, Melendez thought he knew what he was getting with the tempestuous leader.

Today, he regrets that vote.

Melendez says he’s been completely disappointed by Trump because of cuts to federal programs that have gutted health departments in the Valley and made insurance coverage harder to obtain.

“It’s a simple question. When it comes to access to healthcare, am I able to do more now than I was before he became president?” Melendez said. “And the answer is no, I’m doing less.”

But earlier this month, with Election Day approaching, he had yet to decide whether his disillusionment with the Republican party would translate into support for Democrat U.S. Senate nominee James Talarico, a candidate he worried was too far-left. 

Melendez, who says he doesn’t identify with a political party, is among the state’s most politically valuable voters. He’s independent, undecided and Hispanic — which is the state’s largest ethnic bloc. Following the trends of Valley voters, Melendez had previously aligned with Democrats, but moved with conservatives in recent elections. 

In 2024, exit polls showed 55% of Texas Latinos supported Trump in a massive victory for Republicans who have spent decades wooing those voters. Trump also prevailed over Kamala Harris in 14 out of 18 border counties, which is a number that doubled from the four years prior.

This midterm election, all eyes are back on the Rio Grande Valley’s voters again. Two years of higher prices from tariffs and the war in Iran, coupled with aggressive deportation tactics often targeting Texas’ border, have moved an increasing number of Latinos away from Trump. About a quarter of Hispanic voters who picked Trump say that if they had to do it over, they would not vote for him again, according to a survey by UnidosUS, a nonpartisan Latino civil rights group.

With what is expected to be Texas’ most competitive election in decades, Democrats are unlikely to succeed in their statewide bids without a major surge of Latino support. 

But Melendez notes that being anti-Trump doesn’t equate to being against other Republicans running atop the ticket in Texas.

As hundreds of Valley voters were already rushing to the ballot box for early voting, reaching participation levels matching the 2024 presidential election, Melendez was still agonizing over his choice.

“I support the policies on healthcare of Talarico, but I do support some of the more fiscal issues with [Attorney General Ken] Paxton,” Melendez said of the Democratic and Republican candidates for U.S. Senate.

“My soul is torn,” he said.

From left to center

Melendez, who grew up in the border city of McAllen, has been surrounded by people on the political left his entire life. His parents were liberal and now his adult children are, too.

He said he’s always considered himself fiscally conservative, while more progressive on social issues.

His daughter, Ivana Melendez, 30, sees him that way, too. He’s always been supportive of her openly gay sibling and he has opposed outlawing abortions, she said.

“We would always joke around with my dad being like, ‘How could you vote for Donald Trump?’” said Ivana, a law student at Suffolk University Law School in Boston.

In her view, she said her father was primarily motivated by low taxes.

“I really think he was just a one-issue voter in that way because, in other regards, my dad is not conservative,” she said.

She recalled that her mother had a framed photo of her and Melendez meeting President Bill Clinton at a fundraiser in the Valley.

Though Melendez supported Clinton in the 1990s, he said he couldn’t bring himself to vote for Hillary Clinton when she and Trump faced off in the 2016 presidential election.

He had supported the majority of Democratic policies up until that point but, as a veteran who served as a flight surgeon in the U.S. Army, he was disappointed in Clinton’s handling of the attack on a U.S. consulate in Benghazi, Libya, in 2012, when she served as U.S. Secretary of State under President Barack Obama.

He decided not to vote for a presidential candidate that year at all.

Over the years, Melendez has been drawn in by Republican messaging around securing the border.

A majority of Latino voters don’t approve of Trump’s use of mass deportations, according to an NBC News/Telemundo poll. Melendez isn’t one of them. He believes that people with a final deportation order should be subject to removal.

“The law’s the law,” he said.

Melendez said Hispanics and Latinos, especially those who have spent many years in the U.S., put their American values ahead of their heritage, which is why Trump prevailed with those voters in 2024.

“I think that Latinos that were raised in the States … we’re just Americans with Hispanic last names,” Melendez said. “Yeah, we have our own little idiosyncrasies of our culture — tortillas, abuelitas, quinceñeras — but I don’t think that our ethnicity is that big of a deal anymore.”

Melendez said he was unswayed by Harris, the 2024 Democratic nominee, who he felt was inconsistent on her policy positions.

With Trump, he believed he knew what he was getting.

“But guess what? We didn’t get it,” Melendez said. “He turned out to be more disappointing.”

Richard Gonzales, chair of the Hidalgo County Democratic Party, said he understands why some people might remain unconvinced to vote for their candidates.

“We haven’t exactly done the best job of doing things that we need to do, and our messaging has been a little bit messy,” Gonzales said, though he added they’ve done a lot better recently by focusing on the economy and affordability. “I think that these people who are still weary of the party just need to give us an opportunity to show that we’re going to change things.”

The pandemic hits the Valley

In 2020, the global pandemic exploded into the Valley, where high rates of chronic health issues meant people were more susceptible to complications.

The region, where more than half of adults are uninsured, quickly became a hotspot for COVID-19, which brought the Valley’s medical community to its knees. 

At the height of the pandemic, 10 out of 12 hospitals in Hidalgo and Cameron County were at capacity. The death rate there more than doubled the state average.

“People were dying every 7 to 10 minutes,” said Melendez, who was thrust into the national spotlight speaking regularly to national media about the mounting deaths and devastation.

As the top doctor for the county, Melendez was charged with enforcing health laws to try to slow the spread of the coronavirus. He was responsible for issuing recommendations for people to stay at home and to avoid getting together with friends and family. He also urged preventive measures such as wearing masks and, later, getting vaccinated, but that was an uphill battle. 

That role would eventually put him at odds with Republican leaders in the state and nationally who downplayed the need for COVID precautions and falsely questioned the safety of vaccines.

Eventually, the Trump administration would use COVID as an excuse to turn away asylum seekers from the border, fueling right-wing talking points that COVID was being spread by migrants entering the U.S. At the time, Melendez ardently pushed back.

“Is this a pandemic of the migrants? No, it’s a pandemic of the unvaccinated,” Melendez said in August 2021.

Despite those headwinds, Melendez didn’t see Trump as the originator of COVID misinformation. He recalled Trump as someone who followed most, if not all, of the recommendations from Dr. Anthony Fauci, the director of the National Institutes of Allergy and Infectious Diseases and adviser to Trump during the pandemic. 

Republicans in the current Trump administration have since turned on Fauci. Trump himself suggested recently that his former adviser should be prosecuted, after Sen. Rand Paul, R-Kentucky, made a criminal referral to the Department of Justice after Fauci did not answer questions during a hearing.

Melendez also credited the first Trump administration for the accelerated development of a COVID vaccine through Operation Warp Speed.

“Did we find a resistance to solid policy? Absolutely. Did it come, most of the time, from people on the right? It did. But I don’t necessarily feel that it was fed by an organized MAGA system,” Melendez said. “I think it was just fed by anger and just distrust.”

A brief run for office

In 2022, Melendez decided to run for Congress — and he initially wanted to do it as a Republican.

He was inspired to run following his experience with managing politics during the COVID-19 pandemic. He hoped to be an independent voice that truly represented what the community needed.

“What we need down here, in my opinion, is more resources to teach people how to fish,” he said. “And what we have are candidates that just want free fish.”

Texas’ 15th Congressional District had just undergone its decennial redistricting, and the historically Democratic district had been redrawn to tilt in favor of Republicans.

He approached the Republican Party first, but was told the party would not support him, Melendez said. They were already backing Monica De La Cruz, they explained, who had already come close to victory two years prior.

Rebuffed by the Republican Party, Melendez decided to run as a Democrat instead, but his campaign lasted all of two months before he became disillusioned by the process. 

Opposition researchers had dug up legal infractions he’d had when he was younger, such as a charge of public intoxication when he was 17, and they were digging into his family.

“I tried to tell my dad that this is going to get ugly and he was, I think, naive,” Ivana said.

He came away from the experience believing the entire political system was corrupt and viewed the candidates as people who were willing to play the game. 

But he saw Trump as someone who operated outside of that political infrastructure — at least in the beginning. He believed Trump had enough money that he would be unswayed by donors and could do what he wanted.

“[Trump] didn’t play the game,” Melendez thought at the time.

Buyer’s remorse

When Melendez voted for Trump in the 2024 election, he did so believing the healthcare status quo would remain the same. 

He was also aligned with Republicans in opposing Democratic proposals to expand Medicare, a bad program, in his view, because he doesn’t believe it adequately covers the cost of healthcare for most people.

But he did not expect this administration to implement the cuts to health programs that have come to pass since the beginning of Trump’s second term.

The Trump administration cut more than 760,000 people from the Affordable Care Act, President Barack Obama’s milestone healthcare expansion that allowed Americans to access a health plan without going through an employer. Additionally, about 5 million people dropped their coverage after the Republican-controlled Congress did not extend premium subsidies for ACA plans. 

Locally, federal cutbacks led to a staff reduction of more than 30 people at the county health department that had a staff of about 225, Melendez said.

He was also disappointed that the administration had made cuts to vaccine research and changed recommendations for child vaccinations under Health and Human Services Sec. Robert F. Kennedy Jr., whom Melendez referred to as a “kook.”

“All that stuff is, not only counter-science, it just produces a sicker community, and that’s what’s kind of so frustrating,” Melendez said.

He realizes now that, when it comes to healthcare, he is more aligned with the Democrat Party.

Talarico, in July, visited McAllen to share his views on healthcare, participating in a fundraiser for a woman diagnosed with cancer who has been relying on GoFundMe campaigns to pay her medical bills. He said if he wins, he’d reverse cuts to the Affordable Care Act to protect coverage and lower premiums, and he’d support efforts to expand Medicare for all people, regardless of age. 

Paxton, who as attorney general, led a coalition of states in a lawsuit to dismantle the ACA, is touting an economic plan that hinges on a tax deduction of $25,000 per taxpayer and their dependents for all medical expenses, including health insurance premiums.

The 2026 midterm elections

Late last week, Melendez made his way to the polls — but he wasn’t excited to cast this vote. 

In the hotly contested U.S. Senate race, Melendez said he had two bad options.

He views Paxton — who has been plagued by accusations of bribery and malfeasance that he’s never been charged with — as corrupt. 

But he worries Talarico is too far to the left when it comes to gender issues like transgender athletes in women’s sports. Talarico had expressed support for trans athletes during his time in the Texas House but recently reversed course, saying he opposed their participation in girls’ sports “if it endangers safety or fairness.”

Ultimately, Melendez decided to put aside what he described as cartoonish depictions of the candidates being pushed in attack ads and vote for the person who best aligned with his healthcare priorities.

He cast his ballot for Talarico. 

Talarico’s support for expanding healthcare access won out over any culture war concerns Melendez was carrying. And, in some ways, he decided to cast a vote in protest of the last two years under Trump. 

“I think the Republicans really did a lot of harm to us,” Melendez said.

Reporting in the Rio Grande Valley is supported in part by the Methodist Healthcare Ministries of South Texas, Inc.
news.summary: Dr. Ivan Melendez aligned with Democrats for years before moving to the right in recent elections. Ahead of the midterms, he’s weighing his options.

news.title: 'This war is not over': Obama, Trump trade fire in midterms' closing week
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 29 (IANS) Former US President Barack Obama and current President Donald Trump held dueling rallies in Georgia and Ohio five days before the November 3 midterm elections, with Obama attacking the Iran war and tariffs and Trump mocking his predecessor while backing Indian-American Vivek Ramaswamy for the Ohio Governor. Campaigning in the Atlanta area on Wednesday for Senator Jon Ossoff and gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms, Obama said the President had chosen "to start an unnecessary war that nobody asked for and nobody voted for", according to remarks released by his office. "This is the reason why the price of oil is up. This is the reason why the price of diesel is up, the price of just about everything is up," he added. "And by the way, contrary to the promises and statements and declarations that were made seven months ago, this war is not over. It's still going on, which means you are not getting any relief anytime soon." He mocked Trump's trade war with Canada. "And the big trade war he's waging now is that well-known evil empire, that historical adversary of the United States, Canada, the people who gave us maple syrup and Martin Short, the nicest people around, our friendly neighbours to the North," Obama said. "Now, they're booing our hockey games." He also returned to his jibe about White House renovations. "They mobiliSed a whole of government response to that joke, not to inflation, but to that joke!" Obama said, The Guardian reported. Obama urged Georgians to vote early before Friday's deadline. At the same time in Chillicothe, Ohio, Trump rallied for Senator Jon Husted and Ramaswamy, and hit back at Obama over the renovations. "I paid for it myself. I fixed it, and now it's more beautiful and in better shape," Trump said, according to The Guardian, calling Obama someone "who doesn't understand cleanliness, who doesn't understand broken, cracked stone and sidewalk". He also said of Obama's campaigning: "He got involved with Hillary Clinton ... and he lost. He then got involved with Kamala and he lost." Trump attacked the 2015 Iran nuclear deal as "one of the dumbest deals I've ever seen in my life". He again defended Ramaswamy's advertisement featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Amy Acton. "The mother said that Amy Acton, the daughter, is a liar, that she's no good, that she lied about the opponent. How the hell is that his problem?" he said, NBC4 and Al Jazeera reported. NBC4 noted the mother never says in the ad that Acton lied about Ramaswamy. National polls favour Democrats. An NPR/PBS News/Marist poll conducted on October 19-20 gave Democrats a 52-44 per cent lead among likely voters on the generic Congressional ballot. The Harvard CAPS/Harris poll, conducted on October 24-26, put the race at 52-48 among voters and Trump's approval at 39 per cent. Several Indian-Americans are on the November 3 ballot. Besides Ramaswamy, the House's Indian-American members, including Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, Raja Krishnamoorthi, Ami Bera, Shri Thanedar and Suhas Subramanyam, are seeking re-election. Nithya Raman is running for Mayor of Los Angeles and Saritha Komatireddy as Republican Party nominee for the New York Attorney General.

news.title: Maine, Kansas Senate races neck and neck as Democrats lead in Texas, Michigan, poll shows
news.text: High-profile races that will determine which party controls the Senate for the next two years are extremely tight, according to a new CNN poll, as Maine and Kansas remain close and Democrats extended their leads in Texas and Michigan. Democrats, who are widely projected to win a majority in the House of Representatives, need to flip four Senate seats from red to blue in order to gain a 51-seat majority, protecting their majority from the vice presidential tiebreaker. Maine In Maine, Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, is the only Republican incumbent running in a state that went for Kamala Harris in 2024. FOX NEWS POLL: NAIL-BITER IN MAINE SENATE RACE Collins' Democratic challenger is Troy Jackson, the former president of the state Senate who jumped into the race as a replacement for the previous nominee, scandal-plagued Graham Platner. The race has no clear frontrunner, according to the CNN poll, though Jackson holds a marginal lead. COLLINS INSISTS SOCIALIST RIVAL WON'T BEAT HER AS MAINE'S MONEY MACHINE: 'YOU'LL LOSE BIG TIME' Forty-nine percent of respondents told the outlet's pollsters they favored Jackson, compared to 45% for Collins. While Jackson is slightly ahead, at least 12.5% of voters say they could still change their minds. Respondents tied Collins to her party less than any other Republican running for Senate in the nation, with 46% of respondents saying they believe she would choose her constituents over the Republican Party. DAVID MARCUS: THE FUTURE OF THE GOP IN NEW ENGLAND RIDES ON MAINE’S SENATE VOTE Collins was one of seven Republicans to vote in favor of President Donald Trump's second impeachment in 2021, and she joined Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, as the only Republicans to vote against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth's Senate confirmation in 2025. With Collins managing to distance herself from Trump, her race has largely become a referendum on her own career. Three-quarters of respondents from either party told CNN pollsters that their choice was motivated more by Collins than Jackson. DAVID MARCUS: IN BLUE MAINE, NOBODY BELIEVES SUSAN COLLINS WILL LOSE UNTIL THEY SEE IT Michigan In Michigan, despite warnings from some mainstream Democrats and the state's Jewish community, Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed is building a lead over former Rep. Mike Rogers, R-Mich. Respondents favored El-Sayed at 49% compared to the 42% who favored Rogers, according to the poll. CNN's previous poll, released in early September, showed El-Sayed with a 47% share compared to Rogers' 44%, showing the former public health director El-Sayed building on his lead. FOX NEWS POLL: MICHIGAN VOTERS SPLIT BETWEEN EL-SAYED AND ROGERS The Democrat has consolidated his party's support after a contentious primary with Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich. Ninty-five percent of likely Democrat voters say they'll punch the ticket for El-Sayed, up from 90% in the September poll. Rogers voters, meanwhile, are motivated more by dislike for the Democratic candidate than faith in the Republican. 57% told CNN pollsters they were voting against El-Sayed, up from 41% in a previous poll. DAVID MARCUS: THE 5 FACTORS THAT COULD DECIDE MICHIGAN'S TIGHT AND UGLY SENATE RACE Rogers' favorability has also taken a hit, moving from 58% in September to 50% in October. Texas Texas State Rep. James Talarico also built upon a narrow lead over Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, despite Talarico's extended absence from the campaign trail in early October. FOX NEWS POLL: TEXAS SENATE RACE GALLOPING TOWARD A PHOTO FINISH Forty-nine percent of likely voters told pollsters they'd vote for Talarico, while 43% said they would vote for Paxton, according to the poll. Texas, a state that has voted for exactly one new Democratic Senate candidate into office since Lyndon B. Johnson vacated his seat to become vice president, also voted more strongly for Trump in 2024 than in either of his previous elections. TRUMP WON THIS RELIABLY RED STATE BY DOUBLE DIGITS. NOW A DEADLOCKED RACE IS BRINGING HIM BACK Despite the typically steadfast support for the GOP in the Lone Star State, Talarico is riding a wave of favorability and minority support to remain in pole position five days before polls close. CNN's poll says 64% of likely voters of color support Talarico, including 22% of the cohort that voted for Trump in 2024. Talarico is also leading Paxton in favorability within their own parties. 24% of Republicans have an unfavorable view of Paxton, according to the poll. Just 2% of Democrats, meanwhile, view Talarico unfavorably. Kansas In Kansas, a state which Trump won by 16 percentage points in 2024, incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., is falling behind Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton. Forty-nine percent of likely voters say they support Hamilton, 45% say they support Marshall. Hamilton, a relatively unknown candidate, is far outperforming his own party in a state where Democrats are broadly unfavorable. 57% of voters view the Democratic Party as unfavorable while only 38% of them feel the same about Hamilton. Like Republicans in Michigan, likely voters in Kansas appear to be more highly motivated by a dislike for one candidate than strong positive feelings for another. 59% of Hamilton backers say they're motivated by opposition to Marshall. Hamilton, a Christian pastor, is even drawing support from across the aisle. Roughly 12% of Republicans and Republican-leaning likely voters say they support Hamilton, according to the poll. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP CNN conducted its polling via telephone between Oct. 20 and Oct. 27. Registered voters were randomly sampled, according to the outlet. 838 likely voters were considered in Kansas, 783 in Maine, 768 in Michigan and 923 in Texas. CNN tabulated its margins of sampling error at plus or minus 4.5% for Kansas and Maine, 4.7% in Michigan and 4.2% in Texas. Fox News Digital contacted all eight campaigns for further comment.
news.summary: High-profile Senate races in Maine, Texas, Michigan and Kansas are extremely tight, with Democrats leading in all four according to a new CNN poll.

news.title: DHS told '60 Minutes' weeks before segment aired that deported Malian national had once claimed to be gay
news.text: "60 Minutes" was told weeks before the segment aired that a deported Malian husband and father, who was the subject of a sympathetic report on Sunday, claimed to have been gay in his asylum application, Fox News Digital confirmed. Fox News previously obtained records showing Moussa Diawara alleged in his 2009 asylum application that he would face persecution if he were sent back to Mali due to his sexuality. The "60 Minutes" segment depicted an anguished father deported to Africa with his wife and two children still living in the U.S. and noted that a U.S. judge said Diawara could be persecuted, pointing to fears over converting to Christianity. However, the show did not mention that Diawara’s application contradicted his family man narrative and the reason why he claimed he couldn’t return to his native country was because of his sexual orientation. DEPORTED MIGRANT WHO '60 MINUTES' PAINTED AS SYMPATHETIC FAMILY MAN CLAIMED HE WAS GAY ON ASYLUM APPLICATION Fox News Digital has since obtained a copy of an email sent to CBS News by the Department of Homeland Security informing the network about Diawara's claim, which was first reported by The New York Post. The email was sent Oct. 6, nearly three weeks before Sunday's segment aired. A spokesperson for CBS News declined to comment. FROM THE HUNTER BIDEN LAPTOP TO KAMALA HARRIS EDITS: THE LONG HISTORY OF '60 MINUTES' CONTROVERSIES On his 2009 asylum application, Diawara said he feared for his life as a gay man if he was forced to return to Mali. "My asylum application is based upon ground of well-founded past persecution and an undisputable fear of life-threatening [sic] to my person if I were to return to my country Mali. In fact, I had experienced extreme punishment and persecution based on the ground of my sexual orientation," Diawara wrote in his asylum application. "Since I came to the USA I had the possibilities [sic] to express my feelings to men without any embarrassment no reserve. Indeed, my tribal group and community as a whole had reported my sexual orientation to my family back home because such behavior is unwelcome in my society," he continued. "My life is hence worth threatened if I have to go back to my country because I could be executed either by the Islamic group or the community." CBS SHOOTS DOWN 'POLITICAL INTERFERENCE' CLAIMS IN AFTERMATH OF '60 MINUTES' FIRINGS DHS General Counsel James Percival, who was interviewed in the "60 Minutes" segment, took to social media after it aired, saying the newsmagazine made Diawara the "poster child for what it claims are wrongful deportations." "His claimed reason for fearing Mali was that he is ‘gay,’ just in case you’re wondering how bad the immigration fraud problem is," Percival wrote. The segment put a spotlight on Diawara, who was living in the U.S. for 25 years without a criminal record, overstaying his tourist visa and getting nabbed by ICE and sent to Ghana, which ultimately sent him to his home country of Mali. According to the report, Diawara has since fled to an undisclosed African country. During the segment, Percival noted there is "a lot of fraud" in the immigration system and many "fear claims" are untrue. A "60 Minutes" insider previously defended the integrity of the report, pointing to how Diawara's claim that "part of the reason he didn't feel safe" was for religious reasons did make the broadcast. According to the report, he had converted to Christianity, and Mali is a Muslim-majority nation. "The broadcast acknowledged DHS questioned the credibility of Moussa Diawara's fear of persecution, which they're claiming now on social media," the insider told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News' Brian Flood and Brooke Taylor contributed to this report.
news.summary: Fox News Digital confirmed DHS emailed CBS News weeks before "60 Minutes" aired, revealing Moussa Diawara claimed to be gay on his asylum form.

news.title: Nick Fuentes Opts Out of the 2026 Midterms, Unlike Fellow Livestreamer Hasan Piker
news.text:
The sheriffs that morning wouldn’t likely have known that the “Nick” in question was a reference to Nick Fuentes, the 28-year-old white supremacist streamer with some 1.2 million followers on X and one of the largest streaming audiences on the conservative news platform Rumble. They were even less likely to know that O’Brian, a longtime follower of Fuentes—or a “groyper,” as the faithful like to call themselves—says he was swatted because he recently questioned the streamer’s political tactics in a group chat.
“Usually the right fucks with people on the left,” O’Brian tells me on a phone call this past September. “But now the right is fucking with people on the right. Like, how do I explain to the cops that [they’d been called because] I’m not Nazi enough?”
In the world of anonymous online accounts that orbit Fuentes and share his radical “America First” political agenda, O’Brian was a central figure at just 21. Better known by his online handle, Chad Champion, he’d watched Fuentes’s streams from age 14, following him from platform to platform as he was continually banned. O’Brian started posting himself and grew into a far-right microcelebrity. He soon found himself welcomed into Fuentes’s small inner circle, the “groyper generals.”
But it’s not exactly clear where this so-called army is marching. With his increasingly massive following, Fuentes is positioned to be a kingmaker in conservative politics. He’s long spoken of remaking the Republican Party, and he seems to control a loyal voting bloc populated by one of the most coveted demographics in electoral politics right now: young men. But the culture O’Brian describes to me doesn’t sound like a vanguard of white nationalism or anything close to a political organizing operation like the Democratic Socialists of America. Rather, it sounds like most online communities: transient spaces anchored by a celebrity-like figurehead, in this case Fuentes, who, according to O’Brian, was more concerned with gaming and earning money from his nightly streams than true politicking. (A recent report in The Washington Post estimated he earned nearly $900,000 from “superchat” donations between early 2025 and March 2026.) Each night, after Fuentes’s shows on Rumble ended, O’Brian says a select few would be invited to play Fortnite with the influencer.
The community is highly deferential to Fuentes, O’Brian says, eager to gain his favor by clipping and posting moments from his show or attacking his critics online. It can verge into sycophancy as groypers grow consumed with “glazing” the leader, O’Brian adds, to the point that Fuentes has come to resent his own movement. “He hates all of those people,” O’Brian says, referring to Fuentes, “and everyone in the inner circle hated me because I wasn’t dick-riding him.” (Fuentes, when reached for comment, says: “I hate some of them, definitely.”)
But the real problems started for Chad Champion when things moved from online spaces to electoral politics. Earlier this year, Fuentes chose to endorse James Fishback, a groyper-adjacent character who’d embarked on a longshot bid to become Florida’s next governor. Polling at the time had Fishback in the single to low double digits. It was a test for Fuentes’s real-world clout, and it didn’t go well: Fishback went on to win just 10% of the Republican primary vote this past August.
O’Brian voiced his dissent in a relatively small groyper group chat—“the Chadites”—and his heresy was swiftly leaked to the broader community. “Nick is burning his reputation over this dude,” read one of O’Brian’s texts about Fishback. Fuentes was furious, says O’Brian: “Nick told me I was creating ‘problems’ for him.” Soon after, according to O’Brian, Fuentes called him “disloyal” and targeted him in his Telegram chat as an “antifa” collaborator. (Fuentes denies ever targeting O’Brian or labeling him “antifa.”) Soon after came the swatting.
While O’Brian challenged Fuentes, others have been menaced by his followers simply for trying to build public-facing careers as members of his movement, which has no apparent goals in electoral politics as a seismic midterm election cycle plays out. Unlike a certain political influencer from the opposite side of the spectrum, Hasan Piker, who’s ventured out across the country to harness his influence in service of leftist challengers in Democratic primaries, Fuentes has made little effort to insert himself or his online movement into the physical places where the messy work of political organizing unfolds. Mostly, he seems content to sit on stream in his basement, often describing his viewers as “incels” and “retards” while he rakes in their donations.
It’s left many in this world wondering what exactly Fuentes is chasing: Mainstream approval? Power? Online clout? Dollars? Pure chaos? Does he simply feel the tide going out on Trumpism in his young audience? When I reached out to see if Fuentes would like to comment on this story, he first replied over text: “Groyper gossip? Boooooo.” A few hours later, however, Fuentes called me to offer a more thorough response.
To most outsiders, Fuentes’s vision is a horrifying glimpse at the most mutated strain of conservatism on the political spectrum, one shot through with sneering expressions of white nationalism, antisemitism, race science, and misogyny. There’s cheering approval for Adolf Hitler and fascism in general. In the past year alone, Fuentes has suggested that women are “the number one political enemy in America,” that America needs a “dictator,” that Black people “cannot actually sound out words,” and that political asylum seekers are “illiterate peasants.” In October, Vice President JD Vance seemed to reference Fuentes’s long-running hostility toward his wife, Usha, an Indian American. “Theres this podcaster, who goes obsessively at me and my family,” he said. Fuentes responded by calling Vance an anti-gay slur. When it leaked that he’d sat down for dinner with Donald Trump and Kanye West in 2022, the reports created a massive scandal for the former-and-future president. And when Fuentes and a crew of manosphere influencers including Andrew Tate and Clavicular were captured singing along to West’s “Heil Hitler” at a South Beach nightclub this past January, it was the reactionary right on parade.
Fuentes was born in Chicagoland in 1998 and was something of a typical conservative growing up. But he proved a formidable communicator of extreme ideas while attending Boston University, where in 2017 he launched the show that would make his name: America First With Nicholas J. Fuentes. He attended the Unite the Right Rally in Charlottesville a few months later, dropped out of school soon after that, and became a professional purveyor of far-right vitriol.
He was eventually banned from Twitter (as well as YouTube, Twitch, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and Reddit), and his podcast was removed from Spotify for hate-speech violations. But his 2024 reinstatement on Elon Musk’s X has mainstreamed Fuentes’s words and clips. His post crudely mocking a liberal slogan to mark Trump’s victory in that year’s election—“Your body, my choice”—became one of the most viewed political posts of all time. Ever since he appeared on Tucker Carlson’s show last fall, Fuentes has become a kind of mythic figure in conservative circles, representing both the future of the right and all that has seemingly gone awry. This past week, HBO’s John Oliver devoted large part of a segment to Fuentes’s growing reach. “Fuentes has been inching closer and closer to mainstream Republicans over the years,” he said.
But even as the young men with whom Fuentes has influence begin to sour on the president, discerning the streamer’s political goals is increasingly difficult. Over the course of Trump’s second term, Fuentes has mostly played the part of surly dissident, whipping up controversy between the right’s wobbly coalitions. He’s been openly antagonistic toward the Trump administration, and perhaps the most consistent message he’s conveyed to his followers this past year has been the abandonment of the GOP altogether, urging them to “vote Democrat.” For the Ohio governor’s race, one of the rare contests that Fuentes has directly commented on, he’s come out in support of a female Democratic candidate, Amy Acton, over her Republican opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, the Indian American entrepreneur who is a frequent target for the white nationalist right.
Meanwhile on X, many of Fuentes’s posts read like lusty-sounding fantasies about the coming onslaught awaiting Republicans this midterm election cycle. “I can’t wait for Republicans to get destroyed in the midterms and then everyone in the admin to be impeached,” reads one Fuentes post. His increasingly nihilistic streams often veer into political incoherence: He continues to engage in extreme racism and misogyny, said it would have been “better” for Kamala Harris to win in 2024 (to supposedly pave the way for “an American Hitler”), and now maintains the Trump administration is a “criminal enterprise.” His public statements have been laced with melancholy too. This spring he wrote in one post on X: “I’m getting really sick of politics honestly.”
Then there’s the more drastic case of Amy Dangerfield. A former “groypette” and content creator, Dangerfield earned the ire of Fuentes and his generals for the sin of attempting to organize a conference of America First politicians and streamers this past May. Her goal, she claimed at the time, was to bring Fuentes’s political agenda into the real world, and she invited a coalition of right- and left-leaning politicians and influencers to hash out the idea of an “America First” political agenda. The attempt backfired massively. On his Telegram channel, Fuentes claimed that Dangerfield was trying to subvert him, and referred to her as “Amy Dangerslut.”
The claim led to a torrent of stomach-churning abuse and harassment directed at Dangerfield and her husband. A story in The Washington Post described how a flood of torture images and doctored content were unleased against the former Fuentes devotee, all because she hadn’t received his blessing to stage a public event. Today, Dangerfield has largely stepped back from far-right politics and her once-promising streaming career.
For years, Fuentes has claimed that his primary objective is the slow takeover of the Republican Party. He often boasts that the groypers are “inside” the institutions of government, and recent reports in the media have traced how Fuentes’s ideas have permeated the young Republican cadre working in Congress and establishment think tanks such as the Heritage Foundation. Fuentes himself likes to brag about the fellow travelers he says are working within the Trump administration, and O’Brian tells me that he’s heard from groypers in DC that Fuentes has traveled there on occasion to meet with his young allies who work in the White House.
But many on the far right find this slow-burn strategy to be a fantasy—or cover for Fuentes’s unwillingness to take larger political risks. Some believe he actually wants to change lanes.
“I think that he saw that the market opened up following the assassination of Charlie Kirk, which is why he’s coming after everyone who is questioning that narrative,” Dangerfield says when I call her up to ask her thoughts. She’s referring to Fuentes’s clashes with Candace Owens over who killed Kirk and why. “I just think he wants to make his money and go mainstream.”
More sympathetic observers on the right think Fuentes’s disinterested approach to electoral politics is a deliberate choice. Aidan Thompson, who’s behind the widely read America First news platform, AF Post, tells me that Fuentes is holding back out of a sense of “responsibility” to his audience and a refusal to support a flawed GOP slate of candidates.
“I think Nick is tapping out because Trump and the party have just totally fucked him off,” Thompson says. “Like, why would you show up?”
When I eventually get Fuentes on the phone, he takes that tack. “I’ve been very open about why I’m not supporting Trump, and that’s because he started a war with Iran,” he says, claiming that many of his predictions about the second Trump presidency have ultimately come true: the war; a perceived failure to follow through on mass deportations; and that the administration is stocked with neoconservatives, America First’s internecine enemies on the right. “All of those things came to fruition,” Fuentes tells me.
He dismisses criticisms that he’s simply sitting out the midterms or trying to poison the GOP’s chances. “People say I’m just sour grapes over Trump or Peter Thiel,” he says, referencing reports that he pitched the latter for funding and failed. “But I’m very open about my problems with these people. It’s all ideological.” Fuentes goes on to explain his strategy is an attempt to correct a “generational mistake” by previous America First candidates like Pat Buchanan, whose followers ultimately lined up behind the Republican Party. Fuentes has instructed his followers to withhold their votes, estimating that this bloc could add up to some 3% of the general election vote. “We can exercise the veto, and I think that’s the source of our power,” he says.
As the midterms drag on with a sense of grinding doom for Republicans, all that might be too conceptual for a younger generation of conservatives hungry to see a far-right takeover of the party. Will Fuentes and his movement stay stuck on the internet, or can they break out? For her part, Dangerfield suggests the failed Fishback endorsement was evidence that Fuentes doesn’t have the “political pull he thinks he does,” while O’Brian is more blunt still: “He clearly can’t be the guy to take things to the next level.”
news.summary: For close to a decade, the livestreaming extremist has led a growing cohort of young men toward what’s looked like the insidious post-Trump future of the right. But as his movement is consumed by nihilism and infighting, it’s become a fitting outgrowth of Trump’s own cult of personality. When reached for comment, though, Fuentes said he’s moving strategically.
news.author: Nathan Taylor Pemberton

news.title: Abdul El-Sayed Is a Socialist in All but Name
news.text:
When Abdul El-Sayed ran for governor of Michigan in 2018, progressive media hailed him as the next Barack Obama. El-Sayed did not appreciate the comparison. "I get compared to Obama because my name is funny, and I'm brown, and my politics are about inspiring us to believe in each other again," he told Vox at the time.

In El-Sayed's telling, Obama was a "fairly centrist, middle-of-the-road" Democrat. He did not intend that as a compliment. El-Sayed believed the administration's policies were not nearly progressive enough—indeed, he believed Obama had betrayed the agenda he ran on. The far-reaching financial, environmental, and labor regulations that Obama pushed through were not nearly enough for El-Sayed.

El-Sayed ultimately fell short in the 2018 Democratic gubernatorial primary. Eight years later, he's a much savvier political operative; now running for the U.S. Senate, he has welcomed Obama's support this time. Yet El-Sayed's commitment to a left-wing agenda has hardly diminished. If he defeats his opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers (R–Mich.), he will be one of the most far-left politicians to win a statewide election in recent memory—and in a purple-ish swing state that President Donald Trump won twice.

Like his friend and mentor Sen. Bernie Sanders (I–Vt.), El-Sayed is not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA); unlike Sanders, El-Sayed maintains that he is a capitalist rather than a socialist. Yet his political project has much in common with the DSA, and he has given every indication that he will align himself with DSA-affiliated members of Congress—veterans such as Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D–N.Y.) and likely newcomers such as Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, both of New York, who rode similar waves of populist resentment to victory over establishment Democrats.

El-Sayed's left-wing bona fides were evident during his debate with Rogers on October 8. The Democrat proposed giving the federal government vast new powers: up to 50 percent control over AI companies, a socialized health insurance program along the lines of Medicare for All, and price controls on the domestic oil industry. Asked what he would do to bring down the national debt and pay for all the new spending he wants, he had a simple, three-word answer: "Tax. Billionaire. Wealth."

El-Sayed's support for higher taxes exempts one important constituency: seniors. Like many Democrats—and Republicans such as Rep. Nancy Mace (R–S.C.)—El-Sayed wants to exempt retirees from property tax increases, a policy that critics have branded "total boomer luxury communism" because it forces younger, less wealthy Americans to shoulder ever more of the social burden. The new wave of leftist Democrats think that higher taxes on the 1 percent, combined with cuts to the military budget, would be sufficient to pay down the debt while vastly expanding the social safety net.

In fact, El-Sayed has proposed tying Pentagon spending to education, such that an increase in money for the military would necessitate more funding toward schools. Don't expect this to work the other way around: Under El-Sayed's plan, a decrease in Pentagon spending would not force the government to stop throwing so much money at failing schools.

Ann Arbor and Onward

El-Sayed was born on Halloween in 1984. He grew up in Bloomfield Hills, an affluent, predominantly white suburb north of Detroit. His parents divorced when he was young, and El-Sayed lived with his Egyptian father and white stepmother. In high school, he was captain of the football, wrestling, and lacrosse teams. He continued to play on a club lacrosse team at the University of Michigan, which he attended from 2003 to 2007. (We overlapped briefly, though I never met him: I attended Michigan from 2006 to 2010.)

That meant going to Ann Arbor, a progressive college town with a long history of radical activism. Students for a Democratic Society (SDS), the prototypical '60s New Left student activist group, was founded in Ann Arbor in 1960; its first president, Alan Haber, still lives there. The White Panther Party, a sort of hippie counterpart to the Black Panthers, was based in Ann Arbor for a while; in the 1970s, the socialist Human Rights Party won multiple seats on city council. Liberalism, as well as radicalism, has thrived in Ann Arbor: The same year the SDS was born, future President John F. Kennedy came to the town to propose the international volunteer organization that eventually emerged as the Peace Corps. In the 2008 Democratic presidential primaries, the student-run Michigan Daily naturally endorsed the inspirational liberal candidate, Obama, over the establishment favorite, Hillary Clinton.

Over the course of the next decade—as left-wing enthusiasm for the Obama project faded and was replaced by bitter disappointment—El-Sayed enrolled in Oxford University and then Columbia University, pursuing a career in public health. (He never completed a residency, which has led to some scrutiny, even from friendly media figures, regarding his decision to describe himself as a physician.) In 2015, the mayor of Detroit appointed him the city's executive health officer. He resigned that position in 2017 to run for governor. That pattern repeated itself a few years later: He was appointed health director of Wayne County, which includes Detroit, in 2022, and resigned in 2025 to run for Senate.

Unlike in 2018, El-Sayed's hard-left politics and contempt for the Democratic establishment were now well-calibrated to prevail in the primaries. He defeated a more moderate candidate, Rep. Haley Stevens (D–Mich.), in part due to her support for Israel—an issue that El-Sayed frequently discusses. The same phenomenon has played out all over the country, with establishment Democratic figures paying a huge price when perceived as indifferent to voter outrage over Israel.

What works in the Democratic primaries does not always do as well in the general election. But while El-Sayed's politics are well to the left of the state he seeks to represent, the president's unpopularity may be enough to push him over the finish line. El-Sayed is narrowly ahead of Rogers in the latest polling. The Republican has finally resorted to breaking with the president on key policy issues—he has said that he wishes to end some of Trump's tariffs, conceding that "Canada is not our enemy"—but it may be too little too late.

Moreover, El-Sayed's left-wing foreign policy positions, which are not necessarily antithetical to libertarian views, count for more in Michigan than in other places. The state has a significant Arab-American population that politicians have ignored at their peril. In 2024, dissatisfaction with President Joe Biden's failure to curtail Israel's war on Gaza prompted many Arabs in Michigan to cast ballots for Green Party candidate Jill Stein, or even Trump, over Democratic nominee Kamala Harris. Republicans have sought to portray El-Sayed as insufficiently supportive of Israel, but that doesn't always play well in Michigan—particularly at a time when dissatisfaction with Trump's blunders in the Middle East is strong among Democrats, independents, and even many Republicans.

El-Sayed does have a possible Achilles heel on foreign policy: His association with the far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker. To many outside observers, the candidate's courting of Piker reads as a huge unforced error. Not only did El-Sayed seek the approval of an internet personality best known for praising authoritarian governments and evincing sympathy for terrorist groups, but he brought Piker to Michigan, put him in front of a camera, and made him a de facto representative of the campaign. For everyone except the toxically online, Piker is a bizarre and marginal shock jock, a man who says things like "America deserved 9/11." Piker is what happens when you pay too much attention to podcasts. He is also a reminder that while the insurgent left often claims to speak for ordinary, blue-collar working people, its agenda tends to be most popular with the affluent and elite-educated. In El-Sayed's showdown with Stevens, polls had her up 22 points with noncollege voters and 46 points with black voters. (Stevens herself is white.)

Yet El-Sayed prevailed, and he dealt with the Piker issue by shunting him to the sidelines. When asked about Piker, El-Sayed dutifully recites that a Twitch streamer from California has nothing to do with a Senate race in Michigan. (The obvious retort is Well, you brought him here.) He has also adopted right-coded language to explain why he should not be held responsible for Piker's inflammatory comments, telling Politico that he was over "this whole gotcha game, platform policing, cancel culture."

The GOP, meanwhile, may have gone overboard in the other direction. Rogers, a traditional Republican more in the George W. Bush mold than the Trump mold, is not exactly a right-wing firebrand, yet he could not stop himself from suggesting that El-Sayed has some sort of connection to Islamic terrorists. Just as Democrats should genuinely worry that linking up with people like Piker will cost them Jewish votes, Republicans should think more about whether reflexively calling Muslims terrorists is a bad strategy to win in Michigan.

After all, the form of radicalism that El-Sayed typifies is not really Islamic. It's not even foreign. It's the radicalism of left-wing economics, of making the federal government larger and more robust. He wants to prohibit corporations from buying houses and to punish companies like Airbnb over "housing dislocation." He wants to raise the capital gains tax, the inheritance tax, and the top marginal tax rates. He wants to give the Federal Trade Commission expansive new powers. He thinks higher education should be free for everyone. If he makes it to the Senate, El-Sayed will be a reliable vote for the Sanders agenda, including moratoriums on new data center construction, a much stronger Environmental Protection Agency, and, of course, Medicare for All. Indeed, one of El-Sayed's most frequent criticisms of Obama over the years has been that the Affordable Care Act did not go nearly far enough, and that it may have even been counterproductive to the mission of building a socialist health system.

Obama appeared alongside El-Sayed in Detroit on October 24. The candidate was savvy enough not to bring up his thoughts about Obamacare.

This Week on Free Media

I explain why it would be wrong to nationalize Elon Musk's companies.

Worth Watching

I finally watched You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder's quasi-documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes. It was made with considerable technical skill, and there's plenty to like about it—but ultimately I landed in the same camp as Reason's Christian Britscghi. We will discuss the film on this week's episode of Freed Up; look for that later today on the Free Media YouTube page.
