news.title: A creeping crisis threatens the GOP —and it's not the polls
news.text:
This year’s elections arrive amid a political pressure cooker of lawsuits, electoral disputes and accusations of interference by all sides of politics. 

After almost two years of a pliant Republican-controlled legislature, President Donald Trump is bracing for the first nationwide electoral test of his second term.

So, what are midterm elections, and how might the results on November 3 shape the United States until a new president takes the oath of office on January 20 2029?

What are the midterm elections?

Every two years, both chambers of Congress get a shakeup. All 435 members of the lower house, the House of Representatives, are up for election. Around a third of the 100 senators who sit in the upper house face voters, too. This cycle, 36 governorships will also be on the ballot, along with a smattering of state-level contests for legislators and local officials.

When they fall outside a presidential year, these elections are called “midterms,” marking the rough midpoint of a president’s four-year term.

As the US government’s chief legislative body, the make-up of Congress decides each party’s ability to pass federal legislation and scrutinise the president. Most presidents in modern American history have at some point navigated a divided Congress, where the opposition party controls one or both legislative chambers. 

What can we expect?

History tells us the president’s party is almost always punished in the midterms.

In the 2006 elections, during George W Bush’s presidency, Republicans lost 30 House seats. Four years later, the Democrats suffered a whopping 63 net-loss “shellacking” in Barack Obama’s first midterm test as president.

The Republican party is unlikely to defy this trend in 2026. Top election forecaster Charlie Cook has called a Democratic sweep of the House in November a “done deal”. Pundits project the Democrats will pick up at least five and as many as 30 House seats — enough to overcome the GOP’s razor-thin majority and take control of the chamber for the second half of Trump’s term.

However, the Republican majority in the powerful US Senate may be harder to overturn and could come down to the wire. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to win back the chamber, which will likely hinge on the results of about seven hotly contested toss-up races.

Why are Republicans on the back foot?

While these midterms follow a familiar script, they might also be set to break historic patterns.

In the Senate, polling suggests Democrats may be on track for some significant pickups, including in reliably “red” (Republican) states that voted for Trump by double-digit margins in 2024. 

The race in Kansas — currently a dead heat — could see the state elect its first Democratic senator in almost a century. Democrats appear to be competitive in Republican strongholds Ohio, Alaska and Iowa. Polls even suggest they could have a chance in Texas, where the party hasn’t won a single statewide office since 1994.

As the battleground map expands, Republicans are reportedly pouring millions of dollars into advertising to defend safe seats that could now be under threat.

So, why have these Republican strongholds — previously seen as unwinnable for Democrats — come into play this election cycle?

Of course, distinct, local dynamics are shaping individual races, such as the scandals plaguing Ken Paxton’s campaign in Texas and incumbent Senator Roger Marshall in Kansas. In Alaska, Republicans worry that a same-name challenger could confuse voters and siphon support away from Republican Senator Dan Sullivan in a tight race.

But the midterms are ultimately a referendum on the sitting president. And right now, Trump’s approval rating is under water in 47 of the 50 US states.

Americans don’t trust him on trade, immigration or the economy. Seven in ten think the country is headed in the wrong direction. One survey found 48% of Americans say they are financially worse off compared to when Trump returned to office in 2025.

Pollsters are also predicting that a sizeable enthusiasm gap could play into Democrats’ hands on election day. Nearly half of the voters for Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris in 2024 (48%) are very enthusiastic about voting in November. Less than a third of Trump supporters say the same.

Rusted-on Republicans might be unlikely to switch their political allegiance to the Democrats. But it could be just as damaging for the Republican Party if they don’t vote at all.

Is it a done deal?

While many commentators are predicting a “blue tsunami” will wipe out Republicans, others have argued there are reasons for caution when predicting the midterm result.

The Democrats remain deeply unpopular. Gerrymandering has tilted the electoral map in the Republicans’ favour. 

And in what are already the most expensive midterm elections in history, Republicans continue to hold a clear financial advantage. Elon Musk alone has donated more than a quarter of a billion dollars to Republican groups, including his own voter turnout operation.

Moreover, even though polling has been accurate in recent midterm cycles, it has famously missed before.

If Trump is so powerful, do the midterms even matter?

With Trump wielding a level of executive power unmatched in modern US political history, the midterms may seem a minor distraction with little enduring impact on his presidency. In May this year, he said “I don’t care about the midterms”.

Yet, if the Democrats can flip one or both chambers, they would gain the power to launch House investigations and block nominations for top judicial and government. Congress can also pass legislation that overrides or restricts funding for presidential orders. It could even set the stage for Trump to face an unprecedented third impeachment.

The results will also offer an early — albeit imperfect — indication of “where partisan winds are blowing” as both parties eye the presidential primaries that kick off in early 2028.

Regardless of whether the president says he cares about the midterms, on November 3, millions of Americans will show they do.

Ava Kalinauskas, Senior Research Associate, United States Studies Centre, University of Sydney

news.title: Voters hate those political texts. Here's why politicians love them
news.text:
John Michael has two businesses — and two phone numbers — so he gets some 20 political text messages per day. 

He’s not alone. 

Arizona voters say their cellphones are being flooded by a never-ending stream of voter outreach and fundraising pleas this election season. 

“I don't like them, personally, but I think more information is better,” Michael said at a “No Kings” protest in Chandler earlier this month. 

Americans received 15 billion political text messages during the 2022 midterm election year, according to call-blocking service Robokiller. There’s reason to believe that number has grown in the four years since then.

“It's so cheap to send texts,” said Chuck Coughlin, president of the Phoenix public affairs firm HighGround. “You can send out so many of them.” 

For decades, campaigns have used TV ads to reach as many voters as possible. They’re still spending big on TV — $127 million has flooded the Arizona airwaves in the general election, according to AdImpact — but broadcast and cable viewership has been declining for years, Nielsen data show. 

At the same time, voters have never been easier to target on their smartphones. And in the wild west of political texting, many messages arrive unsigned, leaving it unclear who is sending the texts and trying to influence the vote of the recipient.

“Text message spam annoys everyone,” said Alex Logvin, a campaign finance watchdog who lives in Tempe and gets three or four political texts a week. 

Even political campaigns who do sign their texts were reluctant to talk about how many messages they are sending this election season. 

The Arizona Republic reached out to 10 Arizona political campaigns about their texting habits last week. Only one responded.

“Text messaging is an extremely effective method to serve micro-targets with messages that will resonate with an individual the most at the optimal time,” said Brady Smith, strategist for GOP congressional candidate Jay Feely. 

The Feely campaign has seen “excellent responses” to its text messages, Smith said. Texts are especially helpful in getting voters to check out long-form content such as podcasts that are often hard to promote, he noted. 

Targeting is an imperfect science, some voters say. 

Registered Democrat Denise McDougall is bewildered by why Republicans keep texting her. It might be a case of mistaken identity. 

“They always use the wrong name. I'm either Sandra or I'm Peter. So I don't know,” McDougall said at a “No Kings” protest in Chandler. She blocks the Republicans who text her, she added.

Campaign calls and texts are exempt from the Federal Communications Commission’s Do Not Call Registry requirements, though they are subject to other rules. 

As a result, political campaigns are free to send tons and tons of texts.

Political texts are out of control: How to end them in Arizona

Former Vice President Kamala Harris’ presidential campaign sent up to 3.5 million texts per hour during “high-volume periods” in 2024, according to a case study from the texting firm Scale to Win.

The company has worked with Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Arizona, its website said. The state's senior senator is a prolific political fundraiser and texter.

“If you want to raise money, grassroots money, that’s the best way to do it. It works,” said Kelly, who reported having $26.5 million in his campaign bank account at the end of September. 

Kelly reminds annoyed text message recipients that they can text “STOP” to end the deluge. However, he has found that even people who complain about the texts would prefer to keep getting them.

“They do annoy me,” said Chandler resident Auryon Alvarado, 25, who added she gets 10 texts per day from candidates she already supports. “I'm already voting blue, guys. Call those red people, get them on our side.”

Rick Smith of Chandler said he, too, gets flooded with fundraising pleas from campaigns he’s supported in the past. Smith understands that they need to raise cash and compete, he said, since he knows dark money is flooding political races. 

There’s another side of political texting, where shadowy political actors send mysterious or misleading text messages. 

“I don't know all the nefarious (expletive) that's going on underneath the surface on a lot of that stuff,” Coughlin said. “It's to promote voter confusion. It's voter suppression. There's all kinds of motivations. We know that most of them are not good.” 

Some internet communications need a disclaimer under Federal Election Commission regulations, but certain text messages are exempt because of their limited size, FEC spokesperson Myles Martin said in an email.

The Arizona law governing advertising disclosures, ARS 16-925, does not apply to text messages, noted Arizona Citizens Clean Elections Commission Executive Director Thomas Collins.

There were no disclosures on a flurry of texts promoting Republican Kimberly Yee’s campaign for Arizona Superintendent of Public Instruction. The messages read like they had been sent by a friend. They were not signed by any campaign or political group. 

“Ran into my son’s teacher at Fry’s over the weekend and we ended up talking for 10 minutes. Which is why I love this video so much. Teachers don’t usually speak like this,” one such text read. 

The message included a video of a middle school teacher named Kelly endorsing Yee in a selfie-style video. 

The Republic called the number and received a busy signal. Nobody replied to a text message asking who the number belonged to. Yee did not respond to a request for comment. 

Republic reporter Stacey Barchenger contributed to this article.

Stephanie Murray covers national politics and the Trump administration for The Arizona Republic and azcentral.com. She co-hosts “The Gaggle,” The Republic’s weekly politics podcast. Reach her at stephanie.murray@usatodayco.com, on X and TikTok @stephanie_murr and on Instagram @stephaniemurray.news.

news.title: AIPAC Isn’t Retreating. Here’s How It’s Already Shaping the Next Congress.
news.text:
In the words of the biggest name in the outside elections-spending game, “Being pro-Israel is good policy and good politics.” 

This midterms cycle, however, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee’s strategy seems to suggest the opposite. Contrary to its signature slogan, AIPAC’s name has become anathema to voters across the political spectrum repulsed by Israel’s genocide in Gaza and frustrated by Washington’s outpouring of military aid for a foreign government while domestic costs soar.

So it’s going underground. As The Intercept reported in December, AIPAC entered the 2026 midterms by returning to its strategic roots — funding other groups and uniting donors, rather than focusing on direct-to-candidate spending. Now, AIPAC has announced that it will no longer officially endorse or contribute directly to candidates. 

Though progressives welcomed the announcement as evidence of AIPAC’s retreat, it’s far from a sign that AIPAC is backing down. The group is expected to continue spending heavily on elections through its super PAC, which took advantage of campaign finance loopholes to conceal its involvement in several races this cycle until after elections had already passed. To Lara Friedman, president of the Foundation for Middle East Peace, AIPAC’s opting for obscurity shows that “its brand has become politically radioactive.”

But how much has really changed? As AIPAC shifts strategy, a new project by The Intercept reveals the hundreds of candidates still taking its cash, plus how the money paid off for them. The data suggests that though the pro-Israel lobbying giant may be weakened, it’s still dominant.

The Intercept tracked how much the group and its super PAC spent on elections to put pro-Israel candidates on the ballot in this year’s midterms — including the money it tried to keep out of the public eye. While AIPAC makes use of a series of new pop-ups and pass-throughs, it still poured millions directly into 2026 midterm races. Its candidates usually still win.

The new data builds on a 2024 project in which The Intercept documented just how AIPAC shaped the last congressional class. At the time, Donald Trump was preparing for his return to the presidency as Kamala Harris ran a campaign hamstrung by public disillusionment over the Biden administration’s unflinching support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza. To critics of Israel desperate to stop the violence, the two parties looked equally bleak, and the pro-Israel lobby’s grip on Congress appeared unshakeable. 

It’s been different this cycle. Primaries across the country saw candidates win after vowing to cut off or restrict military aid to Israel, and incumbents signed on to legislation blocking weapons transfers in an attempt to keep their seats. But the shift should not be overstated: AIPAC still waded into nearly three-quarters of races, and its candidates still won far more often than they lost.

In total, AIPAC or its super PAC, United Democracy Project, spent on 333 of the 473 seats up for election this year.

These are the dollars AIPAC and UDP spent directly in races. The former makes contributions to candidates, while the latter, as AIPAC’s leading super PAC, makes independent expenditures, like buying ads. They made up the bulk of the pro-Israel lobby’s known elections spending — $53.3 million from AIPAC and $66.7 million from UDP, compared to $53.7 million and $41.4 million last cycle. Simultaneously, the groups took up another tack: making it harder to tell which races they were actually involved in. The group’s donors poured money into races where AIPAC didn’t officially endorse a candidate. AIPAC’s board president hosted a fundraiser for a candidate who swore the group wasn’t backing her. And in a series of races, no one knew for certain that AIPAC had spent on the election until after it was over.

The group tested different strategies in different states, spending directly in the Michigan Senate race, for example, while concealing its spending in several other primaries. In those races, UDP gave money to other committees, including a series of “pop-up PACs,” groups that registered just before primaries, allowing them to delay disclosing their donors until after the election passed. Several of those groups took money from AIPAC’s super PAC, spent on ads against candidates critical of Israel, and then disappeared. 

The pop-ups and pass-throughs represent AIPAC’s most talked-about new tactic, but the lobbying group and its flagship super PAC still sunk the bulk of their spending into key races and high-priority states. The Intercept analyzed where AIPAC employed which strategy, how UDP dollars flowed through pop-up PACs, and which candidates received the most AIPAC and UDP cash in their primaries. 

The Direct Spending

The pro-Israel lobby’s biggest investment in the primaries turned out to be a disappointment. UDP spent more than $30 million on ads attacking Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed in the Michigan Senate race or backing his opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens. Now that El-Sayed is the Democratic nominee, UDP is also battling El-Sayed in his general election contest with Republican Mike Rogers, spending just over $500,000 so far. 

Thanks in part to the deluge of spending, the El-Sayed–Stevens contest was one of the marquee primaries of 2026, pitting a vocal critic of the pro-Israel lobby who could become the first Muslim U.S. senator against an enthusiastic AIPAC cash recipient who famously said: “Israel comes to me in my dreams.” It’s one of the key races where we’re breaking down the money AIPAC and UDP spent in favor of one candidate and against a clear opponent. We’re skipping Democratic House candidate Adrian Boafo, who benefited from $5.7 million in UDP spending, because his Maryland primary included 23 other candidates.

After Stevens and Boafo, the top AIPAC and UDP recipient from this year’s primaries was Rep. Wesley Bell, a moderate Democrat from Missouri who fended off a challenge from former Rep. Cori Bush to return to the House (AIPAC spent millions to oust her last cycle). When UDP spending is excluded, Bell received more AIPAC funding in the primaries than any other Democrat.

On the Republican side, the top beneficiary was Ed Gallrein, the Trump-backed challenger who unseated Rep. Thomas Massie in Kentucky. Massie, a libertarian critic of all foreign aid — including to Israel — was the relatively rare Republican incumbent AIPAC and UDP opposed.

Often, the pro-Israel groups backed Republican incumbents. Two more top recipients were Sen. Tom Cotton, who easily won his primary in Arkansas, and John Cornyn, who lost to state attorney general Ken Paxton in Texas.

But the greatest Republican recipient of AIPAC largesse — ahead of Gallrein, when UDP is excluded — did not face a primary opponent.

Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, now facing a tight general election contest against Democratic candidate Troy Jackson, has been a longtime beneficiary of campaign cash aligned with the pro-Israel lobby. Asked by Zeteo last year for her comment on Americans killed by the Israeli military, Collins shook her head and said only: “I am pro-Israel.” 

The Pop-Ups

On top of the $53.6 million it spent directly on races this cycle, United Democracy Project poured another $13.1 million into Democratic primaries by giving money to other committees whose names or stated agendas indicated no connection to Israel policy. That $13.1 million, more than triple the $3.5 million United Democracy gave through other groups last cycle, helped fund at least three pop-up PACs that formed this year. 

The groups’ names offered little insight into their political agendas, as The Lever recently highlighted. UDP spent the most on popup PACs in a series of Democratic primaries around Chicago, where groups with names like Elect Chicago Women, Chicago Progressive Partnership, and Affordable Chicago Now! used their funds to attack candidates running on rejecting AIPAC money or ending U.S. military support for Israel. Several of the groups also received funding from major United Democracy Project donors, and three of them shut down after the primaries and gave their money back to United Democracy Project. 

In other cases, United Democracy Project funded long-established political action committees with ties to current or former House Democratic leaders, like Bold America, which was formed by former members of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus. That group got almost a quarter of the $12.2 million it reported raising this year from UDP. The UDP share, $2.8 million, was nearly equivalent to the $2.9 million Bold America spent against Darializa Avila Chevalier, a democratic socialist and pro-Palestine activist who defeated incumbent and Congressional Hispanic Caucus Chair Adriano Espaillat in New York.

The super PAC EDW Action Fund was similar. Former Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee Chair Cheri Bustos and former Rep. Annie Kuster formed that group in late 2023 as an offshoot of the political action committee Elect Democratic Women. Like Bold America, EDW Action got about a quarter of its funding from UDP. It also provided more than 80 percent of the funding for Pro-Choice Majority Action, a new PAC that formed in May and spent in 12 primaries. The group presents itself as supporting Democratic women, but Pro-Choice Majority Action notably spent against pro-Palestine candidates like Melat Kiros, who ran a primary challenge against Rep. Diana DeGette, D-Colo., and won. 

In a statement to The Intercept, Pro-Choice Majority Action spokesperson Lenny Young dismissed reporting characterizing the group as a pop-up PAC and said it had backed 23 candidates with a range of views on Israel across the primaries and general election.

“To suggest that we would deny a Democratic woman from being elected to Congress because of her position on Israel, on either side, misses the whole point,” Young said. “We want more Democratic women in Congress because we believe it would improve the lives of women and families. Period.”

Bold America did not respond to The Intercept’s request for comment. Emails to Elect Chicago Women, Chicago Progressive Partnership, and Affordable Chicago Now! bounced back because the groups have shut down.

UDP gave another $2.65 million to groups that did not spend directly on ads in Democratic primaries this cycle. 

In August, United Democracy Project gave $1.65 million to a group called SD PAC, also known as Save Democracy PAC, which registered in 2020 and has supported Democratic candidates in past general elections. The group did not directly conduct any outside spending in Democratic primaries this year, but it funneled money to affiliate groups that did — some of which funded attacks against progressives.

The other recipient of money from UDP, Palmetto Action, formed in May and only spent in South Carolina’s Republican Senate primary. The group backed Sen. Lindsey Graham before his death in July, then received a cash infusion from UDP and started supporting Graham’s sister, Darline, ahead of a special Senate primary. The group did not report any additional spending in its last filing due before the general election.

Palmetto Action, Save Democracy PAC, and EDW Action Fund did not respond to The Intercept’s requests for comment.

If last cycle AIPAC proved that it could leverage its financial advantage to target critics of Israel, its performance this cycle suggests that its money has become a faltering superpower. 

New pro-Palestine groups have sprung up to spend against AIPAC — though their pockets aren’t nearly as deep. When candidates went head-to-head this cycle in primaries defined by U.S. military support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza, pro-Palestine candidates often came out on top. 

For decades before it started spending directly on elections, “AIPAC operated in the shadows,” Friedman, of Foundation for Middle East Peace, said. Its endorsements were once “clear but unofficial,” she added, and its funding operated through “informal understandings with big donors and allied but ostensibly independent PACs.” 

Today, “AIPAC is trying out a sort of middle road,” Friedman said. “It will return in part to the shadows — no direct endorsements, no direct donations — but it will also continue to flex its power directly in elections, via tactics it has been testing and honing these past four years.”

If anything, next cycle could see an expansion of the recent pop-up PAC strategy, making it harder to tell when AIPAC is involved — until it’s too late.
news.summary:
A new project by The Intercept reveals the hundreds of candidates still taking the pro-Israel lobby’s cash, and how AIPAC is obscuring its spending.

news.title: James Talarico’s Final Sprint
news.text:
If Talarico seemed out of place among the retired tías and Mexican goths, it’s because he’s trying to pull off something no Texas liberal has done since 1994: assemble a winning statewide coalition. Since becoming the nominee in March, Talarico has been buoyed by a flood of money (his is the wealthiest Democratic Senate campaign this cycle, having raised more than a hundred and thirty-four million dollars), outsized media attention, and consistent polling showing the candidates within the margin of error. Ken Paxton, the state’s scandal-plagued attorney general and Talarico’s opponent, notched President Donald Trump’s endorsement but has seemingly failed to unify the G.O.P.; many Republicans look askance at his impeachment trial, his estranged wife’s allegations of infidelity, and his corruption charges. Plus, Trump said, “he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen.”
Another headwind for Paxton: many voters remain heated over stubbornly high costs, Trump’s war in Iran, and his Administration’s deportation program. A few moments after Talarico got offstage in Corpus Christi, Aurelia Ramirez and John Herrera wandered through the crowd looking for Talarico. Herrera, a twenty-one-year-old curbside shopper and premed student, cast his first-ever vote for Trump, in 2024. It wasn’t particularly controversial in a county that elected Trump by eleven points. “I was going with the grain on that one,” Herrera said. But they’ve both since soured on the President, owing to rising costs and immigration enforcement. “He thinks about himself too much,” Ramirez, Herrera’s grandmother, said as she walked past two rows of low-riders. “Now I said, ‘Well, I’m going to try Democrat and see how things go.’ ”
Will Talarico be the Democrat who overcomes decades of voter apathy—and antipathy toward his party? “Talarico has to do everything,” Tory Gavito, the Austin-based president of the donor network Way to Win, told me. “There is no one single theory of change to win this state. Every type of Texan has to decide, ‘Enough of it, enough.’ ” Lately, Gavito has seen some ads in which Talarico touts that he helped enact the largest property tax cut in Texas history—and she worries that they send the wrong message at a time when young people are struggling to afford rent, let alone purchase a home. “Property tax is a meaningless concept to them,” she said. It’s reminiscent, she said, of Kamala Harris’s attempt, in 2024, to win over independents by campaigning for President with Liz Cheney: voters might wonder what his policy priorities really are. “Even in the state of Texas, where I am paid to pay attention, I don’t know that I can repeat back three things that Talarico is saying over and over and over again,” she said.
In fact, Talarico has an uncanny ability to say the same things over and over again. His memorized speeches sound as if he is reading from a teleprompter, without false starts or stutters—he repeats himself only when trying to speak over the crowd’s applause. Now, in the final stretch, his closing message attempts to cover everything, from the etymology of the word “Texas” to the mythos of Beyoncé and Selena. At his rallies, he compares himself to the Biblical David, preparing for battle; he tells each city he visits, “You are my slingshot.” He also says that, like Jesus Christ, he was called to serve, not to be served. And he also likes to evoke Coach Eric Taylor from the TV show “Friday Night Lights,” telling his supporters, “This is the last play of the last drive.” On the G.O.P. side, Paxton’s attacks on Talarico are caustic enough to make the Democrat’s put-downs (he is partial to a line about how Paxton is like “that one guy” at a bar who sneakily adds his drink to your tab) sound like constructive feedback.
Christian Menefee, a recently elected Democratic congressman representing Houston, told me that Talarico could do just fine without Obama. “That’s a fantastic way to be approaching this—not looking for a savior here at the last minute,” he said. Within the state, Representative Jasmine Crockett, Talarico’s opponent in the primary, claimed to NBC News that the nominee had not reached out to her for campaign appearances. “You know, I don’t view it as significant that James and Jasmine aren’t in a caravan driving across the state,” Menefee told me. “I view it as significant that we are all working together for the same thing.”
If elected, Talarico would, along with Ted Cruz, represent the state with the largest population of Black Americans in the country. After Talarico beat Crockett, Menefee told him that he needed to show up in Black communities, though he cautioned that people would be angry—at him, at previous campaigns, at a Democratic Party that has overlooked them. “When you come and you just sit down and shut the hell up and listen to people, that means a lot to them,” Menefee said. Other lawmakers and activists have expressed concerns that the campaign is not doing enough to turn out those voters. “For a lot of us, it’s, like, Well, how can this white boy, for real, for real, understand this, when he hasn’t been in these situations?” Chas Moore, the co-founder of Austin Justice Coalition, who overlapped with Talarico at the University of Texas at Austin, said. (Talarico’s spiel hasn’t changed much since he was running for student government, he said.) The risk is that “they either vote for him,” Moore said, “or they just don’t show up—which, to me, is a vote for Paxton.”
At a rally in Corpus Christi, staff verified guests by sticking gold stars on them—a callback of sorts to Talarico’s days as a public-school educator. Among the nine hundred and sixteen guests was Mailey Gonzalez, a nineteen-year-old who said Talarico reminded her of her own teachers in high school. Although she was excited about Talarico’s campaign, she said she wished he talked more about health-care issues affecting women, including teen pregnancy. What’s more, “it really worries me that he came here and they’re not gonna listen to him as much—especially with Trump coming down,” she said, referring to an upcoming rally with Paxton. “It’s worrying me that it’s going one place, but then it’s just going to backtrack.”
On Sunday afternoon, Thomas Saenz, a twenty-three-year-old from McAllen who creates life-style content on social media, headed to nearby Weslaco to see Talarico at an event hosted by the national group Voto Latino. A few days earlier, Saenz had been driving up to Fort Worth to see his long-distance boyfriend when he learned of the event, which included a performance by the superstar Mexican norteño band Los Tigres del Norte. Sensing that the event would be huge, he bought an early plane ticket home to try to interview the candidates. (He was unsuccessful in getting an interview with Talarico, and briefly considered sneaking backstage.) Saenz, whose target audience is Latino and Gen Z, felt that Talarico’s name wasn’t very well known in the Valley, compared to Gina Hinojosa or the Tejano musician Bobby Pulido, two Democrats running for governor and for a congressional seat, who also spoke at the concert. “You’d almost think Bobby was running for Senate,” he told me.
Pulido, a centrist favored to win in a conservatively drawn district that encompasses Edinburg and Weslaco, pointed out that if Talarico wins on Tuesday, “it will be because of the Latino vote.” His community, Pulido said, is rejecting extremism—he’s campaigned effectively against both the excesses of the left and the right, and he suggested that Talarico was doing the same. When Talarico came onstage, and addressed his audience of over eight thousand people, he stuck to his more anodyne fare, vowing to reduce the influence of money in politics; he did not mention immigration at all.“Puro 956!” he said, referencing the informal slogan of the R.G.V.
Some forty minutes away, at an event space in Brownsville just yards from the border with Mexico, Talarico’s supporters grew impatient waiting for the candidate. The room was less than half full, with roughly three hundred people; Talarico came onstage around an hour after the event’s start time. As he criticized Paxton for enriching himself in office, Martha de la Garza and her friend Analisa Martinez decided to leave—they’d seen him speak before. Outside, Martinez quickly mentioned how the ICE raids had driven down business at the secondhand store where she works.
“It is ugly here,” de la Garza agreed. She knew people who worked in immigration enforcement, including one of her friends. “He can’t stand it,” she said. “We talked about it over tequila and whiskey, and yeah, he’s fucking livid. His family is upset with him, but he pays for their bills.” Still, she said, he is planning to vote for Talarico. ♦

news.text:
For the second straight year, center-left Democrats have spent much of the campaign cycle attacking and undermining a compelling Muslim candidate who is also a target of the right. This is shameful and despicable. A Democratic Party that won’t fully accept Muslim candidates isn’t a party that actually practices the principles of democracy, diversity, inclusion, pluralism, and multiculturalism that it preaches. 

After Zohran Mamdani won the Democratic mayoral primary in New York last year, he faced deep hostility from his own party. Many of these Democrats either stated outright or leaked via their aides disagreements with Mamdani on Israeli-Palestinian issues and/or ridiculous claims that he was insufficiently concerned about antisemitism. Kamala Harris said she supported “the Democratic nominee” in the race, refusing to use his name.

news.title: My State’s Democratic Candidate Has Zero Rizz. He Could Decide Control of the Senate. Good!
news.text:
Less than half an hour into the first debate between the two candidates for New Hampshire’s open Senate seat, the moderator put his foot in his mouth. “Do you think that’s important, Chris Sununu?” George Epstein, of the Conway Daily Sun, tried to ask one candidate, before immediately course-correcting: “Excuse me—Chris Sununu is definitely the wrong name to use.”

It was a mistake that said more about the race than any of the candidates’ answers. Yes, John Sununu, Republican, is running against Chris Pappas, Democrat. But Epstein’s error wasn’t an unfortunate mashup of the two candidates’ names: It was a reference to John’s younger—and significantly more popular—brother, Chris Sununu, also the state’s most recent former governor. (John Sununu has served on New Hampshire’s behalf in both the U.S. House and Senate, but he’d been out of office—and out of politics—for almost 20 years, until he joined the race this year.) If you’ve read anything about the New Hampshire Senate race, you might have heard that this is the one where the Republican is trying to ride his brother’s coattails to flipping a seat. This is reflected in his campaign’s perhaps oversimplified yard signs, the majority of which carry only two words “Sununu, Senator,” prompting plenty of residents to wonder if he’s deliberately skipping listing his first name.

Otherwise, on paper, the New Hampshire Senate race has been a bit of a sleeper, despite the fact that it’s a competitive contest in an every-seat-counts struggle for control of Congress’ upper chamber. There are plenty of reasons for that: The September primaries were extremely boring compared to other Senate primaries that demanded national headlines. And unlike other primaries that seemed to point toward where the Democratic Party might be heading in 2028, Pappas’ win hardly felt like a bellwether. He did face a challenger from the left, but Karishma Manzur never put up numbers that made her a real threat, and Pappas beat her handily. Sununu did the same with his further-right challenger, Scott Brown, the former senator who had previously (and briefly) represented Massachusetts. That brought Pappas and Sununu to face off against one another in a Senate race that feels almost like it could be happening back in 2012, with classic establishment candidates from each party promising Granite Staters that they’re the ones who will have New Hampshire’s back in Washington.

By many measures, it should be Pappas’ race. New Hampshire may be purple, but it’s reliably voted Democrat for president every year since 2000, and the delegation it sends to D.C. has been blue over the past several cycles too. Despite a bit of panic earlier this fall (“New Hampshire Democrats Sound an Alarm: We’re Losing” blared a New York Times headline in September), Pappas has pulled ahead in polling in recent weeks.

But I have become particularly interested in New Hampshire’s Senate race, in large part because I live here—I moved a couple of weeks after Trump retook the presidency, soon enough that my town hall was still displaying the 2024 vote count, when 800 residents went for Kamala Harris and 792 went for Donald Trump. And I have come to think of this race not as a sleeper, but as the flip side of the coin to whatever happens with Abdul El-Sayed’s bid for Michigan’s seat or James Talarico’s impressive attempt to flip Texas. This is a race of establishment candidates in a moment when both the Republican establishment and the Democratic establishment are beleaguered.

I wanted to find out what the establishment version of either political party even looks like these days, and whether the most boring Democrat in a midterms year of stars might have something to teach the rest of his party. I also needed to understand whether anyone actually votes a split ticket in our wildly polarized times. Given my own progressive tendencies, I came away surprised by how much close observation of the contest changed my mind.

It’s not that this race feels like it’s happening specifically in 2012, it’s just that it has a retro feeling about it, particularly thanks to the candidates themselves. Jason Barabas, a government professor and director of the Rockefeller Center for Public Policy at Dartmouth College, put it succinctly: “You have the first open Senate race since 2010, but you have two incumbents squaring off.” Chris Pappas served in the House of Representatives for four terms before the Dems nominated him for Senate this year, and Sununu, a former congressman and senator, comes from the state’s biggest political dynasty. (It’s not just John Sununu’s brother Chris—the boys’ father, also John, also served as governor of the state, and as chief of staff for George H. W. Bush, with a memorable legacy.) “If his name wasn’t Sununu, I don’t think he’d be in the position he’s in,” Nicholas Germana, a government professor at Keene State University, told me.

Germana knows what he’s talking about not only because he studies government (primarily German politics, not American ones), but because, like so many New Hampshirites, he serves in the state government himself. New Hampshire’s House of Representatives has 400 members (though apparently no one sits in seat No. 13), making it the second biggest legislative body in the country, just after the U.S. House, and one of the largest governing bodies in the world. This is particularly silly when you consider the small size of the state—with under 1.5 million residents, it’s split into just two congressional districts. But it’s also a huge source of pride and a cause of political engagement here. While reporting this story, multiple state reps reminded me that New Hampshire was the first state to declare independence from England (six months before the country did), and even if the state is losing its first-in-the-nation primary status (Iowa was always a caucus), being demoted from second to third (South Carolina and Nevada are moving up for Democrats) in this upcoming cycle, New Hampshire will still take its task extremely seriously.

Is it people’s political involvement that has given the state its purple nature, with a push and pull back and forth between the parties? Not really. Independents outnumber registered Republicans and Democrats. For years now, the state government has been red—and currently, it’s a united Republican governorship, Senate, and House—while the state votes blue for president and sends a full blue delegation to D.C. Which means that people are splitting their tickets: red for the state, blue for the country.

“That’s something we talk about all the time—marvel at, frankly—is how much ticket splitting there is,” Germana told me. That’s partly because you have a much higher likelihood of actually knowing your House representative, which might get you to vote across party lines. But it’s also because there’s some cultural state pride in “balancing things out,” even in these times. New Hampshire had one of the highest rates of ticket splitters in the 2022 midterms, Barabas told me, and this year, 13 percent of voters have already declared a preference for splitting their ticket. (The likely way this will lean is to send Pappas to Washington while the current governor, Kelly Ayotte, stays in power.)

But the times are making it harder and harder to do that. These midterms are seeing an active effort from Democrats across the state as they respond to some of the more extreme moves made by the united Republican state government. “Republicans in the state had been able to maintain a brand identity that is different than the national Republican Party—rooted in that traditional view of what a Yankee Republican used to be,” Germana told me. But as the Republican agenda has lurched right, that distance has evaporated. In recent sessions, the GOP here has passed culture-war legislation like banning trans athletes from sports. They’ve also taken more aggressive steps to throttle public schools, including voting in a school voucher program that has activated plenty of independent voters. These days, there’s “no daylight between the Republican brand in the state and the Republican Party nationally,” Germana told me, though it’s worth keeping in mind that Germana is not just an observer—he’s technically a member of the opposition party.

All of this makes Sununu’s bid to flip a Senate seat a tough effort, and that’s before you take into account his weaknesses as a candidate. While Sununu says he’s not at all trying to fool anyone into thinking he’s Chris, multiple people told me they only realized which brother was running when the primary came around in September. (Their reaction was not positive—Chris had a lot of cross-party appeal thanks to being “a phenomenal retail politician,” Germana said, which John lacks.) John Sununu’s been out of politics since he lost to Jeanne Shaheen in 2008, and it’s Shaheen he’s looking to replace now. While his absence from politics affords him a certain distance from Trump, when he lost his Senate seat, Sununu resorted to a classic move for the establishment and politicians of both parties: He went into lobbying, something the Pappas campaign has made hay of in both ads and debates.

John Sununu was a Never-Trump Republican who supported John Kasich in 2016 and Nikki Haley in 2024. And yet, he finds himself in a difficult position this race, as D.C. Republicans personally recruited him to run, after failing to get his brother to do so. It feels a bit like he’s trying to run this race as if he could be New Hampshire’s very own Susan Collins, a Republican, sure, but a reasonable one who would hold his party to account. The problem is, Donald Trump endorsed him during his primary race, and here, like everywhere, Trump’s popularity is plummeting. Recent polling found that the number of Granite Staters who approve of the president was the lowest ever—just 19 percent said they approved of Trump in September of this year (compared to the 41 percent who approved of Trump in 2018, during his first in-office midterms). People are mad about tariffs and the Iran war just like they are everywhere—but New Hampshirites get to be extra mad because we share a border with Canada and are heading into winter, where fuel costs will matter more.

All in all, Collins and Sununu seem to be the last individuals trying to claim that it’s possible to be something of a New England Republican—conservative on fiscal issues while being socially liberal—as Trump’s presence and his overwhelming grip on the Republican Party make the viability of that brand more and more difficult. But even Collins is struggling with this message this cycle, and Sununu is not campaigning in the relentless way she is in neighboring Maine. “Sununu is running a low-key campaign with almost no public rallies, few appearances from Republican surrogates, and limited engagement with national media,” the Dispatch reported recently, and he dropped out of what was supposed to be the final debate. I myself tried to engage with his campaign in multiple ways—attempting to RSVP to a meet-and-greet I was told was closed to the press, emailing the campaign, and even eventually texting his campaign spokesman—all to no avail. The main action seems to be in the form of the millions of dollars pouring into the state, where the GOP does have a clear advantage. (In early October, Republicans had spent $39 million compared to Dems’ $23 million, though both campaigns said they have about $14 million on hand for the final few weeks.) The latest ad features Sununu trying to distance himself from Trump, repeating his line that he’s “never met the man.”

Pappas is doing the exact opposite of Sununu. He’s been crisscrossing the state (well, driving up and down—you can’t really drive across in New Hampshire) with bigwig Democrats who are happy to add a stop here in anticipation of 2028. Raphael Warnock, Pete Buttigieg, and Gavin Newsom all came through, and late this month, Pappas was joined by Kamala Harris herself. Which is part of what has gotten Pappas into trouble with members of the left flank of his party: Donald Trump may be toxic, but the Democrats are also dealing with their own intra-party feud. Manzur, his primary challenger, took aim at Pappas’ establishment connections and big money—her signs said “Powered by People, Not Billionaires.” And like Abdul El-Sayed, she tried to make her weak fundraising (in the low hundreds of thousands, not millions) an asset rather than a liability. It didn’t work—Pappas beat her by a ratio of just about 2-to-1—but it doesn’t mean her messaging didn’t land somewhere. I spoke with a group of students at Colby-Sawyer College in New London who were all required by a class to attend a political event on campus, and when I asked what they thought of Pappas, they all groaned and told me he was a “corporate Dem”—basically as bad as Sununu, who they didn’t want to vote for either, mind you. Several were still deciding whether they’d bother to change their state registration to vote here this fall (one knew she wouldn’t because she was “excited to vote against Susan Collins”).

College students will be college students, but they weren’t the only ones I heard lamenting that Pappas might not have what it takes. An AARP poll that found Pappas has the edge also showed that both candidates have underwater favorability ratings. And I have to admit, for a long time, I felt the same way. On primary day, I was personally conflicted about who I’d vote for. (I’m a registered Democrat.) Ultimately, I watched about 30 minutes of the debate between Pappas and Manzur, and decided that Manzur wouldn’t have a chance of making it out of our purple state. I pulled the ballot for Pappas, but really it was a vote for pragmatism, driven by concerns over the ultimate balance of power in the Senate.

Since then, though, I’ve been following him much more closely, and I’ve come to feel differently about my pragmatism vote. That’s largely thanks to the actual campaign that Pappas has knit together—one that has closed the initial gap he faced and looks solid going into November. At one stop I watched him tour a small manufacturing plant, nothing bright or flashy, but Pappas was the picture of politeness, gamely asking questions about how they’d gotten a competitive edge in the niche grips they made. The visit demonstrated what a layup Dems are getting this time around: Tariffs causing this small business problems—check. The war in Iran increasing expenses—check. Healthcare premiums going up—check. Pappas, whose family has long owned the Puritan, an event and conference space with a restaurant that claims to have invented chicken fingers, was able to engage in the minutiae of their business, from a place of true empathy. An on-floor engineer remarked that they sell their scrap metal, and the price has skyrocketed—something they take as a sure indication that the economy is going down the tubes. “Just like when peanut butter sales go up,” the chicken-finger heir nodded solemnly.

At that stop, I spoke with an employee who told me she’s never been into politics herself, but that she’s estranged from both her parents on account of Trump. She stopped talking with her mother the day Roe v. Wade was overturned, she said—she couldn’t take it anymore, and she wants to set an example for her son about how people should behave.

Her story was specific, but the distaste for Trump was second only to “affordability” on the trail, and luckily for Democrats this cycle, the two are intertwined now. You can’t go to a campaign event in New Hampshire without running into at least a few state reps (or candidates for state rep), and many of these people told me that they’re hearing from a lot of independents who are fed up with Trump and prices and are voting blue, and even a few registered Republicans here and there. Many offered praise for Pappas, who is skilled at listening to all sides of an issue and takes his representation of a mixed district seriously, they said—he’s made it easy for right-leaning folks to switch over. “He’s a guy who knows how to win a purple district,” Germana had told me, and he’s calibrated his public persona and strategy around that.

One thing that’s stood out to me is the way Pappas seems to actually decenter himself in these settings, which you don’t need me to tell you is unusual for a politician. If elected, he will be the first openly gay senator in American history. This is not something he ever brings up himself, which, sure, maybe is a nod to the fact that identity politics is truly dead, but I think is more of a representation of his style as a legislator. Also: You’d think the man whose family claims they invented chicken fingers, of all things—what is more American and universally beloved than a chicken finger—would toot that at least a little bit on the campaign trail. But it’s all pretty straight “as a family business owner, I understand the struggle” type stuff. (On a recent visit to the Puritan Backroom, I was struck by two things: how quintessentially New Hampshire it was, which I’ve realized is my code for “caters to Trump voters,” and how delightfully large their Puritan Backroom–branded sauces are—Pappas should be running on his record of ranch portion sizes.) He’s a politician who has done things methodically, which in this day and age means mainly that he paid his dues in both the New Hampshire House and the U.S. House, along with a stint on the state’s executive council, before he went for a bigger office. In his mid-40s, he seems young for the Senate, but that’s just because he has a boyish look and our standards for how old lawmakers should reasonably be are broken. He has a stick-to-the-message-ness that can make him seem rehearsed—or can be interpreted as discipline from someone who is taking his race dead seriously.

At a canvass kickoff event on Oct. 17, the one where Gavin Newsom joined the New Hampshire delegates running for office, I heard more practical praise for Pappas. A state House rep who described herself as far more progressive than he is explained why she voted for him in the primary over Manzur: Pappas pledged to endorse his opponent if he was bested, and Manzur did not. This was not the moment for such games, the rep had concluded. There was a couple who had come up from Massachusetts to canvass who constituted the first real Chris Pappas fans I met in the wild (“I’ve always liked him,” the woman told me, with an almost mothering quality). OK, fine, it wasn’t really the wild—these were people who were giving up their Saturday to knock on doors for Democrats, and would most likely end up at a “No Kings” rally later in the afternoon.

Just two days before, the Pappas campaign had announced a “Country Before Party” steering committee of more than 50 Republicans and independents who were endorsing Pappas for Senate. The big coup on that list was Don Bolduc, the Republican who has been defeated for that exact Senate seat in the previous cycle. “I think that one was kind of surprising, to tell you the truth, and that can be quite powerful,” Barabas, the Dartmouth professor, told me. At the canvass launch, Pappas attributed Bolduc’s endorsement to his military experience, and his recognition of the nightmare the military is currently facing, led by Pete Hegseth into the Iran war. It set Pappas up perfectly for his line that “everyone is welcome on this team: progressives, moderates, independents, Republicans.” It was this plain appeal that made me start to realize what feels good—almost calming—about Chris Pappas’ campaign. There was something fundamentally decent going on here—a representative who truly seemed to understand that the job of an elected official is to represent all of his constituents, not just the ones who agree with him.

One of the most memorable pieces of political journalism I’ve read this midterms cycle was a New York Times Magazine feature from Robert Draper that reported out, via interviews with legislators in both national houses, why Congress is so broken. It turned the entire idea of the midterms on its head for me: “On Nov. 3, American voters will decide which party controls the House and the Senate for the remainder of Trump’s presidency. In theory, at least, the outcome of their decision should be enormously consequential.” In practice, though, Draper is not sure how much any of it really matters, as he goes on to outline exactly how much power the legislative branch has ceded during the mind-bending times of President Donald Trump. There are many reasons for that, including Trump’s astonishing willingness to break norms (see: setting tariffs, something Congress is supposed to have control over). But Trump is also the avatar for how our broader politics have broken over the past decade-plus. Members from both parties explained that the quality of those who choose to join the government has declined, by which they mean that they’re all narcissists now. “What you see now are too many people who come in viewing Congress as their green screen,” David Joyce, a Republican from Ohio, told Draper. “And they’re going to make a name for themselves and don’t give a damn about anything else.”

I’m not trying to suggest that the old Congress was all sunshine and daisies. Bogged down by our resolutely two-party system, we Americans can end up fetishizing Washington bipartisanship (that is ultimately out of step with what most regular people want—there’s a reason both sides are turning on the establishment this cycle). But even compromise is getting a bad name these days. Work too hard to actually get things done, and you might end up primaried by an inexperienced challenger like Manzur who may have plenty of good ideas, but no ability to even make it to D.C. to try them. It’s not that Congress should be populated by only normies, but it’s good to have a solid bloc in the mix. They aren’t exciting, but they’re a decent bulwark against the kind of “exciting” we’ve been living through, with brief interruptions, for a decade now. In the absence of a Congress that passes legislation, we have a Congress full of grandstanders.

Forgive me for my Pollyannaishness, but as I’ve tried to figure out what is happening in my own state, why this tight race isn’t getting as much attention as I think it should, I came to a pretty simple conclusion. Chris Pappas is running to legislate. In 2026, that’s pretty boring. But I found myself convinced by his pitch—that he is actually going to Washington to attempt to solve our problems, even if it means reaching across the aisle or compromising in favor of getting something, anything, done. He won’t do it with a lot of fanfare, and he certainly won’t do it in a tight black V-neck. But he’ll try. Let’s just hope it’s still possible.
news.summary: In a year of insurgents and stars, this establishment-versus-establishment contest is deeply revealing.
news.author: Susan Matthews

news.title: Thune goes all-in on campaign trail as Schumer stays on bench, faces rejection from fellow Dems
news.text: FREMONT, Neb. — Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., likes to joke that he’ll be whatever his candidates need him to be in order to win their races. "I tell all of our candidates, I'll come out for you or against you, whichever helps you the most," Thune told Fox News Digital. Thune’s tongue-in-cheek response came just before he attended a roundtable in Nebraska alongside Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., who is running a tight race against independent Dan Osborn. That stop inside a corrugated metal building nestled among row after row of cornfields was among several visits the top Senate Republican has made across the country this cycle. Since the Senate left Washington, D.C., last month to hit the campaign trail, Thune has been busy, hitting key states like Georgia, South Carolina, Florida, Minnesota, Nebraska, Iowa and Ohio. But as Thune racks up miles on the road, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., has been largely absent. THUNE MAKES BOLD PREDICTION ABOUT REPUBLICANS' SENATE CHANCES AS GOP PULLS MILLIONS FROM KEY RACES Schumer has shifted to virtual events while high-profile surrogates, like former President Barack Obama, former Vice President Kamala Harris and others have descended upon battleground states that could make or break his ambitions of Democratic control of the Senate. His most recent event came earlier this week: a virtual fundraiser for Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon, the Democratic Socialists of America-affiliated nominee running against Sen. Ashley Moody, R-Fla. Many candidates running in key races across the map from Michigan to Mississippi have tried to distance themselves from Schumer or outright said they wouldn’t support him to lead Senate Democrats. SCHUMER SAYS HE'S NOT GOING ANYWHERE, BUT HIS OWN CANDIDATES AREN'T READY TO BACK HIM One of those candidates includes Scott Colom, a district attorney in Mississippi running against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, R-Miss. The Senate Majority PAC, a super PAC closely aligned with Schumer, has teed up $1.2 million in advertising in the state, but Colom isn’t welcoming the top Senate Democrat with open arms. When asked by Fox News Digital if he would support Schumer should he win his race, Colom said, "I don't want to get into hypotheticals, because I don't know what the options are, who the options are." "But I'll say this, I don't like that our party is represented by two people that live in the same borough," Colom said, referring to Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y. "We need to have people that understand rural America. You know, that's part of the problem is we don't have enough rural voices in leadership in the Democratic Party, because we have values and we have a vision that might not be the same as the people in New York," he continued. "And we need to make sure our values and visions are part of the Democratic Party." Others, like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan or Adam Hamilton in Kansas, have been more explicit in saying they won’t support Schumer if they make it to the Senate. SCHUMER, DEMS ARE QUIETLY BETTING BIG ON ONE SLEEPER RACE IN THE DEEP SOUTH Republicans have leaned into that growing schism between Schumer and the ones who could make his wish of a Democratic-controlled Senate come true. "If you look at Republicans, there's not a single Republican running nationally that's saying, ‘Hey, if you elect me, I'll vote against John Thune as leader,’" Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, said. "On the Democrat side, you have virtually every candidate running saying, ‘If you elect me, I will vote against Chuck Schumer.’" "They're going to have a huge problem, because the Democrats are really, really pissed off about Schumer," he continued. "So he's the problem." Meanwhile, as the outlook for control of the Senate remains in the air, Thune has dedicated his time to showing up wherever his candidates need him. "We're getting out and about — It's whatever we can do to help," he said. On the other side of the political coin, Thune argued that the Democratic Party was struggling to find its identity in an election with high stakes for both parties. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He contended that socialists were the rising faction within the party, which was "creating problems for their leadership. And I think it's in both the House and the Senate, you're having to decide, is that what we want to be? Does that really represent us?" And that ascendant left flank of Schumer’s could cause problems in a political environment that could be leaning Democrats’ way, Thune said. "They've gotten so far left that they really are out of the mainstream of where the country's at," Thune said. "And I think that's going to hurt them in this election in what otherwise might be arguably a decent political environment for them, but I just — their party has really, really drifted."
news.summary: John Thune campaigns across key states while Chuck Schumer shifts to virtual events and faces growing resistance from his own party's candidates.

news.title: Ahead of midterms, Missourians defend transgender healthcare
news.text:
CREVE COEUR, Mo. — Reneé Luckfield tries not to knock like a cop.

In fact, the 29-year-old spends a lot of time thinking about how to make strangers comfortable when she shows up at their door to talk about transgender healthcare. A syncopated "tap — tap-tap-tap" sounds friendly even when she knocks loudly. In each encounter, she masks her own unease.

"Honestly, it's not something that I'm entirely comfortable with," Luckfield, a transgender woman, said while walking door to door in this affluent St. Louis suburb. "And it's not fair that we have to do this work."

Transgender issues have become a major theme in this year's midterm elections, especially in Missouri, where voters are weighing a proposed constitutional amendment to bar minors from gender-transition surgery, cross-sex hormone therapy and puberty blockers. The potential ban is part of a proposed amendment to reinstate a near-total ban on abortion in the state.

Voters in four other states will also decide on transgender issues this year: a proposed ban on transgender health care for minors in Colorado, and proposed restrictions on transgender athletes in youth sports in Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska and Washington.

Luckfield is part of an effort by the LGBTQ+ advocacy organization PROMO Missouri to defeat the Missouri measure by knocking on 100,000 doors across five of the state's largest metro areas before the election — an ambitious target the group is trying to reach with a mixture of full-time canvassers like Luckfield, the St. Louis lead, and volunteers who show up on weekends. About one out of every 10 knocks turns into a conversation, and they're aiming to have 10,000 conversations before Election Day. The group celebrated reaching 6,000 in early October, but the process is slow going, intentionally, as canvassers aim for open-ended, "transformative" conversations with potential voters.

The technique, "deep canvassing," has a history of changing people's perspectives on difficult political topics, including a 2012 campaign that overturned a gay marriage ban in Maine and a 2021 campaign for police reform in Minnesota that, while defeated, triggered new debate. Now, organizers in Missouri hope it can help stave off the latest effort in the state to permanently ban gender-affirming care for minors.

In 2023, Missouri's Republican-dominated legislature permanently blocked minors' access to gender-affirming surgeries and temporarily blocked their access to new prescriptions for puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones for four years. The state is one of 27 that enacted restrictions on gender-affirming care for minors in the past five years.

The deep canvass in Missouri began in 2024, as transgender healthcare was becoming a focal point of state and national elections. President Donald Trump's campaign, and pro-Trump groups, spent millions of dollars that year attacking Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris over transgender issues, such as one declaring, "Kamala is for they/them. President Trump is for you."

And in Missouri that year, an amendment to add abortion protections to the state's constitution passed by fewer than 100,000 votes. Opponents argued the measure would also enable the state's ban on gender-affirming care for minors to be overturned. "NO TAX PAID CHILD SEX CHANGE SURGERY" read a sign opposing the amendment.

This year's amendment to reinstate the state's abortion ban and codify the ban on trans healthcare for minors is polling neck and neck, with 43% supportive of the bans, 44% opposed, and 13% undecided, against a margin of error of 4.09%. This most recent poll doesn't ask separately about abortion and gender-affirming care, but polling from February showed stronger support for abortion access. The deep canvassers are trying to reach voters who are against banning abortion but are more ambivalent on trans issues. That means not spending too much time talking to people who are already very opposed or very supportive of the proposed bans.

To discern people's views, canvassers are trained to ask the person they're speaking with to place themselves on a scale from 0 to 10, with 0 being totally opposed to banning abortion and 10 being totally in favor of it. Then they ask the person to use the same scale to rate their feeling toward banning "gender-transition procedures for trans minors" — language similar to what voters will see on the ballot. After each of those questions, canvassers ask why the number the person chose is right for them.

On an overcast Saturday morning in late September, with Missouri's summer heat seemingly broken at last, the sounds of lawnmowers and leaf blowers filled the air as Luckfield began knocking doors in a neighborhood 20 miles west of the Gateway Arch.

The first person who opened their door was a 10/10 in canvasser shorthand — in favor of banning abortion because of her Christian faith and in favor of banning gender-transition procedures for minors because she doesn't think children are equipped to make those decisions and doesn't think parents should either.

"I hear you," Luckfield replied. "That's everything I need from you today. Thank you very much for your time."

The exchange wasn't unusual, Luckfield said. Neither was a conversation she had later that morning with Carol Parsons, who said she was opposed to banning both abortion and gender-transition procedures for minors — a 0/0. Luckfield acknowledged Parsons' support and asked if she had any questions about the process kids go through to get care.

"I do feel that they need to be old enough to realize that that is life-changing," Parsons said. Surgery is the thing she's not sure about, she said.

"It is tricky, and it is scary to think of that happening for young kids," Luckfield acknowledged. "The phrase 'transgender procedures' — that's, I think, very deliberately chosen language to stoke that fear of surgeries in particular."

Gender-affirming surgeries for minors are rare. One study of 2019 insurance claims for nearly 23 million children found surgeries were performed at a rate of 2.1 per 100,000 for those ages 15-17, 0.1 for those 13-14, and none for those 12 and younger. Prescription treatments are also uncommon, given to fewer than 1 in 1,000 adolescents who have commercial insurance, according to another study.

Luckfield explained to Parsons that in addition to banning surgeries and hormone treatments, Missouri's proposed amendment would ban puberty blockers. She said that puberty blockers are reversible and can be prescribed at an appropriate age alongside counseling and social transitioning to give a child time to mature and make an informed decision about further transitions.

"Well, I definitely agree with that," Parsons replied. "I think that would be a good solution."

The final door Luckfield knocked on belonged to Louis Meyer, who had previously spoken to a different deep canvasser and expressed some ambivalence about transgender care for minors. This time, he told Luckfield he was fully against both bans — a 0/0. Luckfield asked what had changed his mind.

"The original question was about where my morals sit and what I would do, which is a different statement than what I want the government to dictate," Meyer replied.

Luckfield knocked on 12 doors in an hour and a half and had conversations with five people, four of whom opposed both bans. Those numbers weren't surprising, Luckfield said, in part because St. Louis County tends to be more liberal than Missouri overall. But she thinks it also reflects something larger.

She pointed to research from the Transgender Law Center finding that when people are asked about their opinions on trans issues, they tend to answer favorably, but when they are asked how they think their neighbors feel, their answers are less certain.

"People are more accepting than they think the people around them are," Luckfield said.

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.
news.summary: The campaign to defend access to transgender healthcare for young people in Missouri is taking an unhurried approach to talking with voters about the proposed ban.

news.title: Kaitlan Collins Schools GOP Rep in Embarrassing Live Segment
news.text:
Kaitlan Collins shredded a Republican congressman’s closing midterm pitch with one blunt truth bomb.

Rep. Chip Roy of Texas went on CNN’s The Source on Wednesday, six days before the midterms.

At one point, Roy, 54, urged President Donald Trump, 80, to talk less about his vanity MAGA projects, including his South Lawn helipad, and to stay on course by talking about lowering high prices. 

Collins had set up the moment by questioning Roy on the cost of living.

Roy’s advice to Republicans was simple. “Talk about the fact we will get gas prices, diesel prices, home prices, food prices down if we cut spending, if we can increase refining capacity,” he said.

“But that’s what President Trump said two years ago,” Collins replied flatly, pointing to Trump’s 2024 promises to tame inflation, get gas to $2, and end foreign wars.

The national average for regular gas currently sits at about $4.29 a gallon, more than a dollar higher than a year ago.

Roy, who is not standing for re-election but failed in a bid to replace Ken Paxton as Texas attorney general, responded with a line that reminded Collins of another president’s words.

He asked for patience. Republicans had “only been in 21 months,” he said, and still had to “finish the job of reducing spending” and “finish the job with Iran.” After listing what he counted as wins on welfare, the federal workforce, taxes, and spending, he summed up his message for voters.

“These are all positive steps,” Roy said. “But yes, look, I say, tell them what the truth is: Let’s finish the job.”

Collins looked unimpressed, pointing to the last president who ran the same slogan. 

“Well, you keep saying finish the job. That was President Biden’s line,” she replied staunchly. “It didn’t work.” 

Collins was referring to Biden turning “Let’s finish the job” into a rallying cry during his 2023 State of the Union, hammering the phrase again and again as he built toward a second run. It became the slogan of his 2024 re-election campaign, which he abandoned that July after a disastrous televised debate against Trump.

Biden was replaced as Democratic nominee by his vice president, Kamala Harris, who lost the presidential election to Trump that November.

Roy pressed on anyway. “Yeah, well, my view is that we’ve had now 21 months of success in pushing the direction,” he said. 

According to him, economic growth, private sector hiring, and the border are among the Trump administration’s wins.

He continued to attempt to defend his quote: “Give us two more years to be able to finish the job. Yes. To get spending down further, get interest down further, to get inflation down further and to get our refining capacity up, get gas prices down, get diesel prices down. And then the American people will be in a position to have massive prosperity for a generation to come.”

“Do you think it’s a good idea to brag about how big the profits are for Big Oil when Americans can’t afford gas?” she asked.

Roy defended Trump, crediting him for being “somewhat critical” of oil companies for “not passing through some of the profits they’ve got to drive prices down.”

Pump prices tell a different story. The national average for regular gas was $4.24 a gallon on Wednesday, according to AAA. That’s $1.20 more than drivers were paying a year ago, and the average hasn’t dipped below $4 since late July.

“So why should voters trust Republicans, when they’ve been in power saying that exactly, in 2026?” 

“My argument would be, is that it takes time, and we’ve only been in 21 months,” Roy said. He added that Republicans also “need to finish the job with Iran,” a war he argued would help “end a lot of these endless wars.”

Then Roy changed course. “I think we need to hold them accountable,” he pivoted. 

Roy’s own political future is already settled. He lost the Republican runoff for Texas attorney general to state Sen. Mayes Middleton in May and will leave the House when his term ends.

CNNKaitlan Collins shredded a Republican congressman’s closing midterm pitch with one blunt truth bomb.

Rep. Chip Roy of Texas went on CNN’s The Source on Wednesday, six days before the midterms.

At one point, Roy, 54, urged President Donald Trump, 80, to talk less about his vanity MAGA projects, including his South Lawn helipad, and to stay on course by talking about lowering high prices. 

Read more at The Daily Beast.
