news.title: Nithya Raman and the Indian-American Rise: From Boardrooms to City Halls
news.text:
When I landed in Baltimore in 1982 as an exchange scientist sponsored by Johns Hopkins University, success for Indian immigrants meant quiet, private steps: a good lab, a steady paycheck, children who studied hard. Had anyone told me that people of Indian heritage would one day run Google, Microsoft and IBM, I would have nodded politely. Had they added that the same community might lead the two largest cities in America, I would have assumed they were teasing me.

That possibility is now on the ballot. When Los Angeles votes on November 3, Kerala-born councilmember Nithya Raman will face Mayor Karen Bass in a race that a recent Berkeley IGS/Los Angeles Times poll shows tied at 40 percent. In New York, Zohran Mamdani, the son of Indian-born filmmaker Mira Nair, took office as mayor on January 1. If Raman wins, people of Indian heritage will govern the country’s two largest cities, together home to roughly 12 million people.

Raman’s path will sound familiar to many Indian families, with one unusual turn. She came to Louisiana with her parents at six, studied at Harvard and earned a master’s degree in urban planning at MIT. Then, instead of heading for a comfortable career, she went back to India to work with slum residents and found Transparent Chennai, a research group on sanitation and city services. In Los Angeles she co-founded a homeless coalition in her neighborhood before winning a council seat in 2020, becoming the first South Asian elected to the city council.

Her mayoral run has been anything but predictable. She filed hours before the deadline, was running third on primary night, and climbed past Spencer Pratt as late mail ballots were counted. She is running on housing affordability and a pledge to halve tent encampments before the 2028 Olympics. Win or lose, a Kerala-born immigrant reaching a dead heat for mayor of the second-largest city in the country is a milestone.

Her run continues a story corporate America has been writing for two decades. Sundar Pichai leads Alphabet, Satya Nadella leads Microsoft, Arvind Krishna leads IBM and Shantanu Narayen leads Adobe, and Indian-origin executives now head sixteen Fortune 500 companies. Politics is the newer frontier. After Kamala Harris and Nikki Haley, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy is in a toss-up race for governor of Ohio on the same ballot day. Indian Americans now lead from both left and right, and one can take pride in that without endorsing any of them.

What links the boardroom and city hall? Education, first. Pew Research Center finds that 77 percent of Indian Americans 25 and older hold at least a bachelor’s degree and 45 percent hold an advanced degree. The median Indian-American household earned $151,200 in 2023, nearly double the national median of about $80,600.

A fair skeptic will say this mostly reflects who America lets in: engineers, physicians and scientists on skilled visas. I was one of them, and the point has merit for my generation. It explains much less about our children. Pew reports that U.S.-born Indian Americans hold college degrees at nearly the same rate as immigrants, 76 percent compared with 77 percent. No consular officer screened Raman at six. Her drive was formed at home.

I would call it culture, and I use the word carefully. Indians are not born smarter than anyone else. What many Indian families do is aim ambition early and keep it aimed: the best school within reach, education as the surest ladder, and the expectation of climbing well past the first rung. Raman’s detour from MIT to the slums of Chennai fits that pattern: a hard goal, chosen early and pursued for years. The summit may be a corner office or a city hall, but the discipline underneath is the same. Habits, unlike ancestry, can be learned, which is why this story matters beyond our own community.

So should Indians feel proud? Yes, of the climb itself, whatever one thinks of any candidate’s platform. The real measure of any mayor will be whether middle-class families can afford to live in the city, and voters will rightly judge that on results, not heritage. For now, it is worth noticing how far a community of immigrants and their children has come since the days when a steady laboratory job felt like the summit.
news.author: Meda Parameswara Reddy

news.title: The Trump paradox: Why Republicans could still defy the odds in midterms
news.text:
By every conventional political calculation, Democrats should be preparing to take control of Congress in November 2026. High prices, economic anxiety, war fatigue and an unpopular Republican president have created almost ideal conditions for an opposition victory. History also tells us that the president’s party generally suffers in midterm elections.
Yet, I predict Republicans will not only retain the Senate but also expand their majority from 53 to 55 seats.
The reason is not that Americans have suddenly become satisfied with the Trump administration. It is that, in my assessment, enough Americans find the Democratic alternative even less acceptable.
If Democrats had remained a party of conventional liberalism, economic concerns and broadly acceptable candidates, I would be predicting their takeover of both chambers of Congress. Instead, the party has developed an image among many voters that could cost it an otherwise achievable victory.
The Democrats’ perception problem
Socialism, communism, Islamism and radical transgender politics have become prominent features of how many Americans perceive the modern Democratic Party. Donald Trump has been relentless in reinforcing that perception, portraying Democrats as having abandoned common sense in favour of ideological extremism.
Whether every Democratic candidate actually embraces these positions is not the central political question. Elections are not academic exercises in determining what candidates truly believe. They are contests over what voters believe candidates represent.
And in politics, perception can be more consequential than reality.
A voter may be deeply unhappy about inflation, grocery prices, foreign policy or Trump's personal conduct and still refuse to support a candidate perceived as representing an unacceptable ideological direction.
Some traditional Democrats may stay home. Others may cross party lines. Independents who would ordinarily punish the president's party may decide that the alternative is worse.
This, I believe, is the central dynamic that conventional midterm analysis risks overlooking.
Maga loyalty
The second factor is the extraordinary loyalty of Trump’s Maga base.
Trump has been working aggressively to keep his supporters politically engaged. His followers may disagree with individual decisions or express frustration over economic conditions, but that does not necessarily translate into abandoning the political movement they helped create.
I expect Maga turnout to decline from the presidential election of 2024, but considerably less than the traditional midterm decline. Trump's continuing involvement and his aggressive messaging against Democrats could make November feel to many supporters like another battle for the political future of America.
I am also placing greater weight on actual election results than on opinion polls.
In November 2024, Trump won Texas by approximately 13.6 percentage points, Iowa by 13.2, Alaska by 13.1, Ohio by 11.2, North Carolina by 3.3, Georgia by 2.2 and Michigan by 1.4.
These results establish the Republican electoral foundation in each state. They do not guarantee Senate victories, but they demonstrate the strength of the coalition Republicans can attempt to mobilise.
The crucial question is how individual candidates interact with that foundation.
Michigan versus Georgia
Michigan and Georgia provide perhaps the clearest illustration of my theory.
Trump won both states in 2024. Yet I predict a Republican victory in Michigan and a Democratic victory in Georgia.
The difference is not the presidential voting record. It is the Democratic candidate and how voters perceive him.
In Michigan, Republican Mike Rogers faces Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive whose political identity makes him particularly vulnerable, in my view, to Republican attacks on the ideological direction of the Democratic Party.
I believe concerns about socialism, Islamism and progressive cultural politics could persuade enough independents and traditional Democrats to reject El-Sayed, even if they are dissatisfied with Trump.
Michigan also presents an opportunity for Republicans to improve their standing among Black voters. Republican gubernatorial candidate John James, who is Black, could contribute to that effort. I also believe the longstanding portrayal of Trump as fundamentally racist has lost some of its effectiveness among parts of the Black electorate.
Whether these factors produce a measurable shift remains to be seen, but even modest changes in a closely divided state can determine the outcome.
Rogers narrowly lost his 2024 Senate race despite Trump's statewide victory. This time, I expect the combination of Maga turnout, ideological concerns and possible demographic shifts to carry Rogers across the finish line.
Georgia presents a different situation.
Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff faces Republican Mike Collins in a state Trump won by only 2.2 points. Ossoff has cultivated a more conventional political image and is less easily associated with the ideological controversies that could damage other Democrats.
Consequently, economic dissatisfaction, war fatigue and frustration with the administration may carry greater weight in Georgia than the cultural issues Republicans are emphasising nationally.
My prediction is that Ossoff survives.
These contrasting outcomes demonstrate why I do not expect every state Trump won in 2024 to automatically elect a Republican senator in 2026.
North Carolina
North Carolina is the one Republican Senate seat I expect Democrats to capture.
Former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper faces Republican Michael Whatley in a state Trump carried by approximately 3.3 points.
Cooper has already demonstrated his ability to win statewide elections in a Republican-leaning presidential electorate. His reputation as a relatively conventional Democrat makes it more difficult for Republicans to portray him as an embodiment of the party's ideological extremes.
That matters enormously in the current political environment.
Voters frustrated by prices, economic uncertainty and the administration's policies may find Cooper an acceptable alternative without feeling they are endorsing the more controversial elements of the Democratic Party.
I expect Cooper to defeat Whatley.
His victory, alongside my predicted Republican victory in Michigan and Democratic hold in Georgia, would illustrate a consistent principle: candidate reputation can determine whether national dissatisfaction or ideological concerns become decisive.
Minnesota is my boldest Republican Senate prediction.
Kamala Harris carried the state by approximately 4.2 points in 2024. Minnesota has not voted Republican in a presidential election since 1972, and it has not elected a Republican US senator in nearly a quarter of a century.
But the massive public programme fraud scandals have created an extraordinary political vulnerability for the state's Democratic leadership.
Hundreds of millions of dollars intended for vulnerable people have been stolen in schemes that exposed serious weaknesses in government oversight. The scandals have generated prosecutions, convictions and intense public scrutiny.
For Republicans, this is more than a corruption issue. It is an opportunity to challenge the competence and accountability of an expansive government bureaucracy.
Republican Michele Tafoya, the former national sports broadcaster, is challenging Democratic Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan for the Senate. Tafoya can make the argument that voters should not reward the administration associated with these failures by promoting one of its senior officials to the United States Senate.
I believe the depth of public frustration over fraud and government accountability, combined with Republican voter mobilisation, could produce an electoral surprise.
My prediction is that Republicans capture Minnesota's Senate seat.
New Hampshire
New Hampshire is another state where candidate identity could overcome the presidential voting pattern.
Harris won New Hampshire by approximately 2.8 points in 2024. Republican John E. Sununu, a former US senator, now faces Democratic Congressman Chris Pappas.
Sununu's advantage is that he is not simply another candidate whose entire political identity depends on Trump.
His willingness to distance himself from Trump on certain issues could help him attract traditional Republicans, independents and even some Democrats uncomfortable with their party's direction.
At the same time, Maga voters who regard preventing Democratic control of the Senate as essential have a strong reason to support him.
Sununu could therefore assemble a coalition broader than Trump's personal base: voters who support Trump, voters who tolerate Trump, and voters who dislike Trump but are more concerned about the Democratic Party's ideological direction.
I expect that combination to give Sununu a victory.
Texas offers a different test of the same political dynamics.
Trump won Texas by approximately 13.6 points in 2024. That is a formidable Republican advantage, even in a difficult midterm environment.
Republican Ken Paxton enters the Senate contest against Democrat James Talarico with political and personal controversies that could make him vulnerable. Under different circumstances, Democrats might have an excellent opportunity.
But elections are choices between actual candidates, not hypothetical alternatives.
I believe Talarico's progressive political identity and positions on cultural issues will make it difficult for him to overcome the perception that Democrats have moved too far from the political mainstream of Texas.
The Democratic primary also deserves attention. Talarico's defeat of Jasmine Crockett raises questions about whether every segment of the Democratic coalition, particularly some Black voters who supported Crockett, will participate with equal enthusiasm in November.
I am not assuming those voters will automatically support Republicans. Reduced Democratic enthusiasm alone could matter in a competitive election.
Ultimately, I expect Trump's substantial 2024 margin, Maga mobilisation and concerns about Talarico's political direction to outweigh Paxton's vulnerabilities.
Texas will remain Republican.
Other seats
My prediction assumes Republicans retain their remaining Senate seats, including Maine, Alaska, Iowa, Kansas and Ohio.
These states are not politically identical. Maine, for example, has repeatedly demonstrated that voters can support a Democratic presidential candidate while electing Republican Senator Susan Collins.
Alaska and Iowa have their own competitive dynamics, while Ohio and Kansas offer Republicans stronger presidential voting foundations.
I recognise that a Republican presidential victory does not guarantee a Republican Senate victory. Mike Rogers' narrow Michigan loss in 2024 is a reminder of that.
Nevertheless, I expect the combination of incumbency where applicable, candidate strength, Republican organisation and Maga mobilisation to preserve these seats.
That expectation is essential to my overall forecast.
Election integrity
Trump’s pursuit of voter ID requirements, citizenship verification, cleaner voter rolls and tighter election procedures is another factor I believe could work towards a Republican advantage.
The SAVE America Act has stalled in the Senate, and courts have blocked some proposed federal election procedures. However, the Supreme Court has temporarily permitted expanded federal citizenship database checks, while several Republican-led states have pursued their own election integrity measures.
Although the actual effect of these initiatives on voting outcomes remains uncertain, I expect Trump's emphasis on election security to reinforce confidence and enthusiasm among voters who regard election integrity as a priority.
My prediction: A 55-45 Republican Senate
The arithmetic is straightforward.
Republicans will lose North Carolina to Roy Cooper but gain Michigan with Mike Rogers, Minnesota with Michele Tafoya and New Hampshire with John E. Sununu.
Jon Ossoff will retain Georgia, Ken Paxton will win Texas, and Republicans will hold their remaining Senate seats.
That produces a net Republican gain of two seats, expanding the Republican majority from 53-47 to 55-45.
I am not necessarily predicting the same outcome in the House of Representatives, where district boundaries, local candidates and different electoral dynamics could produce a different result.
The Senate is a collection of statewide contests in which candidate reputation, ideological perceptions and the political character of individual states can matter enormously.
Democrats have the economic environment on their side. They have dissatisfaction with the president on their side. They have the historical midterm pattern on their side.
But Republicans have an energised political base, Trump's formidable 2024 electoral coalition and an opposition party whose public image has become deeply troubling to many voters who might otherwise support it.
If Democrats had remained the party of conventional liberalism and broadly acceptable candidates, I would be predicting their takeover of both chambers of Congress.
Instead, I see a party whose perceived embrace of socialism, communism, Islamism and radical transgender politics has created an opening for Republicans even in an unfavourable political environment.
My prediction: A 55-45 Republican Senate. Not because Americans are universally happy with Trump, but because enough Americans may be even less comfortable with what they believe the Democratic Party has become.

news.title: US midterms: Decoding the high-stakes game
news.text:
PTIPresident Donald Trump speaks at a campaign rally

The November 3 US midterm elections will determine whether Donald Trump continues to rule the US a Congress largely aligned with his agenda, or faces two years of heated resistance from an opposition empowered to challenge each and every decision of his.With all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats up for election, the results will shape the balance of power in Washington, influence key policy decisions and set the stage for the 2028 presidential contest.Also read | Trump and Obama trade barbs in closing week of US midterm electionRepublicans currently control both chambers of Congress, giving the president a legislative advantage. Democrats are seeking to break that hold and turn Congress into a check on executive power. The outcome will decide not only the administration’s ability to advance its priorities but also the extent of congressional oversight during the remainder of Trump’s term.What are midterm elections and why do they matter?US presidents and vice-presidents are elected every four years. Midterm elections take place halfway through that period, when voters elect members of Congress and several state-level officeholders, but not the president or vice-president.Live EventsUnlike presidential elections, which use the Electoral College to determine the winner, midterms decide the composition of Congress. Historically, the president’s party tends to lose congressional seats in these elections, reflecting voter approval or dissatisfaction with the administration. This trend is not inevitable, but it makes the midterms a crucial test of a president’s political standing.The newly elected 120th Congress will convene in January 2027. Its composition will determine how much legislative support Trump retains for the final two years of his presidency.House of Representatives: A narrow path to controlThe House is expected to be the most closely contested battleground. A September 2026 analysis by the European Parliament’s research service put the Republican strength at 219 seats against 214 for Democrats, with two vacancies. Reuters reported on October 12 that Democrats would need a net gain of four seats to secure a majority.Although the numerical gap is small, the contest will depend on individual districts with different political preferences, local concerns and candidates. Congressional boundaries are another factor. Mid-decade redistricting, which allows states to redraw electoral maps between the usual ten-year census cycles, has altered the competitive landscape. Republican-led efforts in some states have created additional obstacles for Democrats, even as other districts remain susceptible to changing voter sentiment.Races in Pennsylvania, Arizona, Michigan, North Carolina, Florida and Washington are among those to watch. Vulnerable Republican incumbents and open seats could prove decisive in determining which party controls the chamber.Also read | Bloomberg, two trading firms agree to pay Truth Social for faster access to Trump's posts, sources sayA Democratic victory would give the party the House leadership and greater scope to launch investigations, issue subpoenas and scrutinise the administration. Republicans, meanwhile, would retain an important legislative advantage if they hold their majority. Democrats do not need to win every competitive race; they need to gain enough seats while protecting their own vulnerable incumbents.Senate: The battle over judges and appointmentsThe Senate presents a different challenge for Democrats because several Republican-held seats are in states that Trump won comfortably in 2024. Republicans currently have 53 seats, while Democrats and independents who caucus with them hold 47. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to reach a majority of 51. The vice-president can break a 50-50 tie, making the precise arithmetic dependent on the chamber’s composition and control of the vice-presidency.According to Reuters’ October 12 assessment, key contests include Georgia, Michigan, New Hampshire, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, Alaska, Iowa, Texas and Kansas.In Alaska, Republican Senator Dan Sullivan faces former Democratic Representative Mary Peltola. Trump won the state by 13 percentage points in 2024, while its ranked-choice voting system adds uncertainty to the contest.Also read | US judge denies federal request to block 20,000 voters, says it would 'wreak havoc' on US midterm electionsIowa has an open seat following Republican Senator Joni Ernst’s decision not to seek re-election. Republican Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek are competing for it, with economic concerns and the Iran war featuring in the debate.Kansas is another race attracting attention. Republican Senator Roger Marshall faces Democrat Adam Hamilton, while immigration enforcement has become a point of disagreement within the Republican camp. The contest illustrates how national policy debates can complicate elections even in states that strongly backed Trump.Control of the Senate has implications beyond legislation. The chamber confirms federal judges, Supreme Court nominees and senior executive appointments. A Republican majority would preserve the president’s ability to advance nominees with support from his party, subject to Senate rules and individual senators’ votes. Democratic control would give the opposition greater leverage over appointments and the legislative agenda, although it would not automatically enable the party to reverse every presidential policy.Governor and state legislature electionsVoters will also elect governors in 36 states. The current national tally stands at 26 Republican governors and 24 Democratic governors. Of the governorships being contested, 18 are held by Republicans and 18 by Democrats.Republicans are defending governorships in New Hampshire and Vermont, both states won by Kamala Harris in 2024. Democrats, meanwhile, are defending governorships in Arizona, Kansas, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, all won by Trump in 2024.Governors influence state budgets, healthcare, education, public safety, energy development and the implementation of federal policies. They also play important roles in emergency management and the administration of elections under state law.Several contests have particular national significance. In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms faces Republican Rick Jackson in a race with implications for healthcare and data-centre regulation. The state remains politically important following disputes over the 2020 election.In Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy are competing for the governorship, which carries influence over state policy and election administration. Wisconsin’s contest between Democrat David Crowley and Republican Tom Tiffany is significant in a state that has repeatedly been closely divided in presidential elections. Nevada is also drawing national attention, with economic pressures and the cost of living central to its political debate.These contests will reflect local candidates’ records and policy priorities as well as national political sentiment. State legislative elections are equally consequential because lawmakers determine whether governors’ proposals become law, shape abortion policy and establish election rules. Depending on state laws and the timing of redistricting, legislatures may also influence future congressional boundaries.Which issues will determine the outcome?The economy is the leading concern among voters, according to a Pew Research Center survey of registered voters conducted between September 28 and October 4. Some 84% rated it very important to their vote. The future of democracy, healthcare and education followed, while immigration and foreign policy also featured prominently.Economy and cost of livingInflation, housing, energy and everyday expenses are likely to influence how voters judge the party in power. Republicans will seek to persuade voters that the administration’s policies are delivering results and that continued congressional control is necessary to sustain them. Democrats will look to economic dissatisfaction to challenge the administration’s record on household finances.The Iran conflict adds another dimension, with fuel prices and the war’s economic consequences becoming part of the political debate, including in traditionally Republican states. How voters connect these pressures with presidential policies could influence closely contested races.Immigration and border enforcementImmigration remains central to Trump’s political agenda, particularly his efforts to expand deportations and intensify enforcement. Republicans argue that stronger enforcement is necessary to control illegal immigration and protect national security. Democrats have challenged aspects of the administration’s approach, citing its effects on communities, workers and families.Pew found that 72% of voters supporting Republican congressional candidates considered immigration very important, compared with 53% of those backing Democratic candidates. However, enforcement has also produced disagreements within Republican ranks over the extent of the administration’s actions.Healthcare, education and abortionHealthcare is a particularly important issue for Democratic voters. In the Pew survey, 82% of Democratic-candidate supporters rated it very important, against 53% of Republican-candidate supporters. The results could influence debates over healthcare funding, insurance coverage and federal policy.Education is important to both parties, although they differ over school governance, curriculum and the role of government. Abortion remains politically significant following the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision overturning the constitutional protection previously recognised under Roe v. Wade. State governments now have greater authority over abortion policy, raising the stakes in gubernatorial and legislative contests.Democracy, investigations and foreign policyThe future of democracy was rated very important by 73% of registered voters in Pew’s survey. The issue covers election administration, political accountability and confidence in democratic institutions.Investigations into the Trump administration are another dividing line. Some 63% of Democratic-candidate supporters rated the issue very important, compared with 7% of Republican-candidate supporters.Foreign policy, including the Iran war, tariffs and America’s international role, could also influence assessments of presidential leadership, security and economic priorities. The election will not determine the course of a conflict directly, but congressional control could alter the political constraints under which the administration operates.How the midterms could shape 2028The results will influence both parties’ strategies for the next presidential election. Retaining control of Congress would allow Republicans to argue that Trump has maintained political support during his second term. Losing either chamber would prompt questions about the administration’s economic record, political strategy and ability to mobilise voters beyond its core base.For Democrats, capturing the House or Senate would provide a platform to challenge the president and raise the national profiles of emerging leaders. It could also sharpen internal debates over the party’s future direction and the balance between progressive candidates and more centrist figures.The immediate contest is about control of Congress and state governments. Its wider significance lies in determining how much political room Trump has to govern, how effectively Democrats can challenge him and the conditions under which both parties will prepare for 2028.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Are the midterms the beginning of the end of the Trump political project?
news.text:
When Donald Trump won the 2024 US election against Kamala Harris, he pulled together a coalition of voters that don't have much history voting Republican.

Working class and lower income voters helped deliver him key swing states like Pennsylvania, Michigan and Wisconsin, while Hispanic voters helped turn the sun belt states of Arizona and Nevada red.

Research from Pew found that Trump voters were markedly more racially and ethnically diverse in 2024 (20 per cent non-white) than they were in 2020 (14 per cent) and 2016 (10 per cent).

Virtually all demographic groups swung to Trump in 2024, but a New York Times analysis concluded the biggest shifts were among young Black and Hispanic voters.

At the time of that election, strategists wondered if Trump had catalysed a political realignment in the country that would continue to work in Republicans' favour.

But converting irregular voters into reliable members of the Republican base is not easy.

Two years on, as the cost of living bites, they don't appear to have stuck around, and the Hispanic voters that swung behind Trump have either swung right back to the Democrats, or are choosing to sit this election out.

The Republican Party appears almost certain to lose control of the House of Representatives in next week's midterm elections. Democrats also lead in polls in more than enough Senate races to be able to take control of that chamber as well (although many of those leads are within the margin of error).

Among the list of prizes that Democrats are hoping to pick up next week, the state of Texas glistens seductively.

Democrats haven't won a senate seat in the state since 1988, but this year, their candidate James Talarico is leading Republican candidate Ken Paxton in polling.

Republicans appear to be vulnerable in deep red states, and in recent weeks Trump has held rallies on Kansas, Iowa, Oklahoma and Alabama. That is not the strategy of a party that's feeling confident.

Donald Trump isn't on the ballot this year, but at rallies he has repeatedly asked voters to "pretend" he is.

"They say that Trump does great when he's on the ballot, but when he's not on the ballot … his people don't come and they don't vote for senators, congressmen," he said at a rally in South Carolina in August.

Part of the Trump campaign's strategy in 2024 was to increase turnout rates among people who would usually stay home. Among the group of people who voted in that election but not in 2020, Pew estimated Trump had a 12 percentage point lead over Harris.

High turnout helped him two years ago. This year, it may be part of his undoing.

Trump wants voters to be thinking about him when they consider voting, because last time that drove lots of people to the polls.

The trouble is that, in 2026, the president is very unpopular.

Nobody's ever seen a president so disliked

American politicians are, as a general rule, held in much lower regard now than they used to be. But amidst an unpopular bunch, Donald Trump is reaching new depths.

YouGov and the Economist have been regularly tracking views on US presidents by asking voters whether they approve or disapprove of the job the leader is doing.

In his first term, Trump was into net negative territory effectively from the moment he took office. President Biden was in the negatives within seven months.

But in his second term, Trump has plummeted. A week out from polling day, the Economist recorded a net approval rating of -27, with 34 per cent of voters approving of the job he's doing and 61 per cent disapproving.

That is a lower net approval rating than any other president has recorded just before their midterm elections since World War II.

Given the president's party nearly always goes backwards in the House of Representatives, and that the Republicans only need to lose three seats to lose control of the House, it's not hard to see why forecasters are tipping a Democrat win.

If the midterms go as poorly for Republicans as opinion polls suggest, it could threaten Trump's command of the public's attention, as well as his authority over his party.

While he'll be in office for another two years, there's always an election around the corner in the US, and once the midterms are behind us attention will start to shift to the 2028 presidential election.

The results of these midterm elections will be an important moment in defining Trump's political legacy, as candidates start to position themselves for potential runs.

The current president regularly backs his preferred candidates in Republican primaries, and he believes his endorsement carries weight.

But will Republicans in the future be keen to embrace the Trump political project, or will they be keeping their distance the moment he's seen as a lame duck president?
news.summary: Donald Trump wants American voters to "pretend" he's on the ballot these midterm elections. Voters don't need to be reminded how much they dislike him.

news.title: Trump, Obama trade barbs at dueling primetime rallies days before midterm elections
news.text:
President Trump and former President Barack Obama took swipes at each other Wednesday night at competing rallies less than a week before the midterm elections.

Trump, who was stumping for Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy in the Buckeye State, went after the former president over his handling of Iran and accused him of letting the White House fall into disrepair as commander-in-chief. 

“The bricks were falling. The stone was broken. The monuments were coming off. The beautiful windows were cracked,” Trump said of the state of the executive mansion when he took office last January. “It looked terrible. And I fixed it very inexpensively. I paid for it myself.” 

Trump argued Obama “doesn’t understand cleanliness” or that “having asphalt going through a main entrance is not the right thing.”

“We’d like to have granite with marble. We’d like to have it look nice,” the president said. 

Trump noted he “took heat” from Obama over his White House renovations. 

“He said, ‘Why is he spending so much time fixing up the White House? Why is he doing that?’ You know why? Because the White House is the number one symbol of our country, and we can’t have a White House with broken windows, with broken stone that hasn’t been taken in 30 years,” the president argued. 

Trump is in the final stretch of a whirlwind tour of predominantly red states with tight midterm races, hoping his rallies will help Republicans maintain control of the House and Senate. 

Obama has likewise been on the stump since last week, campaigning for Democrats in Michigan, Ohio and Georgia. 

“I always worry when he campaigns against me,” Trump said sarcastically. 

“He got involved with Hillary Clinton … and he lost. He then got involved with Kamala [Harris] and he lost,” the president continued. 

Trump said his reaction upon learning Obama will be rallying for Democrats ahead of the midterms was “that’s good.” 

The president also touted having “terminated” Obama’s Iran nuclear deal, which he described as the “road to a nuclear weapon for Iran, and one of the dumbest deals I’ve ever seen in my life.” 

At the same time Trump was speaking in Chillicothe, Ohio, Obama went on stage in Atlanta, where he spent a good portion of his remarks going after the 45th and 47th president. 

“The current president chose to make a series of bad decisions, the most important of which was to start an unnecessary war that nobody asked for,” Obama said, referring to the Iran war. 

“I put in place a deal that everybody acknowledged, kept them from getting nukes,” he said of the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) Trump scrapped in his first term. 

Obama, who compared Trump’s White House renovations to a Cheesecake Factory run by former Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein over the weekend, dismissed conservative criticism that the zinger was elitist. 

“I am the father of two daughters. You think I could have survived their childhood without going into Cheesecake Factory … that was my jam for about a decade,” he said. 

“The president wasn’t even mad about the Saddam Hussein comparison,” Obama argued. “That part didn’t bother him, but he was very upset about the Cheesecake Factory comment.” 

The Trump administration “mobilized a whole of government response to that joke,” Obama marveled, noting that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had lunch and spoke to reporters at a Cheesecake Factory in Washington, DC. 

Obama went on to compare the Trump administration to a reality TV show. 

“I want y’all to know Michelle [Obama] has love for the Real Housewives, but we gotta keep reality TV on Bravo. Leave it to the professionals. We don’t need it in the White House,” he said.
news.summary: “I always worry when [Obama] campaigns against me,” Trump said sarcastically. “He got involved with Hillary Clinton … and he lost. He then got involved with Kamala [Harris] and he lost."

news.title: Darline Graham Hit with Troubling Poll One Day Before Trump Rally
news.text: Darline Graham, Republican candidate for U.S. Senate in South Carolina, received a potentially troubling poll on Wednesday, just one day before President Donald Trump is scheduled to appear in the Palmetto State. The poll from The New York Times/Siena Research Institute shows that Graham and Democratic candidate Dr. Annie Andrews are tied at 48 percent and 3 percent don't know. The poll comes as Trump is set to rally with Graham on Thursday in Rock Hill, South Carolina. Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during them. Trump won South Carolina during the 2024 presidential election versus then-Vice President Kamala Harris. The late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, Darline's brother, won the seat in the 2020 election cycle along with the primary in June. He died from aortic dissection due to arteriosclerotic cardiovascular disease, a preliminary examination by the D.C. Medical Examiner determined. He died in July at 71 years old, following what his office described as a "brief and sudden illness." Following his death, Darline was sworn into his seat just three days later, with the backing of Trump. Meanwhile, Trump's overall approval rating and ranking on specific policy issues like the economy, immigration, jobs and the ongoing war in Iran have recently slipped as households across America are consistently flagging affordability concerns. The polling lows come as Trump has crisscrossed the country in the lead-up to November 3 to rally for potentially vulnerable GOP candidates, including previous stops in South Carolina. Newsweek reached out to Graham and Andrews' campaigns via email on Wednesday for comment. What To Know The poll shows that men prefer Graham 55 percent to Andrews' 40 percent, and the reverse for women, with 54 percent backing Andrews while 43 percent support Graham. Fifty-seven percent of Independents back Andrews versus 37 percent who support Graham. Graham landed majority support from white, 45-year-olds and up, white with and without a college degree, and Republican likely voters. The survey shows that 89 percent of 2024 Trump voters backed Graham compared to 8 percent of Trump voters who support Andrews. Graham's favorability in the poll is 44 percent compared to a 41 percent unfavorable rating. Andrews' favorability is 45 percent compared to a 29 percent unfavorable rating. The survey shows that 51 percent think Andrews would do a better job on the economy compared to 43 percent who say Graham would. On immigration, 50 percent said Graham would do a better job versus 44 percent who said Andrews would. Forty-nine percent said Andrews would do what is best for ordinary South Carolinians compared to 46 percent who said Graham would. The poll surveyed 707 likely voters in the state from October 19-26, 2026, with a 4.3 percent margin of error. The Cook Political Report rates the race as lean Republican and prediction market sites Kalshi and Polymarket both show Graham leading on Wednesday afternoon. D. Stephen Voss, political professor at the University of Kentucky, told Newsweek on Wednesday, "Polls have been trending toward the Democrats with increasing margins, so surprises would not be impossible if that trajectory continues after most polls have left the field. Even the best polls are only snapshots in time; they cannot predict the future. Still, most voters have made their decisions by late October, so Republicans can have a reasonable hope that their standing has bottomed out and that they'll still hold on in states like South Carolina that have been consistently tilted their way. "The big question mark hanging over all of these polls is whether Democrats will continue to exhibit the big enthusiasm gap in their favor that the party has enjoyed in lower-turnout special elections. Greater mobilization among Republican voters for these competitive statewide races would offer a cushion that the GOP until now has been lacking." Grant Davis Reeher, a professor of political science at Syracuse University, also told Newsweek on Wednesday, "It’s hard to believe, but that appears to be the poll at present. I think in the final couple days, a lot of Republicans are likely to 'come home,' out of sympathy if nothing else. But if Democrats can win there, then it’s hard to imagine that the Senate will remain out of their reach." What Other Polling Shows An InsiderAdvantage poll showed Graham with 46 percent compared to Andrews' 45 percent, Libertarian Kasie Whitener with 2 percent, Constitution Party nominee Mark Hackett with 3 percent and 4 percent were undecided. The poll surveyed 1,200 likely voters in South Carolina from September 28-29, 2026, and had a margin of error of 2.83 percent. A previous InsiderAdvantage survey last month also showed Graham with a slight lead with 45.1 percent compared to Andrews' 43.2 percent. The survey shows that 3.2 percent said another candidate while 8.5 percent were undecided. That poll surveyed 1,200 likely voters from September 8-9, 2026, and had a margin of error of 2.83 percent. news.title: Democrats are deploying volunteers wearing blue on Election Day. Here’s what they’ll do.
news.text:
Thousands of Election Day observers are expected to be dispatched by the Democratic Party to monitor potential voter intimidation at polling places around the country.The Association of State Democratic Committees, a branch of the Democratic National Committee representing state-level parties, trained more than 4,000 volunteers to notify the party’s voter protection programs if federal law enforcement is deployed while voters are casting their ballots on Tuesday. The individuals will be wearing blue on Election Day, according to a memo shared with MS NOW.

The volunteers will “provide a peaceful, secure presence at polling locations — countering intimidation, including from ICE and other federal agents, and reinforcing public confidence in the vote,” the memo states.President Donald Trump and his allies have floated ordering Immigration and Custom Enforcement officers, National Guard troops and Federal Bureau of Investigations agents to polling sites, fueling concerns about election interference in the midterm elections, which historically favors the political party out of power in Washington. Testifying before the Senate earlier this fall, FBI Director Kash Patel, did not rule out sending agents to the polls, saying, “Election integrity is of paramount importance. This FBI will not shy away from that effort.” Federal law prohibits armed federal agents or military personnel at polling locations.For years, Trump has pushed unsubstantiated claims about widespread voter fraud in the United States, and never conceded his 2020 election loss to former President Joe Biden. On Tuesday, Trump told reporters that he would respect the results of the midterms “if they’re honest.” Ahead of the midterms the Trump administration has threatened states over alleged noncitizen voting, arguing those cases have reached “emergency” proportions in California. MS NOW has found, however, that federal prosecutions based on those allegations remain low in California and across the country.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris taped a video message, first reported by MS NOW, for volunteers from the program, known as “Democracy Protectors” who are gathering on a virtual call on Wednesday.

“Thank you so very much for the work you do every day that is about lifting up the people, lifting their spirits, lifting their voice, lifting the importance of all people having the dignity they so rightfully deserve,” Harris says in the video.

Harris has been campaigning across the country, showing up in Wisconsin earlier this week and is expected to be in Georgia Thursday to stump with Sen. Jon Ossoff.

In addition to the blue-shirted volunteers, a senior Democratic lawmaker told MS NOW’s Stephanie Ruhle that Democrats will have 15,000 lawyers volunteering at poll sites across the country on Election Day.

news.title: Hasan Piker Puts Ted Cruz on Notice After $72M Lawsuit Against Jennings
news.text: Left-wing political commentator Hasan Piker took aim at Ted Cruz on Wednesday after the Republican senator shared allegations similar to the ones that led to conservative commentator Scott Jennings getting sued by the streamer for $72.5 million. “Hey ted you seen this?” Piker wrote on X, sharing a news report about his lawsuit against Jennings. Cruz had posted that Piker was “calling for Black people to be lynched,” sharing a clip and a link to footage that Piker alleges was edited to strip his remarks of their original context. It appears to be the same or very similar footage to the video of Piker that featured on the August 11 episode of The Scott Jennings Show. Newsweek has reached out to Jennings, Cruz and Piker for comment. The filing comes as prominent political figures on both sides of the aisle increasingly turn to the courts to challenge statements they say have damaged their reputations. Why Did Hasan Piker Sue Scott Jennings? Piker's complaint, filed in a federal court in Washington, D.C., Tuesday, alleges that Jennings combined footage from three different livestreams, rearranged Piker's comments, and removed the YouTube debate that the streamer had been responding to, in order to remove the context of his remarks and falsely suggest he was advocating racial violence. Jennings falsely told listeners that the streamer had a “plan of returning our country to lynchings,” while airing the edited video of Piker, according to the filing. Piker argued in his lawsuit that he had been reacting sarcastically to a Black conservative commentator in the debate who blamed “woke DAs” for policies harming Black Americans. The left-wing commentator is seeking $27.5 million in compensatory damages and $45 million in punitive damages from Jennings. “You have to remember, this is not just about Scott Jennings, although he certainly messed up,” Piker said about the lawsuit. “This is about truth in the media.” President Donald Trump has made litigation against media organizations a prominent feature of his political career, filing lawsuits over coverage and commentary he says have misrepresented him. Trump's legal strategy extended beyond news organizations to political adversaries. In 2022, Trump sued Hillary Clinton and others over what he alleged was a conspiracy to undermine his presidential campaign. A federal judge dismissed the case and later ordered Trump and his attorney to pay nearly $1 million in sanctions. Meanwhile, California Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, has brought a separate multimillion-dollar defamation suit against Fox News. Cruz and Piker's Escalating Feud Cruz and Piker have clashed publicly in recent weeks. In September, Piker accused the Texas senator and other Republican officials of trying to prevent him from speaking at the University of Texas at Austin, framing their opposition to the event as a threat to his First Amendment rights. Cruz had called Piker an “America-hating Marxist” and accused him of celebrating political violence against Republicans. Cruz continued his criticism of Piker at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas on September 10, invoking the streamer's past comments about the September 11 attacks while attacking Democrats associated with him. “When Hasan Piker says America deserved 9/11, believe him,” Cruz said. He later questioned why Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed had not disavowed Piker. Cruz's remarks refer to comments Piker made during a livestream in August 2019, while responding to an interview in which Republican Representative Dan Crenshaw discussed the September 11 attacks and U.S. foreign policy in the Middle East. Piker said, “America deserved 9/11, dude,” prompting widespread criticism. Piker subsequently walked back the remark, calling it inappropriate and saying he had expressed himself poorly. He argued that U.S. military interventions and support for armed groups in the region had contributed to the conditions that led to the attacks, describing the relationship as a “boomerang effect.” Trump’s History of High-Profile Defamation Lawsuits Trump has repeatedly used lawsuits to challenge media organizations and, at times, political opponents over claims he says have damaged his reputation or undermined his political standing. Several cases have sought billions of dollars in damages, including disputes over television editing and reporting about his conduct. In December 2025, Trump sued the BBC for $10 billion over a documentary that edited excerpts of his January 6, 2021, speech. His complaint alleged that the editing misleadingly combined separate portions of the speech, creating the impression that he directly encouraged violence while omitting remarks about peaceful protest. The BBC apologized for the editing but denied that it defamed Trump and has said it will defend the case. The litigation remains ongoing, with a federal judge ordering Trump to sit for a deposition by December 11. Trump also sued ABC News and anchor George Stephanopoulos in March 2024 after the anchor repeatedly said on air that Trump had been found liable for rape in the civil case brought by E. Jean Carroll. A jury had found Trump liable for sexual abuse and defamation, rather than rape under the narrow definition applied by the jury. ABC settled the lawsuit in December 2024, agreeing to contribute $15 million toward Trump’s future presidential library and pay $1 million in legal fees. The network also published an editor’s note expressing regret. In another case, Trump sued CBS News over its editing of a 60 Minutes interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris during the 2024 presidential campaign. Trump alleged that the editing deceptively presented Harris’ answers in a way that benefited her campaign. He initially sought $10 billion, later increasing the demand to $20 billion. CBS parent company Paramount Global agreed in July 2025 to pay $16 million to settle the case, with the money allocated to Trump’s future presidential library and legal fees. The settlement did not include an apology, and Paramount maintained that the lawsuit lacked merit. Gavin Newsom’s Lawsuit Against Fox News In June 2025, Newsom sued Fox News for $787 million, alleging that the network and host Jesse Watters misrepresented a phone conversation between Newsom and Trump and had falsely accused the California governor of lying about it. The dispute followed public disagreement over when the two politicians had spoken during a period of unrest in Los Angeles. Newsom alleged that Fox’s coverage distorted the timeline and damaged his reputation. Fox denied the allegations and sought to have the case dismissed. A Delaware judge rejected that effort in April 2026, allowing the lawsuit to proceed. The Delaware Supreme Court declined to consider an early appeal in August, and a trial was scheduled for March 2028. The case remains ongoing. Other Recent Defamation Cases Involving Democrats Other cases involving Democratic politicians illustrate how defamation disputes can emerge from political campaigns, social media and internal party conflicts. Virginia Democratic state Delegate Dan Helmer filed a $15 million defamation lawsuit in 2025 against fellow Democrats and a lawyer after allegations of sexual misconduct surfaced shortly before a congressional primary he ultimately lost. Helmer denied the allegations and claimed they were politically motivated. The case was settled with all parties by January 2026, but the terms were confidential. In Arkansas, former Democratic gubernatorial nominee Christopher Jones sued Republican state Sen. Bart Hester in May 2024 after Hester accused him on social media of taking a “Pro Hamas Terrorist position” in response to Jones’s comments about student protests over the war in Gaza. Jones argued that Hester had falsely conflated support for protesters with support for Hamas. Hester defended his comments as political speech. Jones voluntarily dismissed the lawsuit in May 2025. What Happens Next? While it's unclear if Piker will pursue legal action against Cruz, Piker’s lawsuit against Jennings is in its early stages. The streamer alleges that Jennings' portrayal of Piker harmed his reputation, caused emotional distress and threatened his professional interests. He is pursuing claims including defamation, defamation by implication and false light. Jennings will have an opportunity to respond and could seek to have the case dismissed. The parties could also reach a settlement before trial. If it proceeds, the legal battle is likely to focus on whether Jennings’ portrayal of Piker’s remarks constituted defamation. Under the standard established by the Supreme Court in New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, public officials must generally prove that a defamatory falsehood was published with “actual malice”—meaning knowledge that it was false or reckless disregard for whether it was false. The standard also applies to public figures under related Supreme Court decisions. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Hasan Piker took aim at Ted Cruz over his X post, warning him he'd sued a conservative commentator for similar comments.
